text:
California consumers are showing two different instincts on electric vehicles at once. Rising gasoline prices appear to be pushing more shoppers toward plug-in cars, even as many voters resist a possible future requirement to purchase one.

That tension is surfacing at a pivotal moment for California, which has long viewed cleaner cars as central to its future.

Here's what to know

According to a new POLITICO survey of 2,418 registered California voters, most respondents said the state should not continue toward its 2035 goal of ending sales of new gas-powered vehicles. The survey was conducted in English and Spanish from Sept. 8 to Sept. 14.

GV Wire reported that views varied sharply by party, noting that support for staying with the phaseout reached 49% among Democrats but only 7% among Republicans. Opposition, meanwhile, stood at 32% among Democrats, 90% among Republicans, and 57% among independents.

Overall, the findings indicate voters may be more comfortable with policies that encourage EV adoption than with rules that require it. And as gasoline prices rise around the world and especially in California, where they now average over $6 per gallon, it may not even take that much encouragement anyway to nudge people to at least move toward hybrid and plug-in hybrid options if they don't feel ready for full EVs.

More background

New sales data suggest EV demand in California is picking up again, even as backing for the 2035 phaseout softens. The California Energy Commission reported that EVs and plug-in hybrids made up 19.1% of new vehicle sales in the state from April through June.

Compared with the first quarter of 2026, that share was up 3.3 percentage points.

The increase from April through June still leaves California below its earlier peak. In summer 2025, EVs and plug-in hybrids accounted for nearly 30% of new vehicle sales as buyers rushed to secure $7,500 federal tax credits before those credits expired earlier than expected.

The state remains far ahead of the national market. Nationwide, EVs account for 5.8% of new vehicle sales.

What's being done?

Trends in California suggest interest grows when drivers can point to an immediate payoff, such as tax credits, lower operating costs, or some protection from gas-price swings.

"When we asked this question in previous polls, there was a much higher number of people who said 'no, stick with the plan to phase out gas engines.' But now, partly because of what's going on in the world, that support has disappeared," said Jack Citrin, a political science professor and co-director of the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll.

Source: General Motors

History is, again, repeating itself.

Given that the brands have abandoned selling small and fuel-efficient cars - not to mention sedans - reports have come in that Ford and General Motors are losing market share, and not just a little. Amidst skyrocketing gas prices, people are straying away from buying larger SUVs and shockingly expensive trucks.

Source: AutoGuide

According to Reuters (via Cox Automotive), Ford sales are expected to drop 8.8% through the first three quarters of 2026, which would drag it down to a 12.5% market share. General Motors, meanwhile, is looking at 6.2% shrinkage so far this year, which brings it down to 16.7% market share. There's (somehow) good news for Stellantis, though, which is expected to gain market share through the third quarter of the year.

Even so, the three American companies together are looking at a market share of only 36%, an all-time low.

Source: General Motors

Unsurprisingly, the Ford/GM market share drop is largely a reflection of their portfolios. The brands are leaning further into trucks and full-size SUVs than ever before, case in point being the new 8.3-liter Duramax that General Motors is putting into its new heavy-duty trucks and a brand new pair of V8s for its half-tons. GM doesn't have any hybrids but does have multiple electric vehicles, while Ford at least has one hybrid pickup truck and only one more traditional passenger-oriented EV.

Meanwhile, brands like Hyundai and Kia - which both have plentiful hybrids in their lineups - are thriving. This could help bring these automakers to sell more cars than Ford in the first three quarters of 2026 for the first time ever. Over at Toyota, the brand is looking at a 1.1% sales jump for this same period, while Honda is hoping for a 5.6% rise.

"Despite this volatile year, the new vehicle ​market has actually held up surprisingly steady," said Erin Keating, Cox Automotive executive analyst. That's the good news since so much of the world feels like it's crumbling.

title: Climate's new messaging rift - POLITICO
description:

text:
With help from Benjamin Storrow and Zack Colman in the U.S., Charlie Cooper in the United Kingdom, Ben Munster and Zia Weise in Belgium, Nicolas Camut in France, Mike Blanchfield in Canada, and Brian Dabbs in Singapore.

Surge Preview

Officials criticized efforts at Climate Week to repackage the climate issue as an affordability problem.

Europe braces for potentially severe consequences from Donald Trump’s diesel threats.

Satellites see a data center slowdown in the U.S.

CLIMATE SPEAK: Climate Week is exposing a growing rift among advocates over whether climate change needs a rebrand.

“Everyone’s like, ‘Well, we can’t talk about climate to people because people don’t care about climate and they care about affordability,’” said Catherine McKenna, the former climate minister of Canada. “Good news: Climate action is also an affordability opportunity.”

This year’s event has reflected political headlines, with panels and lectures heavy on energy demand and the growing costs of data centers. It comes as President Donald Trump works to erase climate policy — and as leaders around the world start to speak about energy security and affordability as proxies for climate change.

Many Democratic lawmakers in the U.S., including climate champions, have shifted gears to emphasize the need to lower energy costs instead of reducing carbon emissions.

“I just want to give everybody room to talk about this in ways that are maximally impactful,” Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) told Surge. “Back home in Hawaii, nobody has an objection to me saying climate change. But if they did, I would figure out some other way to say it, and it wouldn’t be some moral failing of mine. It would just be that you try to talk to people in a way that is useful to them.”

But some officials and environmentalists argue that climate hushing is wishful thinking at a time when the world is on the cusp of breaching temperature limits and irreversible impacts.

“If we don’t talk about it, others will, and they’ll use the space to pedal lies and disinformation,” Helen Clarkson, CEO of the Climate Group, which organizes Climate Week, said in her opening remarks.

“There’s very intelligent people who disagree with me on that,” she later told Surge. “But I just think without talking about climate, you lose the urgency, you lose why we have to do this right now, and the speed at which we have to go.”

In Europe, many leaders continue to acknowledge the continent’s vulnerability to climate change, but they now talk about acting on it for different reasons. Attention has turned increasingly to energy security, as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine make the continent vulnerable to higher costs of imported fuels.

“Clean electricity gives us independence, energy security, and it is affordable,” Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said at a United Nations climate summit Wednesday, noting this summer’s extreme heat.

The shift in messaging can also be seen ahead of this year’s U.N. climate talks. The hosts of COP31, Turkey and Australia, are pushing for accelerated electrification — rather than for the more polarizing goal of phasing out fossil fuels, the main driver of rising temperatures.

McKenna argued that leaders need to stop side-stepping the issue.

“They need to actually talk about climate as a massive risk,” McKenna said Thursday on a Climate Week panel about climate diplomacy. “So how are we going to adapt, and how are we going to actually do the real things to tackle it and put it in the frame of opportunity and costs.”

WELCOME TO SURGE: I’m Sara Schonhardt, your host reporting from Climate Week. Reach out with tips and ideas at sschonhardt@politico.com.

Power Players

DIESEL DISTRESS: Global energy markets continued to brace themselves Friday for a potential U.S. ban on diesel exports.

“We’ve reached a limit where there is no spare capacity, and that’s why we see record diesel prices today in Europe and the rest of the world,” said Debnil Chowdhury, who heads the Americas and Europe fuels and refining division at S&P Global Energy.

Halting exports could quickly fill U.S. diesel inventories, prompting refiners to cut back production of other fuels like gasoline and jet fuel.

The impact would be “absolutely incalculable,” Frances’s far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen said at a POLITICO event in Paris, adding that surging fuel prices are already “hitting people very hard.”

Rystad Energy, a consultancy, estimates it would result in the loss of 2 million barrels a day of gasoline production at Gulf Coast refineries and another 250,000 bpd in California.

“The benefit of lower US diesel prices could be offset by higher prices at the gasoline station,” Oxford Economics wrote on Friday.

There couldn’t be a worse time for an export ban, Chowdhury said. Diesel demand is set to spike as harvest season approaches in the U.S. and Europe, while planting season enters full swing in Brazil. Fall is typically maintenance season for U.S. refiners, who have been running full tilt to compensate for the loss of Middle Eastern supplies.

That means strategic oil stock releases, energy subsidies and demand destruction, which will more likely fall on consumers rather than industry and agriculture where demand is less flexible.

"Europe will have to drive less, Europe will have to fly less,” said Chowdhury. “We’re at a point where the demand side of this story cannot continue. ... It would need to be even more significant than what we’ve seen so far.” — Ben Munster and Nicolas Camut

FUSION FUTURE: When it comes to our future power systems, there’s a wild card in the pack: fusion. Surge sat down with Bob Mumgaard, CEO of Commonwealth Fusion Systems, the world’s biggest privately funded fusion company, to talk about its (potential) future.

(Not) waiting on a miracle: The old cliché about fusion is that it’s always 30 years away. But Mumgaard — who’s backed by Bill Gates and Google — says the “road map” to commercial fusion no longer has a phase in which “a miracle happens.”

Only a few years ago that wasn’t the case; any fusion power plant would have needed to be huge and impractical. But the development of super-powerful magnets in the early 2020s — enabling smaller, more economically viable designs — “was a huge deal,” Mumgaard says. The sector is still “at the edge of human knowledge,” but the path ahead is clearer.

AI helps fusion: The advent of advanced AI has sped up computer modeling of how tokamaks (fusion machines) will behave. Modeling that used to take a month now happens in days. “AI allows people to take complex systems and make them much, much easier to optimize, easier to harness,” Mumgaard says.

And fusion helps AI: But AI needs power. Mumgaard sees a symbiotic relationship. “AI makes complexity easier … [it] makes fusion easier. Fusion makes electricity. It makes AI easier.”

Baby steps: The next step is SPARC, a fusion machine CFS is building in Devens, Massachusetts, which the company aims to start up in 2027 and, shortly thereafter, produce more energy than it took to power the fusion process. That’s a milestone that has already been achieved, but CFS thinks their approach will be the first to be “commercially relevant.” They then plan to follow up with the ARC Power Plant in Chesterfield, Virginia, which they hope will be the “the world’s first grid-scale fusion power plant” producing 400 megawatts from the early 2030s.

The 10 times bigger world: Mumgaard says he can “easily see civilization using 10 times more energy” than it does now, as low-income countries use more, AI expands and transport electrifies. Fusion — low carbon and unconstrained by geography — is the “the only thing that gets you there,” he predicts.

But ... when? At the “low end” of expectations, by the 2050s, fusion will be “making a dent” in global power demand, Mumgaard forecasts. But “at the high end,” by then, “it’s a big deal.” — Charlie Cooper

Driving the (global!) day

HOLD YOUR CATERPILLARS: America’s data center boom is expanding, just not as quickly as some analysts projected. That’s the takeaway of an eye-catching note from financial analysts at Jefferies on Friday.

The investment bank used satellite imaging from SynMax to keep tabs on new U.S. data centers. The images suggest between 16 and 18 gigawatts of data center capacity will be added in the U.S. this year, up from 11 GW last year. SynMax thinks it will reach into the low 20s GW in 2027, Jefferies noted.

Those are big numbers, but they fall short of what chip orders imply, the bank said. Chip orders suggest almost 16 GW of new data center capacity in 2026, 35 GW in 2027 and 54 GW in 2028.

Jefferies pointed to several constraints on data center development. Chips are in short supply, and so is the advanced packaging needed to make them usable. Another critical bottleneck: a lack of locations suitable for data center development that have access to the grid.

“If the U.S. cannot energize sites fast enough, advanced chips may flow to other regions that can provide power, meaning the question is increasingly where packaged compute can actually be connected to the grid,” Jefferies wrote. — Benjamin Storrow

PUSHING PAUSE: The eye-in-the-sky analysis from Jefferies comes as an Nvidia executive is saying AI projects shouldn’t move forward without community involvement.

“If your electric consumption is changing the current cost of energy for the community, if your current consumption is absorbing capacity that diminishes the local capacity, then you need to pause and engage the community for that matter,” Calista Redmond, vice president of global AI initiatives, said Thursday.

Context: Nvidia produces the chips that train and run AI models. Powering that compute requires huge amounts of energy, and often water, at a time when energy demand is soaring.

I’m sorry, what? Redmond was speaking on a panel in New York about whether AI could help bring more reliable power to communities in Africa. That’s a project the Rockefeller Foundation is pursuing through its Mission 300 Accelerator, which uses philanthropic capital to bring more electricity to Africa.

The idea: The foundation is working with mini-grid developers in four countries to test whether compute demand could create revenue for energy systems in places where they need more paying customers.

Roughly 600 million people across Africa still lack reliable electricity. The concept the Mission 300 Accelerator is testing is whether it can use small computing tasks to support new power infrastructure as local demand grows.

The asterisk: Rockefeller says it’s focused on generating proof of concept before scaling.

“These mini grids are being built out for communities that don’t necessarily have demand for all the electricity being produced,” said Andy Herscowitz, head of the Mission 300 Accelerator. “So we see this as actually the opposite problem of what we’re seeing in the U.S.” — Sara Schonhardt

SHINE ON: Happy 860m day to all who celebrate. The U.S. Energy Information Administration released its monthly statistics on American power plants Thursday, providing a first look at the new facilities that were built, proposed or retired last month.

Surge crunched the numbers. They show that solar continues to lead the pack in terms of new power plant installations through the first eight months of 2026 with more than 14 GW through August. The annual record for U.S. solar installations is about 31 GW, set in 2024. EIA expects another 26 GW to come online before the end of 2026, setting the U.S. up for a potential record-setting solar year.

Batteries are the other big story, with more than 10 GW of capacity installed through August. That eight-month total would have been an annual record as recently as 2023. The U.S. installed 743 MW of battery capacity in August, with much of that coming from a new 530-MW plant in Georgia. (There are 1,000 MW in a gigawatt.)

The McGrau Ford Battery Storage Facility caught the eye of Surge because it’s in a state with rising electricity demand and relatively little in the way of batteries. Georgia’s battery fleet (including McGrau) stands at 742 MW. EIA predicts that another 12 GW of capacity will be added to the grid before year’s end.

Installation totals for other technologies rank as follows: onshore wind (6.2 GW), natural gas (3.1 GW), and offshore wind (800 MW).

Vibe shift: The strong renewable installations are a holdover from the Biden-era, when power companies were racing to green their electricity supplies. But that is expected to change in the coming years due to rising power demand and the Trump administration’s moves to slash pollution regulations.

EIA is expecting 65 GW of new natural gas plant capacity by the end of the decade. When the year began, EIA was predicting 48,000 GW by 2030. The higher projections reflect the rush to build new gas plants to meet rising energy demand from data centers. — Benjamin Storrow

Our open tabs

CALIFORNIA REAMING: A majority of California voters oppose building new data centers in the state, and even more say they oppose putting one in their own community, according to a new poll by POLITICO and its partners.

TOXIC HAZE: Millions of people in Indonesia have been living for months beneath a stifling blanket of haze, reports The New York Times. The wildfires have not only been fueled by a drought brought on by El Niño, but also years of land clearing for cash crops, including timber and palm oil. So far, the fires have burned between half a million and 2.2 million acres of land.

That’s all for today. Thanks for reading!

text:
Set to open in early 2027 at 585 East Fordham Road, the Bronx Green Jobs Center aims to connect Bronx residents with career opportunities to establish a clean energy workforce development hub in New York.

The center will provide a hub for hands-on training, solar panel installation, electric vehicle charging, infrastructure, energy efficiency, urban agriculture and help support growing areas of New York’s green economy.

The center will also feature New York’s first dedicated green economy entrepreneurship support center, an event space and a street-level café showcasing locally produced goods.

“Through the center, we are deepening our commitment to community, and leading into our power at university to bring together the leaders in clean energy and sustainability under one roof, bringing our shared work to scale in order to ensure New York meets its climate and clean energy goals as a leader in the world,” said Fordham University President Tania Tetlow.

Earlier this year, The Bronx Green Job Center was awarded $1.4 million in state funding as part of the initiative to support clean energy workforce development programs statewide.

The center is located in some of the most environmentally unjust zip codes in the entire U.S.

The Bronx has historically been disproportionately impacted by climate injustice and climate change, with the borough left behind in investments in clean energy and sustainability solutions, now that is changing.

“This is a place where the Bronx will have the green economy lead,” said Bronx Borough President Vanessa Gibson. “With this new center, we are ensuring that our residents have access to the training, skills and resources and opportunities that they need to lead our great economy.”

This 12,000 square feet, formerly vacant industrial site will be converted into a state-of-the-art facility with modern laboratories and learning spaces.

“This gift will have an enormous impact on this community because with the renovation of this more than 100 year old facility, we will open doors and create opportunities for the Bronx New York’s green economy,” Tetlow said.

The dedicated space will be the first of its kind to support startups and help aspiring green entrepreneurs launch their small businesses.

The project took two years for design and construction, but the introduction of a dedicated green workforce and entrepreneurship hub idea dates back to 20 years ago under Mayor’s Bloomberg plan for a greener NYC in 2007, but has never been operationalized until now.

According to Vice President of External Affairs at Fordham University Travis Proulx, Fordham University brought in community based organizations, K-12 partners to create pathways to skilled careers for high school students, experts from other universities, and brought in industry and hiring partners.

“It is critical that we prepare people from this community to successfully compete for jobs that actually exist in the growing green economy,” Proulx said. “We’re bringing in experts together under one roof, to be able to expand all of these goals at a scale that is unheard of across the country.”

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Steve Daines penned an op-ed for the Washington Times reflecting on Montana’s energy wins during his time in the U.S. Senate. Read it below.

Montana energy is back and better than ever

Senator Steve Daines

Washington Times

September 24, 2026

Montana is famous for world-class fly fishing, and some of America’s greatest national parks. But Montana is also rich in natural resources. Our energy sector provides thousands of jobs and contributes millions to our economy, which is why bolstering Made-In-Montana energy has been a priority of mine. As I reflect on my tenure in the Senate, I believe we’ve made substantial progress in unleashing the full power of Montana energy.

I was a newly elected Senator during President Barack Obama’s second term, which was an era of climate hysteria. One of the first actions I took as a senator in 2015 was to hold an official Senate hearing at Crow Agency in Montana to push back against President Obama’s radical anti-coal rules.

Montana breathed a sigh of relief when President Donald Trump was elected in 2016 and began to roll back many of the radical ideas that extreme environmentalists were pushing. We passed tax reform to bolster Montana energy jobs, struck down rules that harmed our coal mines and supported Montana hydropower dams. But when Joe Biden became president in 2020, Montana energy was once again under attack.

This was the time of the Green New Deal. President Biden wanted to force us all to drive electric vehicles and shut down Montana’s coal mines and power plants. Every day, Montana’s energy sector was blasted with frivolous litigation, bureaucratic red tape and burdensome regulations that hindered our critical industries. Montana has more recoverable coal than any other state in the nation. Despite this, Biden supercharged his attacks on coal, oil and gas and stalled projects throughout the state, threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of hardworking Americans. He even pushed through a rule prohibiting all new coal development in Eastern Montana. By the end of Biden’s term, all of Montana’s large-scale active coal mines and the Colstrip Power Plant were on the brink of closure.

That’s why it was so important when President Trump took office once again in 2025, and we acted swiftly to unwind the Biden administration’s radical anti-energy agenda.

The first victory was saving the Bull Mountains Mine. On Independence Day 2025, President Trump signed the Working Families Tax Cuts and Jobs Act into law, which included my provision to keep the Bull Mountains Mine up and running. This was a huge win and saved over 250 mining jobs. I visited the mine shortly after this victory and met the miners whose jobs we had saved — many of them were the multi-generational coal miners. They work hard, support their families and are true examples of the American spirit.

The Working Family Tax Cuts Act also included my bill to restart federal oil and gas leasing in Montana, which had all but ceased under President Biden. My bill, the Supporting Made-In-America Energy Act, ensures that the Bureau of Land Management holds quarterly oil and gas lease sales in Montana, as well as many other states. This will keep royalties, jobs and taxes growing in our rural communities long into the future.

A few months later, we had another important victory, when President Trump signed my bill repealing Biden’s disastrous Miles City Resource Management Plan Amendment (RMPA), which unlocked mining in Montana’s coal-rich Powder River Basin. The Powder River Basin is America’s largest coal reserve and is critical for our energy independence. In caving to environmental hysteria, the Biden administration ignored the local community and locked up two million acres of land, which would have cost Montana more than $4 billion in future revenue. Reversing this wrongheaded policy was a huge win, not just for Montana’s jobs and economy, but for our nation’s energy security as a whole.

As my time serving in the U.S. Senate draws to a close, I’m grateful for the opportunity to have fought together with President Trump, Gov. Greg Gianforte, Sen. Tim Sheehy, Rep. Ryan Zinke, and Rep. Troy Downing on behalf of the Treasure State. Montana is the best state in the nation, and we are paving the way for a bright future — a future that will create hundreds of jobs and ensure our nation remains the global leader in energy production.

text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Longtime climate warrior Al Gore sees victory within Earth's grasp. But he worries that it could still slip through humanity's fingers.

“While we're in grave danger, but I think there is a possibility that 2026 will be looked back upon in the history books as the beginning of a positive tipping point,” Gore said in a sit down interview with The Associated Press during New York Climate Week. He sees a good chance the world is peaking its use of coal, oil and gas, which cause global warming, as solar and other renewable power is overtaking dirtier fossil fuels.

History makes the former U.S. vice president hopeful. He compared the effort to make a cleaner world to the U.S. civil rights movement, Nelson Mandela's anti-apartheid movement and women's equality efforts as “the other great morally based challenges that humanity has confronted in the past.

“And in all of those prior movements,” he said, "there were times when the advocates felt despair but they kept going because courage is not the absence of fear, it's the determination to go forward in spite of it."

Nature makes him nervous because Earth's warming is accelerating and with it extreme weather, such as heat waves and the deadly glacier collapse and flooding that killed 1,300 people in Nepal.

“I’m temperamentally optimistic, but the dangers are extremely grave, getting more so all the time,” said, Gore, often accused of being a doomsayer by nonscientist political opponents. “We’re seeing these extreme events come fast and furious. They’re worse as well as more frequent. ... It’s like a nature hike through the book of Revelation.”

A race between old and new power

“This is a close race between the unfathomable risk we are taking, the unacceptable damages we are enduring on one hand, and the incredibly exciting advance of all the clean, cheap, job-producing alternatives that people not under the sway of the fossil fuel industry are adopting in droves,” Gore said.

He ticked off factoids such as Africa installing 100,000 solar panels per day, that 91% of the new U.S. electricity generation was renewable and that 30% of all new car s sold globally this year will be electric. And, he said, in Pakistan the common dowry now includes three solar panels.

Who will win the race? “The answer is in our hands,” Gore said. “The last chapter of this story won’t come for a while, but I think we really are at a turning point."

Ten years ago, 55% of the world's investment was in fossil fuels and 45% in renewables. Now it's 65% renewables, Gore said. He said society changes when a new technology becomes cheaper than the old one, much like cellphones supplanting, then replacing landlines.

Experts say Gore is right to be optimistic

Three climate scientists basically agreed with Gore's assessments of both increasing dangers, but also still had an optimistic outlook.

"I agree with Al Gore that we have incredible progress on exponential rise in adoption and decline in price for renewable electric green solutions," said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany. “But the dilemma, so far, is that they largely meet growing energy demand. We are not yet bending the curve on oil, gas and coal.”

Climate Analytics CEO Bill Hare of Australia said he's generally optimistic like Gore “about what we can achieve particularly with the rapid development of clean technology." But, he said, "I am the at the same time fearful that this is not fast enough and is being held back by the fossil fuel industry.”

Even though change isn't fast enough, the University of Pennsylvania's Michael Mann said Gore's tone is crucial: “Doomism, despair and disengagement is the greatest threat at this point. We must not fall victim to it.”

Gore is having none of that. At 78, he thinks he'll see meaningful bends in the carbon pollution curve in his lifetime. But even if it takes longer, that's OK, Gore said, paraphrasing the Jewish Talmud:

“You are not required to finish the work, but you are required to undertake it.”

description:

text:
In a new report, Sierra Club takes aim at electric utilities across the United States for their slow transition to clean energy sources. The analysis included less than flattering grades for the state’s two investor-owned power companies, Entergy Mississippi and Mississippi Power.

The marks — an “F” for Entergy and a “C” for Mississippi Power — came in the latest edition of the national environmental advocacy nonprofit’s “The Dirty Truth Report,” released Wednesday.

The report graded the country’s utilities using three criteria: the retiring of coal plants by 2030, not adding new gas-powered production and building clean energy sources to replace fossil fuel loads by 2035. For the second year in a row, the nonprofit gave the country’s utilities as a whole an “F.”

“As artificial intelligence data centers drive demand for energy, utility companies are rushing to expensive and dangerous fossil fuels, leading to soaring electricity prices and worsening air pollution,” said Sierra Club Chief Program Officer Holly Bender.

The nonprofit highlighted the large amount of planned new gas generation this year, which was more than in any of the previous five years.

The report gave Entergy a failing grade largely because it plans to add nearly 3,500 megawatts of gas-powered energy to its system by 2035. The utility is growing its power capacity, in part, to meet the needs of Amazon data centers across central Mississippi. It’s unclear, though, how much those plans were fueled by Amazon’s arrival because of limited oversight over the companies’ agreement.

Sierra Club gave the utility a poor grade despite its plans to retire all of its coal units by 2030 and Entergy’s recent investments in renewable sources, which includes a 100-megawatt solar power plant that came online in 2022.

The utility is building three new, 754-megawatt gas plants: one in Greenville, set to be ready in 2028, which will replace an existing plant and is designed to use hydrogen in the future; another plant in Ridgeland, expected to be in service in 2029; and one in Vicksburg, which will open in 2028.

Entergy said in a response to the Sierra Club report that it aims to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

“We continue to invest in renewable power and storage projects, with approximately 3 gigawatts either already approved or pending regulatory review,” the company said Thursday in a statement to Mississippi Today. “Driven by strong economic growth and rising customer demand, we are developing new baseload generation capacity to power these exciting opportunities while continuing to make meaningful progress toward a net‑zero future. Changes to available tax credits for carbon‑free resources are also shaping how we optimize our clean energy investments.”

Mississippi Power, which received an “F” in last year’s edition, improved to a “C” this year. It plans to retire all of its coal power units by 2030 and is planning for 548 megawatts of new gas production by 2035.

The utility received the best grade of any subsidiary of Southern Company. The report panned the energy giant for extending the lives of its coal units. Last year, Mississippi Power received approval from the state to push back the retirement of its coal units at Plant Victor J. Daniel in Jackson County. But the utility later proposed to convert the units to gas in 2029, the Sierra Club report said.

The report, though, gave the company a “0%” in its plans to replace fossil fuel generation and load growth with clean energy. The company’s power supply has included roughly 160 megawatts of solar power for nearly the last decade.

In a Thursday statement, Mississippi Power pointed to those projects as well as its low rates, 22% below the national average.

“The company continues to reliably meet our customers’ ever-evolving energy needs and is in a strong position to ensure adequate capacity and the ability to serve our customers as the state experiences robust economic growth,” the utility said.

The company also mentioned the potential benefits from a solar power battery storage project in Walnut Grove, which it called “one of the nation’s most advanced green microgrids.”

“Lessons learned from the project are helping inform how renewable energy and battery storage may be integrated into our system in the future,” Mississippi Power said.

text:
The Clean Energy Generation is making progress every day here in the Southeast. From solar and farmland thriving together, to electric school buses powering the grid, to a Costco distribution center going solar, our clean energy future is becoming a reality. Take a look at just six of the many amazing signs of clean energy adoption in the Southeast we’ve seen over the past few months.

Solar and Farmland Thrive Together in North Carolina

“Solar and agriculture can thrive together,” and it’s thriving right here in the Southeast, including in North Carolina. In fact, according to the SEIA, “Solar development uses a very small amount of farmland compared to many other common land uses, while also delivering affordable energy, local tax revenue, and reliable income for farmers and landowners.” Read more.

Electric School Buses Send Power to the Grid

“School buses will be a critically important backbone of V2G capacity.” The batteries of more than 200 electric school buses are sending power back to the grid, easing the strain as soaring temperatures create skyrocketing demand. At least 31 utilities in 21 states are taking advantage of this V2G technology, with hundreds more electric school buses expected to come online. Read more.

Costco Florida Distribution Center Adds Solar and Storage

Stocking up on sunshine! Popular club retailer Costco is powering its Port St. Lucie, Florida distribution center with a combination of solar energy and battery storage. Built in response to surging energy demand and rising energy costs, this new system not only powers the whole distribution center, but also the on-site chargers for the company’s electric fleet. Read more.

Atlanta Requires New Roofs to be Reflective

“They’re not overly expensive, they’re on the market, they’re available right now.” Atlanta is requiring that new roofs be reflective. Doing so will not only reduce temperatures within the buildings themselves, but within the surrounding areas—by as much as six degrees is some of Atlanta’s hottest neighborhoods. And because their homes won’t get as hot, residents can then spend less on air conditioning. Read more.

Tennessee Rebate Program Brings EV Charging to Apartments

Apartments are plugging in! Tennessee’s new rebate program will help multifamily housing properties afford electric vehicle charging infrastructure. Owners, property managers, homeowner associations, and authorized lessees with a minimum of four units can apply for rebates for up to 10 charging plugs per site. Read more.

Retired Wind Turbine Blade Repurposed as Bus Stop

Huntersville, North Carolina has turned a retired wind turbine blade into an artistic bus-stop bench. This impressive piece of public art is part of a growing effort in the U.S. to find practical uses for retired wind turbine blades. Though most parts of a wind turbine can be recycled, composite components such as blades are traditionally harder to process. Read more.

Bonus story: To see another innovative use of a decommissioned wind turbine, check out how a Colorado blade became the perfect footbridge across a previously-uncrossable creek in an Atlanta park. Read more.

These stories highlight just a few of the positive things happening in our area! Every day, we see signs of hope. The Clean Energy Generation is creating a future powered by clean energy that leads to clean air and water, good jobs, and vibrant communities.

Would you like to see more stories like this? We’ve got just the thing for you! Every Thursday, we share the latest clean energy news on Instagram with #CleanEnergyNews. Join us as we celebrate the progress and signs of hope in the clean energy transition.

text:
As part of a coordinated U.S. Department of Energy initiative, a new transmission line through the Oklahoma Panhandle will connect the Southwest Power Pool with the Western grid, allowing the export of excess energy, relieving grid congestion and bringing down power costs.

On Thursday, Energy Under Secretary Kyle Haustveit visited Oklahoma to announce the Three Corners Connector project, a name referring to the Oklahoma-Colorado–Kansas tri-point known as 8 Mile Corner. That tri-point is set to act as the pass-through for a 300-mile high-voltage transmission line with endpoints in Guymon and Pueblo, Colorado.

The project will connect the Southwest Power Pool, which covers all or part of 17 central U.S. states, with the Western Electricity Coordinating Council, which oversees 1.8 million square miles across 14 western states, British Columbia, Alberta and part of Baja California, Mexico.

“We’re ensuring that the lowest cost electron is what comes to you in your home, to your business, to keep downward pressure on prices,” Haustveit said. “We recognize the Trump administration is working very hard to make sure that we push prices down. Affordability is a top priority, and that’s why we’re making this investment today.”

The Three Corners Connector is estimated to cost about $832 million, and the federal government has granted $250 million through the DOE initiative. According to the project website, the line could be operational by 2031.

During Haustveit’s visit, Oklahoma Corporation Commission Chairman Kim David celebrated the project.

“Oklahoma has always been a big powerhouse state,” David said. “We have natural gas. We have wind. We have other forms of generation. For us to be able to export that power for economic growth benefits every one of our ratepayers. When we get a line like this, that helps move that energy back and forth, so we ensure that we get the cheapest power going on that grid, being able to push those prices down.”

According to SPP, demand for energy in Oklahoma is set to double in the next decade, while seven of the 10 most congested points on the SPP grid are in Oklahoma. Grid congestion drives up consumer electricity rates by forcing operators to bypass cheap power and run expensive local generators instead.

“Oklahoma has a lot of congestion,” Haustveit said. “We have a lot of generation capacity that are not always able to get to market. Connectors like this will allow you to get your product to market. When you run your equipment at a higher capacity factor, the effective cost per unit of energy falls. That’s how we’re going to continue to put downward pressure on prices while protecting resiliency, reliability for Oklahomans and Coloradans.”

text:
ST. THOMAS, ONT. – PowerCo Canada has named EllisDon Corporation the general contractor for its $7 billion St. Thomas gigafactory, marking a key milestone as the project advances into its next phase of construction.

The project is now moving into the core infrastructure and structural phases that will support future production.

Work includes the production-building shell, mechanical, electrical and plumbing installations, energy and utility systems and supporting site services. Approximately 60 EllisDon workers are currently onsite, expected to ramp up to roughly 1,300 workers at peak, alongside additional personnel supporting parallel project activities, a release reads.

At 1.5-million-square-feet, the plant will be the size of 210 football fields just for the factory alone. The entire industrial park itself amounts to 1,500 acres, or an area of 850 football fields.

“The PowerCo facility represents a transformative investment in Canada’s industrial future, and EllisDon is proud to play a role in its delivery,” said Max Mantha, president, construction at EllisDon in a statement. “As a Canadian-headquartered, employee-owned company, we are committed to building the infrastructure that will help support Canada’s growing electric vehicle and battery manufacturing sector. This project will create opportunities for skilled tradespeople, local businesses, and communities across southwestern Ontario, and we look forward to working with PowerCo and our partners on this landmark development.”

Ground was broken in 2025 on the project, with Magil Construction Canada leading foundation construction for three major buildings and Steelcon Group of Companies fabricating and erecting structural steel components.

PowerCo has stated it is also aligning the project’s timeline and product strategy “with evolving market demand, technological advancements and the Volkswagen Group’s long-term strategy.”

St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029. PowerCo had previously said initial battery production was targeted for 2027.

“The St. Thomas gigafactory remains a cornerstone of our North American strategy,” said Joel Karlsberg, chief procurement officer with PowerCo Canada.

“We are continuing to build now while determining how and when the facility scales over time. This is about getting the pacing right — not stepping back — to protect our long-term investment, support regional jobs, and position Canada, Ontario and St. Thomas to benefit in a dynamic and evolving market.”

text:
New York state could catalyze a widespread clean energy transition and address its affordability issues by leveraging one of its most important resources – homes – according to a new report from the Climate Jobs Institute at Cornell University.

“The disaggregated and piecemeal approach with which we’ve done residential decarbonization work is not working and is creating a lack of safety protections for workers,” said Lynda Nguyen, the report’s lead author. “We need to think about how we’re doing this work – rehabbing as many homes as we can while also creating pathways out of poverty into the middle class.”

“Bringing Unions Home: A Blueprint for Labor-Led Residential Decarbonization in New York,” was launched during an in-person event held on Sept. 22 at the ILR NYC Conference Center.

The panel of speakers included:

Harry Bronson, New York State assemblymember, District 138

Mete Coban MBE, deputy mayor of London for environment and energy

Brendan Griffith, president, New York City Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO

Katie Schwamb, managing director, Building Energy Exchange

Audrey Zibelman, chair, New York State Energy Research and Development Authority

Lynda Nguyen, climate jobs associate, Climate Jobs Institute

Reyna Cohen, research and policy development associate, Climate Jobs Institute

Grennan J. Milliken, climate jobs associate, Climate Jobs Institute

Lara Skinner, executive director, Climate Jobs Institute

Zach Cunningham, assistant director of labor education, Climate Jobs Institute

The authors of the report found that the average age of existing residential buildings in New York is 65 years, and that more than half the three million residential buildings rely on fossil fuels. They argue that the current suite of building upgrade programs is insufficient to meet the needs of the state’s aging housing stock, while the promise of high-quality union construction careers has eroded over the last several decades.

They suggest that the state must implement a comprehensive, worker-centered strategy to address the inequities in affordability, deferred maintenance and labor issues in its private housing industry.

By doing so, the state could meet the dual needs of scaled emissions reduction and energy efficiency by creating good union jobs.

title: EV drivers get reprieve on annual fee. But it might be temporary - USA Today
description:
This fee is being considered because EV drivers do not pay the federal gas tax, which traditionally funds the Highway Trust Fund.
That means EV drivers won’t have to begin paying the proposed national fee on Oct. 1.
The USA TODAY Cars team examined why Congress is considering an EV fee and what it could mean for EV owners.
The proposal differs from other ideas that have been floated to replace gas tax money that isn't collected from EV drivers.
A new $135 annual fee for EV drivers could eat into those savings.
text:
A proposed annual fee for electric vehicle owners has been delayed because the bill containing it has stalled in Congress.

The fee would start at $135 for EV owners and $35 for plug-in hybrid owners to help fund road and transit projects.

This fee is being considered because EV drivers do not pay the federal gas tax, which traditionally funds the Highway Trust Fund.

Electric car owners are being spared an annual fee to help pay for roads as soon as next month because the bill containing the fee has stalled in Congress.

A new proposed EV fee that will start at $130 annually beginning in October 2026 was included in a new bipartisan draft of a five-year surface transportation funding bill that the U.S. House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee is considering. Under the proposed legislation, dubbed the BUILD America 250 Act, the fee can be increased by $5 each year until it hits a max of $150 annually. Plug-in hybrid owners would be hit with a $35 fee starting in October that can be increased to as much as $50 by the end of the legislation in 2031.

The proposed fee was lowered from a earlier proposal that would have started at $135. It included in a larger bill to reauthorize surface transportation funding that is set to expire on Sept. 30. The measure was approved by the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, but has not been approved by the full House or Senate. The last transportation funding measure approved by Congress was signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021.

With progress on the larger transportation bill that includes the proposed EV fee stalled, Congress passed a temporary extension of federal government funding that extends spending until Dec. 11, according to the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO), a nonpartisan and nonprofit organization that advocates for consistent transportation funding.

AASHTO said the temporary transportation funding bill allowed lawmakers to "prevent a federal government shutdown on October 1 and continue Highway Trust Fund programs and annually appropriated general fund programs" at the 2026 fiscal year levels until the new December deadline.

That means EV drivers won’t have to begin paying the proposed national fee on Oct. 1.

The USA TODAY Cars team examined why Congress is considering an EV fee and what it could mean for EV owners.

Why is Congress considering adding an EV fee?

The federal government currently collects 18.4 cents per gallon on every U.S. gasoline purchase to help pay for road and transit construction projects, and most states also tack on their own fees. EV drivers don’t pay that tax because their vehicles don’t use gasoline.

The money goes into the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Highway Trust Fund and is then distributed to states to help pay for road and transit construction projects. As cars have become more fuel-efficient and more drivers have opted for EVs and hybrids, less money per mile driven has been collected despite increased use of roads. Lawmakers have looked for ways to close that growing gap in federal gas‑tax revenue.

The federal gas tax hasn't increased since 1993, and it brings in about $40 billion a year at its current level, according to the Tax Policy Center. President Donald Trump and some lawmakers in Congress have recently proposed suspending the federal gas tax as the average price of gas hovers around $4.50, according to the AAA Auto Club.

The federal government typically spends about $60 billion on transportation projects, and infrastructure advocates say that amount is just enough to maintain the nation's roads and transit systems. Most states also levy their own gas taxes to fund local road projects.

Supporters of the proposed fee say it's time for EV drivers to contribute to the fund that helps pay for the upkeep of the roads they use. Rep. Sam Graves, a Republican from Missouri who chairs the U.S. House Transportation Committee, said in a statement that the EV fee "ensures that electric vehicle owners begin paying their fair share for the use of our roads."

Rep. Rick Larsen, a Washington state lawmaker who is the top Democrat on the panel, said the bipartisan highway bill agreement represents "a commitment to bipartisan lawmaking means finding compromise."

How would the new EV tax be collected?

Electric vehicle owners would have to pay the new fee when they register their cars. The proposal differs from other ideas that have been floated to replace gas tax money that isn't collected from EV drivers.

Vehicle-miles-traveled, or VMT, programs tax drivers based on miles they drive on U.S. roads instead of how much gasoline they purchase.

Mileage-based road tax proposals have long been controversial in U.S. transportation funding debates because critics question how the government would monitor drivers' traveling habits without infringing on their privacy.

Supporters of the current highway bill draft note that unlike previous mileage-based highway fee proposals, the current EV tax proposal would involve no tracking or reporting from drivers about their travels. EV owners would simply pay the $135 annual fee upon registering their vehicles each year.

What would the new fee mean for EV owners?

Electric vehicle owners save an average of about $8,811 in ownership and maintenance costs over 200,000 miles compared with owners of best-selling gas-powered vehicles in the same class, according to Consumer Reports.

A driver who opts for a new or used EV could save $2,200 annually on gas, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Hybrid drivers can save $1,500 on gas each year, according to the agency.

A new $135 annual fee for EV drivers could eat into those savings. EV supporters have argued that additional annual fees increase the cost of owning an electric vehicle.

When state lawmakers in South Carolina were considering a new user fee for EV owners of 4.5 cents per kilowatt-hour on electricity consumed at publicly accessible charging stations, the Electrification Coalition, which lobbies for EV-friendly policies, said in a February 2026 statement that the state's proposal "imposes significant additional costs on EV drivers without increasing the state gasoline tax."

text:
Chinese electric vehicles’ ultrafast charging is only getting faster.

On Wednesday, Geely Auto unveiled technology that can charge an electric vehicle battery from 10% to 70% in just 4.5 minutes, a leap analysts called a significant development for the Chinese auto group.

Geely is joining the ranks of BYD, which last year overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest EV maker, as well as CATL, the world’s largest EV battery maker, both of which this year rolled out around 5-minute EV ultrafast charging.

By comparison, some of the fastest-charging EVs available in the U.S. currently can take roughly 20 minutes, analysts said.

“China is way, way, way ahead in terms of multiple players engaged in the charging competition,” said Lei Xing, an independent analyst of China’s auto industry based in Easthampton, Massachusetts.

Geely, BYD and CATL lead ultrafast charging race

Chinese automakers are seeking to eliminate the “ultimate barrier” to EV adoption – range anxiety – by narrowing the gap between EV charging and the roughly five-minute refueling experience of gasoline vehicles, explained Stephen Chan, an analyst at S&P Global Ratings.

At a launch event Wednesday, Geely Auto announced its new system that can charge an EV from 10% to 70% in 4.5 minutes, and 10% to 97% in just 8 minutes and 40 seconds.

BYD in March launched a new generation of its “blade” EV battery that it said can charge an EV from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes, and from 10% to 97% in 9 minutes. In April, CATL rolled out technology that can charge an EV from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes and 44 seconds, and from 10% to 98% in 6 minutes and 27 seconds.

Despite the breakthroughs, experts cautioned there are other obstacles.

“The real challenge is whether the battery can accept that level of current quickly and repeatedly without overheating, excessive degradation or internal bottlenecks,” said Chris Liu, a Shanghai-based senior analyst at Omdia, a technology research and advisory group.

EV makers face intense competition inside China

With more than 100 domestic passenger car brands, Chinese auto makers face intense competition. Domestic car sales have fallen for months in China as automakers are exporting more cars overseas. A focus on technological advancements like ultrafast charging is a way to set themselves apart and try to improve sales.

But success will depend on factors including the scale of companies’ charging network.

For one, the majority of China’s public charging stations still operate below 1 megawatt, while Geely, BYD and CATL’s ultrafast charging technologies rely on higher charging power to reach their full potential, said Chan at S&P. That means network expansions or grid updates will remain as hurdles for large-scale adoption.

Some in the industry are already taking ambitious steps. China’s BYD, for instance, is targeting 20,000 superfast charging stations by the end of this year, followed by 30,000 more in 2027 and 40,000 in 2028, bringing the total to 90,000 stations by that time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis.

China leading the world in EV fast-charging

Other countries including the U.S. is still behind China when it comes to ultrafast EV charging.

In the U.S., EV fast-charging sessions typically take roughly 20 to 40 minutes to charge from 10% to 80%, according to S&P, although newer models from brands like Hyundai, Kia and Porsche can reduce charging times to approximately 18 to 20 minutes under optimal conditions.

“Overall, while the battery-charging network in the U.S. is growing at a rapid pace, it is still well behind China’s ultrafast charging speeds by orders of magnitude,” said Neal Ganguli, a partner and managing director in the automotive and industrial practice at consultancy AlixPartners.

But Ganguli also believes the U.S. may not be attempting to match China’s “megawatt race” in EV charging at least in the near future, but to pursue a “more moderate” path to upgrades.

Today Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01), a founding member of the Congressional Lowering Utility Bills Caucus, announced he is introducing three new pieces of legislation to lower energy costs. The bills would increase federal support for heating assistance, expand eligibility to more families, and lower gas and diesel costs.

“President Trump’s reckless war with Iran is making it more expensive for Granite Staters to get to work and heat their homes. James, a Navy veteran from New Hampshire, had to come out of retirement because he couldn’t make ends meet. People like James, and countless others who have seen their energy bills more than double, need relief now,” said Congressman Pappas.“New Hampshire families have spent an extra thousand dollars at the pump and filling their fuel tanks because of this war. My legislation would give people the breathing room they need.”

The LIHEAP Act would expand the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), one of the most successful programs aimed at reducing energy costs for working families.

The American Homes First Act would increase funding for LIHEAP by redirecting $1 billion from President Trump’s ‘Board of Peace’ slush fund.

The Consumer Fuel Prices Relief Act would provide federal fuel tax relief until the end of September 2027 by pausing the gas tax, the diesel tax, and the aviation fuel tax, while ensuring the benefit is immediately passed on to consumers in full. The legislation builds on his bicameral Gas Prices Relief Act of 2026, introduced in March, which would have suspended the federal gas tax through October 1, 2026. The legislation safeguards and maintains funding for roads, bridges, and gas spill remediation, and holds corporations accountable if they fail to pass along savings to individual consumers.

Pappas is a fierce advocate for efforts that lower energy costs for Granite Staters and programs that help low-income families pay their bills. text:
By MARISSA GONZALEZ

Capital News Service

LANSING – Some environmental advocates are expressing concerns about a Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy (EGLE) proposal that would remove some ozone pollution data from Detroit’s air quality records.

Under the federal Clean Air Act, states may exclude pollution data due to exceptional events such as smoke from wildfires, including those in Canada, that increasingly bring smoky air to Michigan.

According to a posting by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in the Federal Register, EGLE in 2022 first requested Detroit to be redesignated as an “attainment” area, which means it meets the EPA’s air quality standards.

EGLE submitted a more recent draft of the request this May.

If approved by the EPA, the change will result in the removal of 21 days of ozone pollution data over a four-year period from Detroit’s air quality records, according to the Michigan Environmental Council.

The group says that would make it look like Detroit meets the air quality standards, when it does not.

During a recent virtual roundtable discussion hosted by the council, several experts said the state department’s proposal is not a good idea and will cause more harm than good by disregarding the actual ozone pollution levels that Detroiters live with every day.

According to Nicholas Leonard, the executive director of the Great Lakes Environmental Law Center, most of Detroit’s ozone pollution is not due to wildfire smoke, and he said that wildfires should not be considered an exceptional event under the law.

“It’s almost a ‘get out jail free card’ for regulators. By excluding data, states are allowed to pretend air quality is meeting the standard, when it is not,” said Leonard.

He said that according to EGLE’s own studies, even on days when wildfire smoke is present, the vast majority of ozone pollution in the Detroit area comes from other sources.

Leonard said that “85-90% is actually caused by our local industry. Only a small amount, 5-15%, is caused by wildfire smoke.”

Sandra Turner-Handy, the interim executive director of Detroiters Working for Environmental Justice, said she wants EGLE and the EPA to advocate for clean air in Detroit rather than seeking to exclude data.

According to the American Lung Association, Detroit was named the sixth-worst in the nation for year-round particle pollution in its 2025 report. In the 2024 report, the Detroit metro area was graded an F for ground-level ozone pollution.

“Our city has always been out of attainment – it’s a low-income community of color. Who cares but us that are living this lower quality of life?” said Turner-Handy.

Turner-Handy said it is an environmental justice and racism issue and that the health of low-income communities of color needs more consideration.

Poor air quality in Detroit negatively impacts residents and stunts children’s growth and development, according to U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Detroit.

She said children can be more vulnerable to the negative effects of air pollution since their bodies are still developing.

“We already know that children cannot learn when they are being poisoned by our air and our water,” said Tlaib.

Children are at risk of getting hurt from natural causes that they cannot control, according to Mary-Jacqueline Muli, a climate justice nurse.

Speaking at the panel, she said she is doing a fellowship with the Alliance of Nurses for Healthy Environments to teach kids how to protect themselves and protect the air within their rooms.

However, Muli said that even when people make all the right choices, it still doesn’t fully protect them from complications from air pollution.

“It suggests that if a patient just makes the right choices that they will be safe. But how many people are making the right choices and are still not safe because of the environmental harms that we face?” said Muli.

According to EGLE, the department’s ultimate goal is to protect public health and improve air quality for Michigan communities.

An EGLE statement said the proposal would not hide air quality data and would not undermine negative health effects on the Detroit community.

“The use of exceptional events are in no way intended to minimize or discount the health of community members or the potential impacts of wildfire smoke. The data is a permanent part of the public record,” according to its statement.

text:
Catch up on C40’s highlights from New York Climate Week 2026

As New York Climate Week comes to a close, one message stood out above the rest: mayors aren’t waiting for the future. They’re acting now.

Across energy, housing, extreme weather and resilience, city leaders spent the week sharing tangible results and scalable solutions.

Cities are preparing for extreme heat

Extreme heat remains the deadliest climate threat facing 1 billion people living in C40 cities. Throughout the week, city leaders treated heat adaptation as a top priority.

Through the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator, mayors showed how fast-moving local action saves lives:

Building on a successful pilot, New York City has secured $350,000 to roll out its cooling pop-ups for outdoor workers across all five boroughs in 2026.

In Miami, Mayor Eileen Higgins is using data from 156 heat sensors to protect high-risk neighbourhoods before extreme heat hits.

Before 2023, we only had about 14 days where the heat was over 105 degrees. This August alone, we had 17 days in a row over 105 degrees.

Mayor of Miami, Eileen Higgins

To turn local action into long-term resilience, C40 and Harvard’s Salata Institute brought together the Mayors of Freetown and Paris, the Governor of Jakarta and experts in health, data, and finance to explore how cities can plan for a hotter future.

Countries with robust early warning systems experience nearly six times fewer disaster-related deaths.

City leaders shared how they’re strengthening these systems to get life-saving information to residents before severe heatwaves hit.

The heat is with us; it’s no longer a distant threat. As mayors, we also need to track the health impacts; the risk is no longer a risk – it’s reality.

C40 Co-Chair and Mayor of Freetown Yvonne, Aki-Sawyerr OBE

US cities are showing what bold urban climate action looks like in real time

Across the United States, city leadership is strengthening clean energy, good jobs and heat adaptation.

Under Mayor Brandon Johnson, Chicago has transitioned its municipal operations to 100% clean energy. In Boston, Mayor Michelle Wu is strengthening the clean energy workforce by rolling out training placements for more than 4,500 jobs.

In Miami, Mayor Eileen Higgins is championing climate solutions expected to create thousands of green jobs, while Mayor of Phoenix, Kate Gallego, is tackling extreme heat and water shortages side by side: planting nearly 30,000 new trees, installing 500 shade structures and advancing water recycling infrastructure.

Building climate-resilient, equitable cities

A new report from C40 Cities and Ramboll, ‘Where Housing Meets Climate’, shows that expanding access to affordable housing and cutting building emissions go hand in hand. The research highlights that cities don’t have to rely on new construction alone. They can retrofit existing buildings, create more homes close to public transport and jobs and lower the cost of city living by addressing energy, transportation and rent together.

At the launch, Copenhagen Lord Mayor Sissel Marie Welling, Global Ambassador for GCoM and former Mayor of Paris Anne Hidalgo and UN-Habitat Executive Director Anaclaudia Rossbach explored how cities can protect residents from rising utility bills and climate risks at the same time.

We cannot delay housing. And we cannot delay climate action. We must deliver both. Teachers, nurses and families need homes they can afford, but the way we build those homes will also shape our climate for decades to come.

Copenhagen Lord Mayor Sissel Marie Welling

Youth leadership also took centre stage. C40 Co-Chair and Mayor of Freetown Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr, Governor of Santiago Claudio Orrego Larraín and New York City Chief Climate Officer Louise Yeung joined young leaders, including winners of C40’s Youth Reinventing Cities competition. The session, hosted by Gensler with support from the Holcim Foundation for Sustainable Construction, explored how youth-led design can shape more inclusive and resilient cities.

It’s our responsibility to ensure that the views of young people are embedded into the decisions we are taking.

C40 Co-Chair and Mayor of Freetown Yvonne, Aki-Sawyerr OBE

Smarter, sustainable urban growth

As demand for infrastructure skyrockets, mayors, investors and industry leaders discussed how cities can manage data centre growth without straining local power grids, water resources or energy affordability. Leaders highlighted C40’s Global Urban Data Centre Pact as a benchmark for responsible growth that doesn’t come at the cost of local communities.

Mayor Kate Gallego, who co-led the call for a Global Urban Data Centre Pact with Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece, shared how cities can meet the growing demand for data centres while protecting local communities and building a cleaner energy future.

US cities are at the forefront of defining the next era of digital growth and urban development. It’s essential that we work to ensure our cities, and our peers around the world, establish a standard for how our residents get the benefits of the AI and digital economy while protecting the communities that make that growth possible.

Mayor of Phoenix, Kate Gallego

The Pact is a vital tool for cities, investors and industry to unite around a shared vision for responsible growth. The City of Chicago is proud to be part of the Pact and to put its principles into action by developing robust regulatory standards for data centre development. Working with partners in industry, finance, academia and government, both locally and globally, we can build a future with clean energy, clean air and shared prosperity.

Mayor of Chicago Brandon Johnson

With food systems generating one-third of global emissions, cities discussed how they could partner with others to create healthier, more sustainable networks. C40’s upcoming research shows how stronger urban-rural partnerships can help cities:

improve their food security

support farmers and local economies

create green jobs

cut consumption-based emissions.

Local leadership, global impact

At the UN SDG Media Zone, São Paulo’s Camila Assis joined former mayors Eric Garcetti and Anne Hidalgo for a panel hosted by WIRED. They shared how city action on jobs, extreme weather and a fair transition away from fossil fuels could offer a blueprint for national governments.

Mayor Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr also outlined how Freetown is preparing for climate impacts by building resilience to protect communities.

UNFCCC Executive Secretary Simon Stiell reinforced that city leadership remains the driving force behind global climate momentum.

Climate action is not a burden on prosperity. It’s how we secure it for everyone, everywhere.

UNFCCC Executive Secretary Simon Stiell

It was clear throughout the week that local action is keeping climate progress moving. As national governments negotiate, mayors are on the ground delivering cleaner energy, healthier neighbourhoods and resilient infrastructure. By turning ambition into delivery, city leaders are setting the pace for global climate action and proving that a fairer, climate-resilient future is already underway.

text:
HOUSTON—The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), in coordination with the White House National Energy Dominance Council (NEDC), the U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI), and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) hosted G20 Energy Ministers at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, Texas, from September 14–16, 2026.

Under President Trump’s leadership, the U.S. recentered G20 conversations on affordability, reliability, and security—affirming the essential role of hydrocarbons, nuclear energy, and advanced technologies in delivering energy abundance and driving economic prosperity.

G20 Energy Ministers reached consensus on four outcomes: advancing energy access and closing the clean cooking gap, supply chain security, infrastructure development, and water resilience. The outcomes reflect the significant progress following nearly a year of dialogue with the G20 to support the commonsense solutions that President Trump has championed to increase access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy; speed the development of critical infrastructure; and reduce vulnerabilities in energy supply chains.

Under U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright’s leadership, G20 Energy Ministers endorsed a clean cooking access declaration(link is external) to support affordable, reliable, and scalable solutions for closing the clean cooking gap—including the use of liquefied petroleum gas, or LPG, which has accounted for roughly 75% of global gains in clean cooking access since 2010. This declaration can help mobilize greater attention and resources for the two billion people still living without access to clean cooking, so they can breathe cleaner air at home and spend less time collecting traditional biomass for fuel.

Building on this achievement, Secretary Wright and Corporate Council on Africa President and CEO Florie Liser hosted a side event on clean cooking that convened G20 representatives alongside private sector executives. The event examined how stronger public-private partnerships can accelerate access to clean cooking solutions, particularly across Africa, to help translate this year’s G20 commitments into action.

“Energy is the essential ingredient that enables everything we do,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “A highly energized society brings health, wealth, and opportunity. The consensus reached in Houston advances cooperation to expand the affordable, reliable, and secure energy, infrastructure, and supply chains needed to support prosperity, resilience, and opportunity throughout the world.”

The investments and agreements announced in Houston demonstrate how the U.S. energy abundance agenda is fostering job creation, expanding economic opportunity, strengthening U.S. and global manufacturing partnerships, and advancing the energy infrastructure that will power the future:

The Japanese company Hitachi Energy announced a $528 million investment to build a new power transformer manufacturing facility in Gallman, Mississippi, expected to create 654 new jobs.

Houston-based Caturus announced a five-train expansion of its Commonwealth LNG export facility in Louisiana that would add 7.75 million tonnes per annum of capacity—or approximately 7% of total U.S. capacity in 2025—and nearly double the project’s planned capacity to approximately 17.25 million tonnes per annum.

Continental Resources signed a memorandum of understanding with Venezuela’s PDVSA to develop and operate the 126,000-acre Ayacucho 2 Block in the Orinoco Belt, which Continental estimates contains approximately 30 billion barrels of oil.

Representatives from the following nations and unions were present at the Energy Abundance Ministerial: the African Union, the Argentine Republic, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Federative Republic of Brazil, Canada, the People’s Republic of China, the European Union, the French Republic, the Federal Republic of Germany, the Republic of India, the Republic of Indonesia, the Italian Republic, Japan, the United Mexican States, the Republic of Poland, the Russian Federation, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Republic of Korea, the Republic of Türkiye, and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

The hands-on display is designed to help visitors of all ages better understand how solar energy works and how the sun can be used to create clean, renewable electricity.

“We wanted to find a way to make solar energy something people can actually see, touch and interact with,” said Amy Schirf, CCRRA Education Coordinator. “It’s one thing to talk about solar panels and renewable energy, but it’s much more fun when you can actually experiment with it and see what happens.”

The display complements CCRRA’s own solar energy project, which includes more than 1,600 solar panels installed across three Authority buildings.

CCRRA could save more than $2 million in electricity costs over the life of the array.

The system is part of CCRRA’s broader commitment to sustainability and provides an opportunity to turn the Authority’s facility into a real-world learning experience.

The new interactive display will be incorporated into CCRRA’s educational programming, including facility tours, school visits and community events.

Visitors will be able to explore the basics of solar energy while seeing how renewable energy connects to CCRRA’s own operations.

Local media are invited to come see the new display in person! CCRRA would be happy to provide a demonstration, answer questions and give media an opportunity to photograph and experience the display.

To arrange a visit or interview, contact Amy Schirf at aschirf@ccrra.org or 814-238-7005.

CCRRA would like to thank and recognize West Penn Energy Fund for their generous support of the project as well as the artists who spent their time and energy creating this amazing educational display.

text:
Power Electronics a global company specializing in solutions for solar energy, storage, data centers, e-mobility, and drives, celebrated the groundbreaking of its future campus in Houston, Texas, marking a major milestone in the company’s long-term growth and industrial strategy in the United States.

The ceremony brought together Power Electronics’ executive leadership, government officials and authorities, customers, industry partners and members of the Houston business community to recognize the beginning of a new chapter in the company’s U.S. operations.

Located on more than 53 acres, the new campus represents a significant expansion of Power Electronics’ manufacturing footprint in the United States. The project will include two buildings of approximately 150,000 and 700,000 square feet, bringing together Logistics, Production, Electronics Manufacturing, R&D, Training, Corporate Offices, and other key functions within a single industrial campus.

Once fully operational, the Houston campus is expected to deliver up to 40 GW of annual production capacity and create over 400 new jobs in the Houston area.

Designed to become Power Electronics’ most automated inverter production site to date, the campus will incorporate advanced production technologies and processes focused on efficiency, quality, scalability and reliability.

Strengthening U.S. Energy Infrastructure Through Local Manufacturing

The new Houston campus comes at a critical time for the U.S. energy industry, as accelerating demand from utility-scale solar, storage, data centers and broader electrification continues to increase the need for reliable power conversion solutions and resilient domestic supply chains.

The Houston campus represents more than additional production capacity. It is a long-term investment in American industry, skilled employment, technological innovation and the infrastructure required to support the next generation of the U.S. energy system.

“For the first time in many years, the United States will be able to meet its growing need for sustainable power generation capacity and energy resilience through local manufacturing, supported by the most advanced technology in the world. Our 40 GW Houston Campus will help shape the future of energy and AI growth globally,” said David Salvo, CEO of Power Electronics.

Built on Decades of Power Electronics Expertise

With 40 years of experience and more than 116 GW installed in the U.S., Power Electronics has built its position as a global industry leader through a continued focus on innovation, advanced manufacturing and service.

The United States has become a key market in the company’s global strategy. For more than a decade, Power Electronics has steadily strengthened its presence across the country, building local teams, operations and technical expertise to serve some of the most significant and demanding energy projects in the U.S.

By continuing to invest in manufacturing, engineering, talent and service resources, Power Electronics is reinforcing its long-term commitment to the market and its role in advancing the infrastructure needed for the next generation of energy development. With the addition of the Houston campus, Power Electronics will further strengthen its global manufacturing platform and reach up to 105 GW of annual production capacity worldwide, combining its operations in the United States and Europe to support customers with greater scale, proximity and resilience across key energy markets.
