Climate cooperation, for it to be durable, needs a separate track of its own, one that can advance specific interests and opportunities in clean energy.
For India, a more useful frame and approach is managed or selective interdependence, advancing commercial engagement on clean energy issues while limiting strategic exposure.
India-China bilateral clean energy engagement offers scale, but it likely remains hostage to the broader political relationship.
Dr Karthik Nachiappan is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Institute of South Asian Studies (ISAS), an autonomous research institute at the National University of Singapore (NUS).
text:
Summary

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s recent visit to New Delhi for the BRICS Summit reopened diplomatic channels but largely left intact India’s structural dependence on Chinese goods. Moving forward, India should pursue managed interdependence by engaging China and regional institutions to build up domestic capacity rather than unconditioned dependence or decoupling.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September 2026 has been read as a resetting of India-China ties: restored flights and visas, a pledge to work toward resolving the border dispute and language on structural trade imbalances. Climate and clean energy cooperation, however, were absent from the outcomes.

The lesson is not that the thaw is meaningless but that it is running on a different track from the underlying economic rivalry. The ongoing detente lowers the temperature in terms of political engagement; it does not resolve the structural tension between India’s dependence on Chinese goods, especially clean energy inputs and its general and overriding wariness of that dependence. Climate cooperation, for it to be durable, needs a separate track of its own, one that can advance specific interests and opportunities in clean energy.

The debate on India-China clean-energy cooperation is often framed as a binary: engage or not. Neither is sufficient. China holds dominant positions across solar manufacturing, battery chemistry, electric vehicles, power electronics and mineral processing that India cannot replace in the near term; attempting to do so quickly would raise costs and delay deployment.

However, wholesale, unconditioned engagement risks converting engagement into a potential vulnerability.

For India, a more useful frame and approach is managed or selective interdependence, advancing commercial engagement on clean energy issues while limiting strategic exposure. In practice, this means differentiated conditions by sector through measures like equity caps, local-content requirements, technology co-development, training, repair and sunset clauses that could be attached wherever infrastructure, data or critical technologies are involved, alongside an effort to nurture and have credible alternative suppliers.

India’s existing investment-screening mechanism also illustrates the gap between the two. It did ostensibly reduce the risk of some investment and acquisitions but did not reduce dependence, since restricted equity simply continued alongside imports of Chinese machinery, components and technical expertise.

Southeast Asia could help navigate this trajectory. Vietnam’s solar and wind boom, built almost entirely on Chinese panels, turbines and engineering services, took installed capacity from negligible to over 16 gigawatts within two years and outran the grid’s capacity to absorb it, producing curtailment and retroactive tariff cuts. Indonesia’s nickel and battery build-out, driven by an export ban that forced Chinese processors to build onshore, created US$ 34 billion (S$43.5 billion) in downstream capacity and with it, a dependency on a technology partner whose processes Indonesia cannot replicate, alongside significant environmental and public-health costs.

Both cases show that Chinese capital and equipment can deliver speed and scale at a pace no domestic pathway could match. Neither, however, shows that capacity converts into capability. The Southeast Asian record should function for India less as a template than as an example to assess and reconfigure. India can institute the safeguards when engaging China through greater ownership, technology transfer, supplier development and enforcement that Southeast Asian countries did not adequately think through.

India-China bilateral clean energy engagement offers scale, but it likely remains hostage to the broader political relationship. This situation calls for engagement through the bilateral and beyond via minilateral platforms such as BRICS and BASIC (Brazil, South Africa, India, China), multilateral development banks, including the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the New Development Bank, city-to-city networks, and Track 1.5 dialogue, among research institutions.

These channels diffuse the political risk that any single government absorbs by engaging China directly, and as Indonesia and the Philippines have shown by coordinating nickel policy give smaller and mid-sized countries more leverage collectively than they would have by negotiating alone. A possible sequence is regional and minilateral engagement first, to build trust, benchmarks and standards, and bilateral second, to deliver cooperation at scale once.

The current window gives India an opening for deepening climate engagement with China. Potential success for India could be measured in terms of whether India has been able to build robust clean energy capabilities at home, found credible alternative suppliers, secured cooperation on grids, storage and energy efficiency that makes a difference.

That outcome depends on Beijing’s intentions and on India’s institutions, the investment screening mechanisms, industrial policy, regional and minilateral partnerships that can add to other engagements. Managed interdependence is not just a strategy; it will be a test of institutional capacity, and one that India must foster.

. . . . .

Dr Karthik Nachiappan is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Institute of South Asian Studies (ISAS), an autonomous research institute at the National University of Singapore (NUS). text:
ALLENTOWN, Pa. (AP) — The Energy Department said Thursday that it will spend almost $2 billion to try to squeeze more electricity out of the nation's aging and stressed power grid, as President Donald Trump's administration steps up efforts to avoid blackouts amid skyrocketing energy demand spurred by artificial intelligence.

The money will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity — enough to power 16 million homes. The projects will use new technologies such as sensors to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested paths, the department said.

The upgrades could improve power reliability and lower electricity costs for about 100 million Americans, officials said.

“This is a quick way to lower electricity prices and increase reliability: using fibers that are already in the transmission lines to analyze what’s the temperature out, what’s the wind out, how can we use this transmission line to distribute more power, but safely and only in the right conditions," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a news conference promoting the grants Thursday at a PPL Corp. facility in Allentown.

The eastern Pennsylvania electric utility says two data centers in its territory came online this year and six more are under construction, with enough other data centers in the advanced planning stages that its peak electric demand could quintuple by 2032.

PPL said it is receiving $71.5 million to modernize an existing high-voltage transmission line across roughly 30 miles in northern Pennsylvania.

The announcement comes amid warnings that AI’s voracious demand for power is threatening to overwhelm U.S. power supplies, as massive new data centers come online faster than new power plants can be built. It also comes as electricity bills rise faster than inflation in many parts of the U.S., blamed in some areas on demand from data centers.

The snowballing opposition to data centers in communities across the country has thrown a wrench into the plans of the world’s richest companies and transformed the midterm election landscape.

Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both major political parties criticize them and many communities try to block them.

In the meantime, Congress and some states are trying to push utilities to expand their use of new technologies to make grids more efficient and to lessen the need to build new power plants.

Julia Selker, the executive director of the WATT Coalition, a trade association for grid-enhancing technologies, said both the projects and the scale of the investment are significant. Utilities in the U.S. are lagging places like Europe in adopting the technologies, despite federal investment in the past to develop and test them, Selker said.

Still, Drew Maloney, CEO of the Edison Electric Institute, a trade association of for-profit utilities, said America's electric utilities are making a “significant investment” every year in new technologies to strengthen the grid and reduce outages.

Wright said that work on the projects should begin right away and that he hoped some efficiencies are in place before this winter to tamp down price spikes when extreme weather sends demand skyrocketing.

Wright said he didn't know whether the projects would have gotten done without federal funding. Many, he said, had been under consideration before the grants were offered, but the grant recipients hadn't “quite pulled the trigger” on them.

Projects being announced Thursday will involve component enhancements on more than 1,500 miles (2,400 kilometers) of transmission lines and technological enhancements across nearly 21,000 miles (34,000 kilometers), the department said.

Projects were prioritized based on those that can be put into operation quickly, officials said. Money for the grants comes from the bipartisan infrastructure law enacted by Congress under then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat. The government's $1.9 billion in funding will be matched by $3.35 billion from the recipients, the department said.

Recipients include utilities, cooperatives and four state agencies. The state agencies — in Colorado, Indiana, Ohio and Oklahoma — were the biggest recipients, collectively drawing $810 million, with the Colorado and Oklahoma projects promising improvements to regional grids.

Trump has vowed to “unleash” the nation's energy sector in his second term, aiming to drive up record-setting domestic oil and gas production, strip away pollution restrictions on power plants and keep expensive coal-fired power plants operating past their retirement dates.

The administration also has pledged nearly $4 billion to buy back offshore wind leases as Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.

His administration meanwhile has pushed to help tech giants build and connect data centers to power plants and high-voltage power lines and convert Cold War-era uranium enrichment plants into data center and power plant complexes.

___

Daly reported from Washington.

Why Capitol Hill Must Finish the Farm Bill For farm families looking to expand, purchase land, or simply cover input costs, the pending federal Farm Bill remains the ultimate key to financial security.

But while speedier approvals will keep many wheels turning this season, long-term stability hinges on Capitol Hill passing a Farm Bill that aligns loan limits with the real cost of keeping an American farm in business.
text:
As skyrocketing input costs, volatile markets, and eroding profit margins continue to pinch Midwestern operations, relief couldn’t come at a more crucial moment. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has announced a series of major overhauls to its farm loan programs—a direct effort to slash red tape, accelerate funding delivery, and get capital directly into the hands of producers when they need it most.

For farmers facing tight cash flow and growing credit demands ahead of the upcoming season, these administrative changes mean quicker access to vital operational capital without getting bogged down in traditional federal bureaucracy.

Slashing Wait Times and Paperwork

The core benefit of the USDA’s updated rules lies in speed and efficiency. A permanent rollout of the USDA’s fast-track application process for qualifying direct loan borrowers is already paying off: early pilot testing proved the system trims processing time by roughly eight days. In a farming environment where equipment breakdowns, seed orders, and land leases wait for no one, over a week saved in loan approval can mean the difference between securing an opportunity or missing it entirely.

Additionally, the agency is granting experienced agriculture lenders expanded authority to process guaranteed loans internally. By removing unnecessary layers of administrative review, producers can work closely with the local lenders who understand their specific regional operations—bypassing the slow-moving paper trails of the past. To ensure these benefits last, the USDA is also shifting away from paper applications in favor of full electronic processing by 2027.

“First, they’re making a fast-track application process permanent for qualifying direct loan borrowers, which has already reduced processing time by about eight days in the pilot,” explains Danny Munch, Economist with the American Farm Bureau Federation. “They’re also giving experienced lenders more authority to process guaranteed loans with less paperwork and fewer layers of review. They’re also moving away from largely paper-based applications toward electric processing beginning 2027.”

The Elephant in the Field: Outdated Loan Limits

While streamlined processing gives farmers immediate breathing room, industry experts emphasize that faster paperwork is only a partial solution to a much larger economic issue. Modern farm operations require significantly higher capital to operate than they did even five years ago, making current federal borrowing limits feel increasingly out of touch with real-world farm budgets.

“Farmland values, equipment costs, production expenses have increased dramatically,” Munch points out. “The proposed farm bill would raise those limits to $850,000 and $750,000, respectively. It would also increase guaranteed loan limits and double the micro loan limit to $100,000. And there’s real demand for those programs.”

While the USDA has pushed its administrative capabilities to the limit to help producers, raising those hard borrowing caps requires a literal act of Congress.

Why Capitol Hill Must Finish the Farm Bill

For farm families looking to expand, purchase land, or simply cover input costs, the pending federal Farm Bill remains the ultimate key to financial security. The USDA can modernize its technology and eliminate bureaucratic hurdles on its own, but only Congressional approval of the updated Farm Bill can unlock the higher loan thresholds necessary to match today’s hyper-inflated farm economy.

“They can cut paperwork at USDA, modernize technology, but it can’t independently raise those limits without a federal law change,” Munch cautions. “That’s why the farm bill is so important. It gives Congress the opportunity to update those limits that actually reflect today’s farm economy, and that’s why we’re hoping to get this farm bill across the finish line soon.”

The Bottom Line for Your Operation

The USDA’s loan modernizations provide a faster, cleaner path to critical funding, helping producers cut through red tape when margins are razor-thin. But while speedier approvals will keep many wheels turning this season, long-term stability hinges on Capitol Hill passing a Farm Bill that aligns loan limits with the real cost of keeping an American farm in business.

State-Level Employment Clean energy employment declined across 35 states during 2025, although the losses were concentrated in some of the country’s largest clean energy job markets.

text:
The U.S. clean energy sector lost 36,949 jobs in 2025, reversing four consecutive years of employment growth, according to E2‘s Clean Jobs America 2026 analysis.

The job losses mark the first annual employment decline since the pandemic-driven economic crisis. The jobs lost during the year were equivalent to nearly 40% of the new positions created in 2024.

The employment contraction affected most major clean energy sectors, with energy efficiency recording the largest absolute decline. Employment in the sector declined by 21,443 jobs, ending 2025 with approximately 2.36 million workers.

Employment in renewable generation fell by 11,584 jobs, to 557,725. Jobs in the clean vehicle sector fell by 9,619, to 388,415.

Storage and grid modernization bucked the broader decline, adding 5,346 jobs during the year. Employment in the segment increased to 173,388.

Biofuels also registered a marginal increase, adding 350 jobs to reach 42,270.

The decline in clean energy employment came alongside a broader contraction in the U.S. energy workforce. The Department of Energy estimated that the country’s overall energy sector employed 8.4 million workers in 2025 and lost approximately 86,000 jobs during the year.

Clean energy accounted for roughly 43% of the total energy sector job losses.

Despite the contraction, clean energy remained the largest segment of the U.S. energy workforce, with more than 3.5 million jobs. E2 said oil and gas companies employed approximately 958,000 workers, while coal and nuclear companies employed 125,000 and 70,000, respectively, in 2025.

Clean energy employment also remained 16% above 2020 levels. However, the report notes that the sector’s recent trend of adding around 100,000 or more jobs annually appears to have ended.

State-Level Employment

Clean energy employment declined across 35 states during 2025, although the losses were concentrated in some of the country’s largest clean energy job markets.

The five states recording the largest declines accounted for approximately 82% of the nationwide net job loss. Four were among the 10 states with the largest clean energy workforces.

California recorded the largest decline, losing 20,655 clean energy jobs, or 3.7%. The state’s losses accounted for more than half of the nationwide net decline.

Illinois lost 2,958 clean energy jobs, representing a 2.2% decline, while Maryland lost 2,395 jobs, or 2.8%. Massachusetts recorded a decline of 2,212 jobs, or 1.7%, and Michigan lost 1,926 jobs, or 1.5%.

Florida led clean energy employment growth among states, adding 3,801 jobs, an increase of 2.1%. Georgia added 830 jobs, followed by Iowa with 797, New Mexico with 754, and Idaho with 518.

New Mexico recorded the highest percentage growth among the five leading states at 5.4%. Florida added more clean energy jobs than the next four highest growth states combined.

Project Cancellations

The employment decline coincided with a significant increase in clean energy project cancellations and downsizing.

According to E2, companies canceled or downsized 142 clean energy manufacturing, generation, and storage projects during 2025. The projects represented $57.8 billion in planned investment.

The canceled or downsized projects were expected to create about 84,400 jobs. These positions are separate from the 36,949 existing clean energy jobs lost during 2025 and are not included in the Department of Energy employment figures.

Combining the actual employment decline with the jobs associated with canceled projects results in more than 120,000 existing and planned positions affected, according to E2.

E2 linked the reversal in employment and project activity to changes in federal support for clean energy and electric vehicles that began in January 2025 under the Trump administration and Congress.

Clean energy manufacturing investment in the U.S. continued to slow in the first quarter of 2026, with businesses announcing $758.3 million in funding across 12 new electric vehicle, solar, battery, and grid projects between January and March. This is a decline from the $3.45 billion invested in Q1 2025.

text:
GE Vernova & Eneva's Azulão I gas plant in the Amazon has bespoke features to safeguard its turbines from grid oscillations on a 1,200-mile link

Brazil is banking on wind and solar, which raises an awkward question about what keeps the lights on when the weather turns.

The government's Ten-Year Energy Expansion Plan expects renewables to account for more than 85% of electricity generation by 2035.

That said, grid operators need plants that can ramp output quickly and supply firm power at peak demand when renewables fall short.

Azulão I, deep in the Amazon rainforest, was built for that role.

A gas plant in the jungle

The 295MW plant is built around GE Vernova's 7HA.02 gas turbine and was developed by Eneva, which GE Vernova describes as Brazil's largest thermoelectric generator, meaning a producer that burns fuel to make power.

Because the turbine can adjust its output as grid conditions change, it counts as dispatchable, meaning operators can call on it when needed.

"Providing dependable power when renewables fluctuate makes flexible gas generation a critical complement to lower-carbon technologies," says Marco Vera, General Director and VP of New Units for GE Vernova's Gas Power business in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The trouble with a 1,200-mile line

Azulão I feeds the Tucuruí–Macapá–Manaus transmission corridor, a route stretching nearly 1,200 miles.

Moving power that far requires series capacitors, devices that increase the amount of power a line can carry.

They carry a serious side effect, however, because they can set off oscillations in the grid known as sub-synchronous resonance (SSR), which occur below the grid's normal operating frequency.

Left unchecked, these oscillations can cause large-scale outages, damage machinery and break transmission lines.

They can also snap a generator's shaft in half.

A filter tuned to the site

After GE Vernova flagged SSR as a risk in early talks with Eneva, engineers modelled the network in detail, examining capacitor configurations, maintenance outages and the frequencies at which the network and turbine generator could interact.

Standard equipment could not provide the necessary protection, and the precise frequencies depend on the local network and the generator, so the team built a bespoke blocking filter.

Installed in the generator's output path, it acts as a barrier to the problem frequencies and stops harmful oscillations reaching the machine.

"An off-the-shelf component would not account for these site-specific resonances," explains José Geraldo Barreto Monteiro de Andrade, Managing Director for Latin America at GE Vernova's Consulting Services.

"A tailored solution was necessary to ensure the filter was 'in tune' with the risk profile of the turbine generator units," he added.

Such filters are usually added after commercial operation begins, once a problem has surfaced, but at Azulão I engineers built the protection in beforehand.

One system rather than two

Teams from GE Vernova's Gas Power, Electrification and Consulting Services businesses worked with Eneva to fold those findings into the plant's grid connection design.

"Instead of reacting to an SSR problem after the plant entered service, the team addressed it while the system was still being engineered – an outcome enabled by Eneva's trust in GE Vernova's expertise," says Ivette Castillo, General Manager of Grid Systems Integration for GE Vernova in Latin America.

Because the risk of SSR shifts with the configuration of the surrounding network, the team also developed special operating procedures for when nearby equipment is offline or being serviced.

Those procedures were applied during commissioning and testing of the first turbine generators.

The same assessment is now under way for two subsequent units, and GE Vernova will maintain the plant for 15 years under a long-term services agreement.

text:
About Us

The American Clean Power Association (ACP) is the leading voice of today’s multi-tech clean energy industry, representing energy storage, wind, utility-scale solar, clean hydrogen, and transmission companies. ACP is committed to meeting America’s energy and national security goals and building our economy with fast-growing, low-cost, and reliable domestic power. Learn more at cleanpower.org.

The Clean Power Institute (CPI) is ACP’s 501(c)3 affiliate organization. CPI’s mission is to build the public support and workforce to fuel the clean energy future. CPI advances its mission through programming that builds a stable, skilled, and diverse workforce and creates strategic partnerships that promote the benefits of clean energy investments across the country.

Position Summary

The Clean Power Institute (CPI) is seeking an entrepreneurial and highly collaborative Executive Director to lead the organization through its next phase of growth. Reporting to the COO of ACP/President of CPI and working closely with the CPI Board of Directors, the Executive Director will lead CPI’s day-to-day operations and develop the strategies, programs, partnerships and resources needed to expand its national impact.

CPI is building a national approach to clean energy workforce development that connects industry, educators, workforce organizations and communities to create stronger pathways into clean energy careers. The Executive Director will identify opportunities for growth, develop new programs and business cases, strengthen and scale existing initiatives, and build the partnerships and financial resources necessary to execute them. This is a hands-on leadership role, with the Executive Director expected to directly develop and execute key initiatives while leading CPI’s broader strategy and growth.

CPI’s relationship with ACP provides direct access to the companies investing in, building, operating and supplying America’s clean energy infrastructure. The Executive Director will leverage that connection to ensure CPI’s workforce and education programs respond to real industry needs, while expanding CPI’s partnerships across philanthropy, education, workforce development and communities nationwide.

Essential Functions/Major Responsibilities

To perform this job successfully, an individual must be able to perform each essential duty and responsibility satisfactorily. Reasonable accommodation may be made to enable an individual with disabilities to perform the essential functions. Other duties may be assigned to meet business needs.

Strategy & Organizational Growth

Lead the development and execution of CPI’s long-term vision, strategy, and operating priorities in partnership with the CPI Board of Directors and ACP leadership.

Build the organizational capabilities, team, systems, partnerships, and resources necessary to grow CPI from a portfolio of successful initiatives into an integrated national platform.

Identify opportunities for new programs, partnerships, and areas of growth; develop strategies and business cases to evaluate opportunities and bring forward recommendations for investment and execution.

Establish CPI as a nationally recognized leader and convener on clean energy workforce development, education, economic opportunity, and community engagement.

Establish clear goals and measures of success across CPI’s work and ensure accountability for execution and results.

Programs, Workforce & Education

Lead a national workforce strategy focused on building sustainable talent pipelines in the communities where clean energy projects are developed and operated, particularly rural communities.

Build upon CPI’s existing workforce models and expand its reach across wind, solar, energy storage, transmission, electrical trades, manufacturing, and emerging clean energy careers.

Lead the creation of an integrated education-to-career strategy that introduces students to clean energy early and connects them through high school, community colleges, apprenticeships, universities, military pathways, and employment.

Build partnerships with K–12 systems, educators, community colleges, and national youth-serving organizations to dramatically expand clean energy career awareness.

Lead the development and growth of the Clean Energy Academy as the industry’s premier learning platform and the educational backbone of CPI’s national workforce strategy.

Ensure the Academy connects early career awareness, workforce preparation, professional development, and lifelong learning into a cohesive educational ecosystem.

Use data, partner feedback, and program outcomes to evaluate impact, identify opportunities, and guide the continued growth of CPI’s programs.

Partnerships, Fundraising & External Engagement

Serve as CPI’s chief fundraiser and develop a comprehensive, diversified fundraising strategy capable of supporting CPI’s national ambitions.

Build and maintain strong relationships with foundations, corporations, individual philanthropists, and other institutional funders interested in clean energy, workforce development, education, economic mobility, rural communities, STEM, and the future of work.

Develop a compelling philanthropic case for investment that connects CPI’s workforce and education mission with economic opportunity, community impact, and the long-term strength of American clean energy.

Ensure strong stewardship of philanthropic investments through measurable outcomes, effective reporting, compelling storytelling, and sustained relationships with funders.

Build a national network of strategic partnerships across philanthropy, education, workforce development, youth-serving organizations, economic development organizations, and state and regional clean energy associations.

Serve as a national convener capable of bringing organizations with different perspectives and capabilities together around shared workforce and education challenges.

Work with state and regional organizations to translate CPI’s national strategy into locally relevant programs and resources, recognizing that clean energy projects ultimately succeed at the community level.

Serve as CPI’s principal external ambassador and a compelling national voice on clean energy workforce development, education, economic opportunity, and community impact.

Represent CPI with CEOs and industry leaders, philanthropic organizations, policymakers, educators, workforce leaders, community organizations, conferences, media, and other national forums.

Build CPI’s national profile and reputation as a trusted, solutions-oriented organization capable of bringing industry and external partners together to solve complex workforce and education challenges.

Organizational Leadership

Lead CPI’s day-to-day operations and team, establishing clear priorities, accountability, and expectations across the organization.

Develop a strong and highly collaborative partnership with the CPI Board of Directors, engaging the Board as strategic advisors, ambassadors, fundraisers, and champions of CPI’s mission.

Engage individual Board members strategically based on their expertise, relationships, and ability to advance CPI’s priorities, including industry engagement, fundraising, partnerships, and external visibility.

Provide the Board with clear updates on CPI’s performance, major initiatives, and emerging opportunities, and bring forward significant strategic priorities and recommendations for Board consideration.

Make CPI’s relationship with ACP and its member companies a defining strategic advantage for the organization.

Engage ACP member companies not simply as employers at the end of the talent pipeline, but as partners in identifying workforce needs, shaping curricula and credentials, providing career exposure, creating internships and apprenticeships, and investing in workforce solutions.

Position CPI as the place where the clean energy industry can collectively address workforce and talent challenges that individual companies cannot solve alone.

Work collaboratively with ACP leadership and staff, leveraging ACP’s industry expertise, relationships, and organizational resources while establishing a strong identity, strategy, and external presence for CPI.

Lead and develop CPI staff, establishing clear expectations and accountability while building an entrepreneurial and collaborative organizational culture.

Assess CPI’s organizational and staffing needs as the organization grows and recommend the structure, talent, and resources necessary to support its priorities.

Education, Experience & Skills

15+ years of progressively responsible leadership experience, including significant experience in a senior organizational, program, or executive leadership role. Experience in clean energy, workforce development, education, philanthropy, economic development, nonprofit leadership, government, or a related field is strongly preferred.

Bachelor’s degree or equivalent combination of education and relevant experience required; advanced degree in business, public policy, education, nonprofit management, workforce development, economics, energy, or a related field preferred.

Demonstrated ability to develop long-term strategy, translate broad organizational goals into actionable plans, and lead complex programs or initiatives from concept through execution and evaluation.

Hands-on, execution-oriented leadership style with the ability to move between strategy and direct execution as needed to advance CPI’s priorities.

Strong business and financial acumen, including experience developing business cases, managing budgets and resources, evaluating investments and opportunities, and making recommendations that support organizational growth and long-term sustainability.

Proven fundraising and resource development experience, with the ability to build relationships and secure support from corporations, foundations, government entities, philanthropic partners, and other funders.

Strong understanding of workforce and talent development issues, ideally including experience with education-to-career pathways, workforce systems, apprenticeships, skills development, or employer-led talent strategies.

Exceptional relationship-building and stakeholder management skills, with demonstrated ability to develop trusted partnerships across industry, government, education, philanthropy, workforce organizations, community-based organizations, and other external stakeholders.

Demonstrated ability to influence, build consensus, and move complex work forward across teams and organizations where priorities, perspectives, and interests may differ.

Experience working effectively with a Board of Directors and senior executives, including bringing forward recommendations, communicating complex issues clearly, and exercising sound judgment around matters requiring broader leadership or governance involvement.

Demonstrated experience leading and developing high-performing teams, setting clear expectations and accountability, developing talent, and holding leaders accountable for how they manage and develop their own teams.

Ability to lead beyond the immediate CPI team, working across ACP functions and leadership to align priorities, leverage shared resources and expertise, and advance broader organizational goals.

Strong organizational judgment and decision-making skills, with the ability to operate with significant autonomy, assess risk and opportunity, make decisions with incomplete information, and recognize when an issue requires escalation or broader organizational consideration.

Outstanding written and verbal communication skills and executive presence, with the ability to communicate complex ideas clearly, adapt messaging for different audiences, and represent CPI credibly with senior industry leaders, funders, policymakers, educators, community leaders, media, and other external audiences.

Entrepreneurial and solutions-oriented approach, with the ability to identify opportunities, challenge existing approaches when appropriate, and build the strategy, relationships, resources, and organizational support necessary to move ideas forward.

Demonstrated ability to lead through growth and change while maintaining organizational stability, building trust, and creating an accountable, collaborative culture.

Ability to operate successfully within a complex affiliated organizational structure, working collaboratively with ACP leadership and staff while advancing CPI’s distinct mission, strategy, and external presence.

Job Conditions

We are a fast-paced, high-energy organization with a very ambitious agenda and a staff that is highly motivated. This position may experience high-level work demands and independent decision-making under tight timelines. Regular travel across the country for meetings or events may be required. Applicants must be currently authorized to work in the United States on a full-time basis. ACP will not sponsor applicants for work visas.

We reasonably believe that the base salary range for this position is $250,000 to 300,000 annually. A wide range of factors are considered when making compensation decisions including and not limited to skill set, experience, training, education, knowledge, and other business and organizational needs. We offer a 401k, PTO and sick leave, commuter benefits, wellness reimbursement, and professional development/tuition reimbursements for eligible employees.

This privacy notice applies to the processing of personal information that ACP collects about candidates for employment. Throughout the application process, ACP may collect some or all of the following categories of personal information: name and address; email address; age or date of birth; race or other demographic information; occupation and employment history; phone number; education; and/or social security number or other identification data.

ACP provides this information to third-party service providers to store and process this data on our behalf, for background checks, and for regulatory compliance. ACP does not sell any applicant personal information.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) launched the Speed to Power (STP) initiative on September 18, 2025—a federal action to accelerate large-scale generation, transmission, and grid infrastructure development so the United States has the power needed to continue to meet growing demand for affordable, reliable, and secure energy, and win the global artificial intelligence (AI) race.

To inform the initiative, DOE issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking data on large-scale grid infrastructure projects. Responses were due November 21, 2025. DOE received 369 responses and identified 238 unique projects primarily across transmission, generation, and load categories.

This document distinguishes among actions informed by the RFI, separate actions that align with issues raised through it, and recommendations that remain under consideration or require action by other authorities.

The RFI was not a funding opportunity and did not accept applications for financial assistance. Submitting a response did not provide an advantage or disadvantage in any later competition. DOE reviewed the submissions as planning information and did not treat any response as a binding project or policy commitment.

Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades (SPARK)

The Office of Electricity’s approximately $1.9 billion SPARK Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) was designed to accelerate investments in electric grid infrastructure that helps meet growing electricity demand, strengthen resource adequacy, and improve grid reliability and affordability. The funding opportunity prioritized projects that combined durable physical capacity upgrades, such as reconductoring, with advanced transmission technologies that improve operational efficiency and flexibility. Through these investments, SPARK will expand grid capacity and transfer capability while maximizing the value and performance of existing transmission infrastructure.

Some actions respond directly to the Request for Information (RFI); others were already under way, but address issues that stakeholders raised. Unless noted, sources do not establish that an action was created because of the RFI.

For more information about the projects selected under Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and Other Key Transmission Technology Upgrades (SPARK) Notice of Funding Opportunity, go here.

RFI respondents also proposed actions concerning new generation, nuclear and geothermal deployment, long-duration storage, demand-side flexibility, domestic manufacturing and workforce, federal permitting, interconnection and market rules, tax policy, and interagency coordination. The source materials do not establish that DOE has adopted each recommendation or created a new program for each issue. DOE will announce any additional funding opportunity, policy action, study, or engagement process through official channels.

description:
Navitas Solar plans to invest $1.04 billion over five years across Gujarat and Maharashtra, expanding from solar modules into cells, wafers, ingots, storage and power generation.
The expansion also includes a 5 GWh battery storage facility and two solar parks, strengthening Navitas Solar’s position across the clean energy value chain.
Navitas Solar plans to invest $1.04 billion over the next five years to build a more integrated clean energy business across Gujarat and Maharashtra.
The strategy would give Navitas greater control across the solar supply chain at a time when India is pushing to expand domestic clean energy manufacturing.
Battery storage joins the expansion Navitas plans to add battery energy storage to its portfolio through a 5 GWh facility in Vadodara, Gujarat.
text:
Navitas Solar plans to invest $1.04 billion over five years across Gujarat and Maharashtra, expanding from solar modules into cells, wafers, ingots, storage and power generation.

A 2.4 GW solar cell facility is already under development in Gujarat, with its first phase expected to begin operations by July 2027.

The expansion also includes a 5 GWh battery storage facility and two solar parks, strengthening Navitas Solar’s position across the clean energy value chain.

Navitas Solar plans to invest $1.04 billion over the next five years to build a more integrated clean energy business across Gujarat and Maharashtra.

The privately owned Indian solar manufacturer will expand beyond its existing module operations into upstream manufacturing, battery storage and renewable power generation. The investment covers solar ingots, wafers, cells and modules, alongside new energy storage and generation capacity.

The strategy would give Navitas greater control across the solar supply chain at a time when India is pushing to expand domestic clean energy manufacturing.

Building an integrated solar supply chain

Navitas currently has 3 GW of annual solar module manufacturing capacity. Its next phase will move the company further upstream into the components required to manufacture those modules.

A major part of that expansion is already underway in Sisodara, Gujarat. Navitas is developing a 2.4 GW solar cell manufacturing facility there.

The first phase will involve approximately $125 million of investment and is targeted to begin operations by July 2027.

Adding cell production creates a more vertically integrated manufacturing structure. Planned investments in ingots and wafers would extend that integration further upstream.

For solar manufacturers, greater control over these production stages can reduce exposure to external suppliers and improve oversight of costs, quality and availability. It can also support India’s wider effort to build more domestic manufacturing capacity across the renewable energy supply chain.

The scale of the Navitas investment also reflects how manufacturers are broadening their strategies as India’s renewable energy market grows. Companies increasingly face demand not only for generation equipment, but also for technologies that can support grid reliability.

Battery storage joins the expansion

Navitas plans to add battery energy storage to its portfolio through a 5 GWh facility in Vadodara, Gujarat.

The move takes the company beyond solar manufacturing and into one of the technologies increasingly viewed as critical to renewable power systems.

Battery storage can absorb electricity when renewable generation is high and release it when required. That capability becomes increasingly important as grids integrate larger volumes of variable solar and wind power.

For Navitas, the planned facility creates another business line alongside its solar manufacturing operations. It also positions the company across both renewable energy production and the infrastructure needed to manage that electricity.

RELATED ARTICLE: Navitas Drives GaN Sustainability Benefits at Deutsche Bank Conference

Maharashtra projects extend into generation

The five-year strategy also includes direct renewable power generation.

In Maharashtra, Navitas is developing two solar parks with capacities of 200 MW and 25 MW. These projects extend the company’s presence beyond manufacturing into renewable energy assets.

Taken together, the investments create a business spanning several stages of the clean energy value chain. Navitas would have exposure to upstream solar materials, cells, modules, battery storage and electricity generation.

That breadth could become increasingly relevant as India’s power system expands renewable capacity and seeks stronger domestic supply chains.

India’s clean energy manufacturing race accelerates

India has been working to increase domestic production of solar equipment while reducing reliance on imported components. Expanding local manufacturing has become closely tied to the country’s industrial, energy security and climate priorities.

For investors and corporate energy buyers, the growth of integrated domestic manufacturers could influence equipment availability, project economics and supply-chain risk.

The addition of storage is equally significant. Renewable deployment increasingly depends on investment in grids, storage and other flexibility technologies alongside new generation capacity.

Navitas Solar’s $1.04 billion plan brings those elements together under one expansion strategy. If delivered as planned, the company will move from a primarily module-focused manufacturer toward a broader clean energy platform.

That shift reflects a wider transformation underway across India’s renewable energy sector. Manufacturing scale remains important, but the next phase of competition is increasingly about controlling more of the value chain while building the infrastructure needed to support a larger, more flexible clean power system.

description:

Contrarily, U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly calls climate change a hoax, a con job or a scam.
Here are the world leaders in their own words: ___ THE QUOTE: “Until recently, the response to climate change was firmly established at the center of the international agenda.
And more than half of that loss comes from climate change, he said.
___ THE QUOTE: “For those who have declared climate change a hoax perpetrated by geopolitical opponents, the warnings of recent times cannot have been clearer.
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the world cannot “allow countries and cultures to vanish beneath the waves” on Thursday as the General Assembly approved its first declaration on sea-level rise.

This statement is meant to shift the international response to the rise in sea level driven by humans from fragmented initiatives to sustained, coordinated and adequately-funded action. It comes as country after country has lamented the toll of climate change in speeches this week and called for collective action.

Contrarily, U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly calls climate change a hoax, a con job or a scam.

Here are the world leaders in their own words:

___

THE QUOTE: “Until recently, the response to climate change was firmly established at the center of the international agenda. This year, however, the topic disappeared from the debates of the G7 and G20, forums that bring together the largest carbon emitters. It is time to resume the offensive and inflict a defeat on denialism. Nature reminds us every day that we live on one planet. The glaciers in the Himalayas are melting. The super El Nino may cause torrential rains, droughts and forest fires in different parts of the globe.”

— Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, president of Brazil

THE SITUATION: Climate change and deforestation threaten the Amazon. A strong El Nino, a cyclic warming of the equatorial Pacific, causes higher temperatures and drier weather in the rainforest, conditions that worsen wildfires.

___

THE QUOTE: “What we experienced in Nepal was Himalayan tsunami. But the larger looming threat is even more consequential. It is not only the devastation we mourn today; it is for greater danger that lies ahead if the world continues to look away... I call upon you to treat climate action not as a charity, but as a matter of justice.”

— Shisir Khanal, minister of foreign affairs for Nepal

THE SITUATION: Human-caused global warming thinned glaciers and thawed mountain permafrost, likely helping to destabilize the Himalayan slope that collapsed last month and unleashed catastrophic flooding across Nepal, according to a World Weather Attribution report. More than 1,300 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing.

___

THE QUOTE: “To protect the lives of present and future generations, all states must take serious action to tackle global warming. I believe that climate action and economic growth can go hand-in-hand.”

— Sanae Takaichi, prime minister of Japan

THE SITUATION: Japan is working to protect communities from warming and has pledged to slash emissions, but extreme heat remains a threat in the short term.

___

THE QUOTE: “I think this summer was a summer of truth. The recent summer months have been, as we heard from the scientists, the hottest on record, but may be the coolest for the years to come.”

— Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission

THE SITUATION: Europe is heating up twice as fast as the global rate, making it the fastest-warming continent.

___

THE QUOTE: “By the end of this century, 12 to 18% of our coastal areas could be submerged by sea level rise, affecting the livelihoods of tens of millions. Climate change has caused loss and damage equivalent to 1% of our GDP. And our food security is at serious risk”

— Tarique Rahman, prime minister of Bangladesh

THE SITUATION: The low-lying geography of Bangladesh makes it one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change.

___

THE QUOTE: “Cabo Verde speaks with the same voice as other countries that are also living the climate crisis every day. For us, climate change is not a distant risk. It is an existential reality affecting our economies, our food and water security, our coastlines and ultimately our people’s future.”

— Francisco Carvalho, prime minister of Cape Verde

THE SITUATION: Cape Verde, like other small island developing states, is grappling with rising sea levels and increasingly powerful storms that erode shorelines, submerge land and threaten homes and livelihoods.

___

THE QUOTE: “Nearly a third of the world’s tuna is caught in Pacific waters. And it’s moving east into the high seas. More than a quarter of our people live within a kilometer of the shore. Six of our communities have already moved. Two more are moving now. And half a degree is not a rounding error. For us, it is the difference between adaptation and relocation.”

— Naiqama Lalabalavu, president of Fiji

THE SITUATION: Lalabalavu cited projections that by 2050, the fish available to each Fijian is projected to fall by nearly a quarter, from 41 kilograms (90 pounds) a year to about 31. And more than half of that loss comes from climate change, he said.

___

THE QUOTE: “The climate crisis is often referred to as a ‘global group project shared by all 8 billion people on Earth.’ A single country cannot tackle this challenge alone. At the same time, abandoning growth cannot bring everyone on board.”

— Lee Jae Myung, president of Korea

THE SITUATION: The impact of extreme weather worsened by climate change is far-reaching in South Korea. Farmers face higher costs and must use more labor to produce the same or lower yields.

___

THE QUOTE: “We live in a fragmented world. Nations are turning inward. Promises are made loudly and kept quietly, if at all. Each country is tempted to say: It is not my storm, not my coastline, not my problem. The ocean does not recognize that thinking. It is one body of water. What warms in one hemisphere breaks upon another. The sea has never been fragmented. Only we are.”

— Philip Davis, prime minister of the Bahamas

THE SITUATION: Like many other countries in the Global South, Bahamas has a lot of debt from warming-connected weather disasters. Hurricane Dorian, the strongest storm to hit the country on record, caused $3.4 billion in damage in 2019.

___

THE QUOTE: “For those who have declared climate change a hoax perpetrated by geopolitical opponents, the warnings of recent times cannot have been clearer. Melting glaciers, flash flooding, droughts, record-breaking heatwaves, brush fires, hurricanes and other extreme weather phenomena are unmistakable signals of an overburdened planet. Climate change is the ultimate test of global equity.”

— John Dramani Mahama, president of Ghana

THE SITUATION: Ghana faces erratic rainfall, erosion of its coastal towns and accelerating desertification. In June, Mahama said Ghana and coastal West Africa were hit with unprecedented torrential rain that killed 39 people.

text:
The granting of environmental approval for two Queensland renewable energy projects has propelled the Albanese Government past two major milestones, with more than 150 renewable energy projects Australia-wide, including 50 Queensland projects, approved since the May 2022 election.

The 150 projects will generate enough energy to power every home in Australia, reducing greenhouse gas emissions by over 84 million tonnes of carbon dioxide each year which is the equivalent of taking 27.6 million passenger cars off the road.

The projects have also pumped tens of billions of dollars into the national economy.

The projects are located right across the nation and include 64 solar farms, 34 onshore wind farms, 20 energy storage systems, 18 infrastructure and exploration projects (including for offshore wind farms) and 14 transmission projects.

The Bungaban Solar Project in Queensland’s Western Downs region, a joint venture between Windlab and Squadron Energy, was the 150th project to be given the green light, while the neighbouring Bungaban Wind Farm was the 152nd (and 50th Queensland renewables project) to get the green light.

The 500-megawatt solar project was given the green light in just 20 business days after choosing a site on previously cleared and environmentally degraded land.

The 1400-megawatt wind farm received approval following a rigorous assessment process and must follow strict conditions to minimise its potential environmental impact.

Together the Australian-owned projects will reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 4.92 million tonnes of carbon dioxide annually, equivalent to taking 1.83 million cars off the road each year.

The 50th Queensland project, Bungaban Wind Farm, is on the National Renewable Energy Priority List and a successful tenderer under the Government’s Capacity Investment Scheme.

It will also deliver a big economic boost for the region, creating around 1000 jobs at peak construction, 50 ongoing jobs, and injecting around $500 million into the local economy.

Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt said hitting the century and a half milestone showed the Government was delivering a pipeline of reliable, renewable energy to power Australian homes and industry.

“Renewable energy is the cheapest and cleanest form of energy, and these 150 projects are creating jobs, unlocking investment and reducing emissions right across the country,” Minister Watt said.

“The Bungaban projects demonstrate the renewable energy transition in action, with the wind farm expected to help power the Boyne aluminium smelter in Gladstone, as it shifts from coal-powered power to cheaper, cleaner energy.

“These are exactly the type of job creating projects that simply wouldn’t go ahead under the Coalition’s plan to cut investment in energy, which would only drive up power bills.

“Our landmark environmental reforms will continue to help the renewables transition by making approvals faster, clearer and more predictable, while delivering better environmental outcomes.”

text:
Japanese automaker Honda Motor Co. (HMC.US) is reportedly in the final preparation stage to build a brand-new hybrid vehicle production plant in Ohio, with production expected to begin as early as 2030. The total investment ranges from ¥300 billion to ¥400 billion (approximately $1.9 billion to $2.5 billion), reflecting Honda's accelerating shift in North American production strategy from pure electric vehicles toward hybrid models.

Market sources indicate that Honda has not yet made a formal announcement regarding the new plant, and a spokesperson for American Honda declined to confirm details. However, Honda executives have repeatedly stated publicly that North American production capacity is nearing saturation and that the company indeed needs a new plant to expand output. Ohio has long been a key production hub for Honda in the United States, and its selection once again demonstrates Honda's enduring confidence in the state's supply chain and workforce.

Tariff Pressures Drive Localized Production

Honda's accelerated push to build a U.S. plant is closely tied to shifts in American trade policy. In August of this year, the U.S. government announced that starting January 2027, it would impose a 50% tariff on automobiles imported from Canada—double the current rate. Honda currently exports certain models from Japan and Canada to the U.S. market, and higher tariff barriers will inevitably squeeze export profit margins.

Honda Executive Vice President Noriya Kaihara warned last year that if the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) were not extended, the company might need to reassess its investment direction in North America. The plan to locate the new plant in Ohio represents a concrete move by Honda to mitigate tariff risks through local production amid heightened trade uncertainty.

The United States is Honda's largest single market globally, accounting for roughly 40% of total sales. Last fiscal year, Honda sold 1.41 million vehicles in the U.S., and hybrid demand has remained strong this year, with sales outperforming the same period last year. Existing plants have very limited room for additional output.

Strategic Pivot from EVs to Hybrids

Honda's electrification roadmap has taken a notable turn in recent years. The next-generation electric vehicles originally slated for North American launch starting in 2026 have been scrapped. The company has also indefinitely shelved an $11 billion EV and battery production project in Canada and canceled three EV models intended for the U.S. market.

Behind these decisions lies the heavy toll Honda has absorbed in the EV space. The company has cumulatively recognized more than $9 billion in restructuring costs related to its EV business. Combined with pricing pressure from Chinese competitors, Honda reported its first annual loss in seventy years in May.

Honda CEO Toshihiro Mibe stated bluntly at the June shareholders' meeting that battery-electric vehicle market share in the U.S. is far below company expectations. He warned that if the company continued with its original EV sales plan, "the overall automobile business would remain in operating losses for at least five years, possibly as long as seven." He emphasized that this would place the company in an extremely precarious long-term position.

To reverse the decline, Honda is redirecting resources toward hybrids, where it holds competitive advantages, with plans to launch 15 new hybrid models by March 2030, primarily targeting the North American market. Starting this year, Honda has discontinued sales of its only pure EV model in the U.S., the Prologue SUV, and has shifted production of the Civic hybrid from Japan to Indiana for direct supply to the U.S. market.

Software Collaboration and Future Plans

While adjusting its powertrain strategy, Honda is also actively positioning itself in the software-defined vehicle space. Honda and Nissan are reportedly advancing joint development of a central electronic control unit (ECU), targeting commonized components in vehicles around 2029. Mibe has publicly confirmed that the two companies are in discussions on this collaboration.

If the planned Ohio plant comes online as scheduled in 2030, it will become a critical pillar of Honda's U.S. hybrid production capacity. From tariff avoidance and capacity expansion to product strategy transformation, Honda's North American footprint is entering a new phase centered on hybrid vehicles.

text:
Colorado will receive $250 million from the federal government to support a key transmission corridor connecting western states to Texas as part of a national push by the Trump administration to buttress America’s strained energy grid.

Gov. Jared Polis said Thursday that the grant to Colorado — the single largest investment that’s part of $1.9 billion in new spending by the U.S. Department of Energy — will benefit 10 million ratepayers across Colorado, Texas and New Mexico.

“And what does ‘benefit’ mean? It means increased reliability and lower rates,” Polis said during a news conference at the Arapahoe County Fairgrounds, while flanked by state, federal and private sector energy leaders.

The money will go toward a major Xcel Energy project that will move the Colorado side of the Texas grid connector from its current location in Lamar to the May Valley substation in southeastern Colorado. Doing so, officials say, will better link the country’s western and eastern energy grids.

The federal grant will cover about 20% of the project’s overall $1.2 billion cost, the rest of which Xcel will pay for.

The project includes replacing aging equipment and power lines to support greater energy transmission. Officials say the investments will more than triple the amount of electricity that can move between the two regional grids from 210 megawatts to 700 megawatts — and eventually up to 2,000 megawatts — as demand grows.

The announcement comes as Xcel Energy customers are expected to see a roughly $5 monthly increase to their energy bills in the coming months to help pay for a suite of upgrades to Xcel’s power supply system. The company has also faced a list of complaints from developers over electricity delays for new projects.

Xcel Energy-Colorado President Robert Kenney said modernizing the existing Colorado-to-Texas grid corridor is “first and foremost a reliability project” that’s aimed at replacing “aging infrastructure with modern, proven technology.”

In total, 31 projects across 26 states are slated to receive a slice of the $1.9 billion in federal funding. That will be matched by $3.35 billion from project recipients, resulting in about $5.2 billion in total investments. Together, the projects are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity — enough to power 16 million homes.

Rather than creating new infrastructure, the money is targeted at rehabilitating the nation’s energy grid.

“These projects are about getting more out of the infrastructure we already have, and doing it faster,” said Tim Walsh, the assistant secretary for the Energy Department’s Office of Environmental Management.

The projects receiving money nationally will use new technologies such as sensors and other devices to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested or overloaded paths, the Energy Department said. The upgrades could improve power reliability and lower electricity costs for about 100 million Americans, according to officials.

Walsh said the federal funding awards for power grid upgrades build on President Donald Trump’s “Unleashing American Energy” executive order.

The money comes from the bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, signed by then- President Joe Biden in 2021, which Trump at the time opposed.

Walsh and other officials stressed that data centers — a growing, power-hungry sector — must pay for their own electricity.

The investments announced Thursday come at a critical time for the nation’s energy grid, which continues to face growing demand driven largely by the artificial intelligence boom and the proliferation of massive data centers.

Walsh said Trump, an avid supporter of AI and data centers, said the administration was focused on “leading the globe in innovation,” which is why the country needs “to increase our AI data centers.”

But, he added: “We’re not putting them where communities don’t want them.”

Kenney said Xcel has a proposal pending before the state’s Public Utilities Commission aimed at ensuring data centers don’t force their energy costs onto consumers.

Will Toor, the executive director of the Colorado Energy Office, added that the Xcel grid project in southeastern Colorado was contemplated even before the rise of large data centers, saying that energy demands had been building for at least a decade.

“We’ve needed expanded transmission and, in particular, we’ve needed expanded interregional transmission linking the Colorado grid and the eastern grid,” he said.

The Associated Press contributed to this story.

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senators Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) today introduced the Critical Mineral Executive Coordination Act, which aims to strengthen the United States’ ability to address vulnerabilities in global critical mineral supply chains by improving diplomatic training and executive branch coordination. Sens. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Chris Coons (D-Del.), and John Curtis (R-Utah) joined in introducing the bill. With China controlling a majority of rare earth minerals, this legislation would support a more comprehensive critical minerals strategy and bolster U.S. economic and national security interests.

“Critical minerals are the building blocks for advanced technology. From powering our cellphones to our nation’s most advanced weapons systems, they are essential to America’s national security,” said Sen. Scott. “The Critical Mineral Executive Coordination Act supports our efforts to safeguard access to critical minerals, bolstering our national defense, energy security, and economic competitiveness. America’s future should be driven by American strength, and this bill helps make sure the U.S. – not China – leads the way.”

“Georgia’s transformative contributions to national defense and technological advancement call for streamlined access to global critical mineral markets,” said Sen. Rev. Warnock. “This bipartisan bill addresses alarming vulnerabilities by educating our federal workers and diplomats on the importance of securing our nation’s critical mineral supply chains and how to better support our domestic industries.”

“We need critical minerals to build chips for everything from our smartphones to our national defense apparatus. The U.S. must not cede control of global critical mineral supply chains to China,” said Sen. Kaine. “That is why I’m glad to cosponsor this bipartisan legislation to establish a dedicated executive branch critical minerals czar and marshal our diplomatic corps’ expertise in this area. This commonsense and overdue step is crucial to our national security and retaining our technological edge, and I encourage my colleagues on both sides of the aisle and in both chambers to support this legislation.”

“With the People’s Republic of China controlling global critical minerals supply chains, the United States needs a durable strategy to secure reliable access to the resources that power our modern economy,” said Sen. Rosen. “I am proud to help introduce this bipartisan bill to make sure our government has the training, skill, and supply chains necessary to maintain and grow the United States’ critical mineral leadership and ensure we’re not just playing catch-up to China.”

House Foreign Affairs East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee Chair Young Kim (R-Calif.-40) and Representative Ami Bera, M.D. (D-Calif.-06) introduced the House companion legislation.

“America cannot allow Beijing to maintain its chokehold on the critical minerals that power our economy, our defense, and our modern lives. The DOMINANCE Act provides the long-term strategy and tools needed to break that chokehold, which is why it passed both the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House with strong bipartisan support,” said Rep. Kim. “I thank Senator Scott for introducing the Critical Mineral Executive Coordination Act, which advances two key provisions of the DOMINANCE Act, and I look forward to working with him to get our bill to the President’s desk before the end of the year.”

“Strengthening America’s critical mineral supply chains is essential to our economic and national security,” said Rep. Bera. “I’m encouraged to see the Senate continue the bipartisan work we advanced through the House-passed DOMINANCE Act. I appreciate Senators Scott and Warnock’s leadership in carrying forward key provisions that will strengthen our diplomatic expertise and improve coordination across the federal government.”

The Critical Mineral Executive Coordination Act would establish a Foreign Service Institute training program to equip Foreign Service Officers with the resources they need to advance both economic and national security interests in relation to critical minerals and strategic competition with China.

The bill would also establish a permanent position of special advisor to the president for critical minerals and supply chains within the National Security Council, facilitating a coordinated, government-wide strategy to secure America’s critical mineral supply.

text:
“Keep Me In Your Heart” was written by Warren Zevon and appears as the 11th song on his 12th and final studio album, The Wind. The song is a tender and heartfelt farewell to Zevon’s loved ones, asking them to remember him fondly without grief after he was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer. It was the only track on The Wind composed entirely after his diagnosis. The song has been covered by Eddie Vedder, Willie Nelson and Jorge Calderon. Personnel on the record were: Warren Zevon (vocals), Jorge Calderon (acoustic guitar, lead acoustic guitar, bass) and Jim Keltner (drums).

The Wind was recorded from September to December 2002 at Cherokee Studios, Sunset Sound, Groovemasters, Hensen Recording Studios, Masterlink Studios, Fanboy Studios, The Cave, and Snakepit, Billy Bob Thornton's home studio in Los Angeles. Produced by Jorge Calderon, Noah Scot Snyder and Warren Zevon, the album was released in August 2003. It went to #1 on the Billboard Top Independent and #12 on the Billboard 200 Albums charts, and has been certified Gold by the Recording Industry Association of America. It won two Grammy Awards and three nominations. Two singles were released from the LP.

Warren Zevon was an American rock singer, songwriter and musician. His father, William “Slumpy” Zevon, worked for Los Angeles mobster Mickey Cohen. Warren Zevon quit high school at 16 and drove a sportscar his father won in a card game to New York City to pursue a career as a songwriter and folk singer in 1964. He released his first record, as part of the folk duo Lyme & Cybele, “Follow Me,” in April 1966. He spent time as a jingle writer and session musician before releasing his Kim Fowley-assisted debut studio album, Wanted Dead or Alive, in April 1970. He released 12 studio albums, three live albums, seven compilation albums, and 32 singles. He also wrote hit songs for Linda Ronstadt and Terri Clark. Friend and fan David Letterman dedicated a whole 90-minute show of Late Night with David Letterman to Zevon performing his songs. Letterman asked him if he had learned anything about life and death, to which Zevon responded: “to enjoy every sandwich.” He was inducted posthumously into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame by Letterman in November 2025. Zevon died at his home in Los Angeles in September 2003 at 56.

text:
Clean Energy Fuels Corp. has completed the sale of $30.7 million in federal tax credits generated by seven renewable natural gas production facilities, marking the company’s fourth transaction monetizing credits from its RNG projects.

The largest component of the transaction was a $26 million investment tax credit tied to South Fork Dairy, Clean Energy’s RNG production facility in Dimmit, Texas. The facility began producing renewable natural gas in 2025.

The transaction also included all of the Section 45Z clean fuel production credits generated during 2025 by Clean Energy’s portfolio of dairy RNG projects.

Those credits came from seven facilities located across Texas, South Dakota, Iowa and Minnesota, including projects operated through Clean Energy’s joint ventures with bp and TotalEnergies.

Together, the projects produced 2.7 million gallons of negative carbon-intensity RNG for transportation fleets in 2025. Clean Energy develops dairy RNG projects by capturing methane from organic waste and processing it into transportation fuel.

“This is our largest ITC sale to date and a strong result for our RNG business,” said Will Flanagan, vice president of strategic development at Clean Energy. “Successfully monetizing our full portfolio speaks to the value of these projects and the increasing demand for the environmental benefits they deliver.”

The $30.7 million transaction demonstrates another financing mechanism available to Clean Energy as it develops and operates RNG production assets. Rather than retaining the federal tax benefits generated by eligible projects, the company can monetize those credits through sales and convert them into capital.

The South Fork Dairy credit represents the majority of the latest transaction. Its $26 million investment tax credit accounts for approximately 85% of the total credits sold, with the remaining value coming from the portfolio’s 2025 Section 45Z credits.

The sale also reflects Clean Energy’s strategy of combining RNG production with its transportation fueling operations. The company operates RNG production facilities at dairy farms while maintaining a network of fueling stations across the United States and Canada.

Its fuel is used by transportation fleets including airport shuttles, municipal buses, waste collection vehicles and heavy-duty trucks.

Clean Energy has increasingly built its RNG supply through production projects in addition to distributing the fuel through its station network. Partnerships with major energy companies have also become part of that development strategy, with some of the seven facilities included in the latest tax credit transaction held through joint ventures with bp and TotalEnergies.

The completed sale is Clean Energy’s fourth tax credit monetization transaction involving its RNG portfolio and its largest investment tax credit sale to date.

Nasdaq-listed Clean Energy Fuels is focused on producing and supplying renewable natural gas for the transportation market, using methane captured from organic waste as a feedstock. The latest transaction converts federal incentives generated by seven of those production facilities into $30.7 million for the company.

text:
Even as clean energy remained the largest employment sector in the US energy industry in 2025, accounting for more than 3.5 million of the sector’s 8.4 million workers, E2 reported that the sector lost nearly 37,000 jobs during the year.

According to E2’s analysis of US Department of Energy (DOE) data, solar, wind, energy efficiency, clean vehicles and other clean energy sectors went from adding about 100,000 jobs annually in recent years to recording a loss of 36,949 jobs in 2025. This represents nearly 40% of all new jobs created in 2024 (see US Clean Energy Jobs Expanded In 2024; Growth Expected To Slow).

Analysts point out that this was the first time since the pandemic that companies cut jobs in solar, wind, energy efficiency and other clean energy sectors.

Analysts said the decline came in the first year of the Trump administration’s policy actions affecting the clean energy sector.

E2 says the clean energy job loss last year was impacted by the July 2025 passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) under which the administration rolled back tax incentives and programs for clean energy manufacturing, generation and job creation (see US Clean Energy Cancellations Cost $68B In Investments).

Michael Timberlake, E2 Director of Research, said, “America’s clean energy jobs boom didn’t just slow in 2025—it went into reverse. After four consecutive years of strong growth, the industry lost nearly 37,000 jobs—its first decline since the pandemic.”

The largest job loss in the clean energy space last year was visible in clean vehicles with 9,619 jobs lost while renewable generation segment lost 11,584 jobs, and energy efficiency 21,443.

Storage and grid, on the other hand, reported 3.2% growth over the year with the addition of 5,346 jobs.

Clean energy job loss was seen in 35 states, with California leading with almost 21,000 job cuts, followed by Illinois, and Maryland. Florida led the states gained 3,800 positions.

The job losses followed a sharp decline in clean energy project activity tracked by E2 in 2025. Companies canceled or scaled back 142 manufacturing, generation and storage projects, representing $57.8 billion in lost investment and 84,400 expected jobs. Including these canceled positions, total existing and planned job losses exceeded 120,000 in 2025.

On the other hand, oil and gas companies employ 958,000 workers, coal companies 125,000 and nuclear 70,000, according to the analysis.
