name: American Energy
title: A Sunny Week in New York - by Bill McKibben
description:
It is a bold call for dramatically accelerating the pace at which we roll out solar energy around the world.
First, we must build clean power for everyone.
It takes just $15 to give access to clean electricity for one person for a generation.
By the time advocates gather for next year’s New York Climate Week, the landscape may be very different.
But while Pakistan’s rapid, bottom-up solar shift offers a hopeful model for ramping up clean energy, it also offers a warning.
text:
My watch, which tells me lots of things I don’t necessarily want to know (I scored a depressing 56 out of 100 on my sleep last night) informs me I’ve taken 112,000 steps around the city of New York in the last four days, not to mention a considerable number of miles on the B, M, 6, and 3 trains. It’s all been interesting, but a literal and figurative high point came yesterday, on 6th St between Avenue C and D. On this block, in 1982 shortly after his eviction from the White House, Jimmy Carter began his post-presidential career as a Habitat for Humanity volunteer, rehabilitating a six-story apartment building across the street.

I know the number of stories, because I got to carry a solar panel up them, part of the project to make the building even more affordable for its inhabitants.

And the pleasure of that project underscored the best part of the week—the hope for practical solutions even as our overlords dithered and tussled at the UN and in the other corridors of political power. I’d gone to the Lower East Side straight from Solar One, the nonprofit clean-energy outpost on the East River in whose grand new building we’d had an excellent discussion of the rapid spread of balcony solar across the country. Pictured below is State Sen. Ray Ward of Utah, who ushered in the country’s first balcony solar law, now followed by a rough dozen other state legislatures this spring (we’re still waiting for Governors Hochul and Newsom to sign the laws their assemblies have approved).

But of course those hopeful sprouts aren’t going to bloom fast enough at the current pace to put the planet on a new trajectory. The cynical men that run America’s energy policy currently were in town, underlining the trouble. Chris Wright, the Secretary of Highly Expensive Energy, was over at the Times and HeatMap, explaining that despite the pledge of his boss, the US was not going to ban diesel exports, just “tweak where diesel flows out of U.S. refineries.” He also explained to the Times again that “Every day, actually, the sun goes down, it doesn’t produce power at all.” That the man in charge of America’s energy policy is purposefully blinding himself to the rise in batteries across the country—the single most important energy development of his term—is sad but not shocking; he is and always will be a fracking executive, not a patriot. And he won’t be stopped unless we stop him.

What’s missing here in New York is activism. The marches of past years are not boe be seen, though I did get to speak at a small but important rally outside Amazon’s NY headquarters near Bryant Park, scolding them for proposing the country’s biggest source of pollution near Pecos TX. (“Forget Amazon Prime. It’s Amazon Crime—climate crime”). And without a movement to force action, it’s hard to imagine how we manage to really speed up the shifts that have begun but must come faster. I got to listen to Mayor Mamdani speak this morning at a New School conference. From a few feet away, I can assure you he was as charismatic as you’ve been told, and he is good at the necessary task of avoiding specific questions. But he is an organizer at heart, and he took note of how the data center rebellion is offering real openings. Most of the people out at those zoning meetings were, he said, new to political movements; it’s “an opportunity to bring someone into a movement to say that the reason that you are opposed to this — the things that you're worried about in your life — that's what others feel the same about. You are actually part of something bigger than yourself.”

Which brings us to the mural pictured below, tucked under the High Line over on the edge of Chelsea. It’s an early project of newly formed Brightside, which also spearheaded the release of a letter yesterday signed by some of the world’s climate leaders, everyone from Bernie to Jane Fonda to Muhammad Mustafa Amjad of Renewables First who has helped lead Pakistan’s remarkable solar revolution. It is a bold call for dramatically accelerating the pace at which we roll out solar energy around the world.

First, we must build clean power for everyone. For the first time ever we can reliably bring electricity to the 1 in 10 people on earth living without regular access.

We ask everyone who can afford it to donate something so that others can turn the lights on for studying, cooking, and medical care - and never have to think about a gallon of diesel or gas again. It takes just $15 to give access to clean electricity for one person for a generation.

Second, we need to build clean power everywhere, and to make that happen we need to build a movement powerful and beautiful enough to force governments to take large-scale action.

Individual steps alone are not enough: too many of our leaders will resist action, until we demonstrate together how much we want them to move. We must demand that governments stop building coal, oil, and gas projects we no longer need, and start building the clean-energy systems that works - no pollution or wars required.

One important day along this path will be 20 June, as the summer solstice approaches in the Northern Hemisphere, generating the most solar power of any day on earth yet. We will celebrate that day as Sun Day, coming together to celebrate and accelerate this great shift.

I got to write about this new initiative in the Guardian yesterday.

There is one solitary (and very literal) ray of sunshine amidst this gloom: the steady rise of solar, wind and batteries. That clean energy trinity has broken out of its Chinese base and over the last few years expanded quickly across the planet – from Karachi to California to Cuba, solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown. It’s even begun to demonstrate that it can drive emissions down: China seems to have started on its downward slope years before most thought it could, and California has cut the use of gas to produce electricity in half in the world’s fourth-largest economy.

None of it is happening fast enough to catch up with the physics of global warming, though – which is precisely why civil society will now try to double down on this one bright spot, and push for a rapid acceleration of clean energy; this transition is going fast, but it needs to go much faster. And it can – China and India are using barely half their solar panel factory capacity, and too many countries are hedging their bets, using clean energy as additional power instead of replacing fossil fuels.

By the time advocates gather for next year’s New York Climate Week, the landscape may be very different. The physical landscape (there is, I fear, no doubt that El Niño will change the literal map of the world), and the political landscape. If a resurgent movement demands action, we finally have the tools to make that demand matter – a working planet that runs mostly on sun and wind is in tantalizing reach. At the last possible moment, with backs to the wall, we still have our face to the sun.

Every advance we’ve made in the climate fight has come from some combination of engineering and activism. Without pressure from civil society, we wouldn’t have gotten the Paris accords (there were 400,000 people in the streets of New York in September of 2014) nor the promises, now mostly abrogated, from banks and corporations (Greta Thunberg spoke to 250,000 in lower Manhattan in September 2019). We need more pressure. I’ll be talking to you about Sun Day in the months ahead—once we’re past the midterms, it will be time to build that pressure again, here and around the world.

For now, time to get back on the campaign trail. I came to New York from Iowa, and am leaving this evening for Pennsylvania, ready to knock on doors and help Third Act rally voters. If you happen to be in the area come join us, but by all means find somewhere else to help. From now through November 3 our greatest leverage is electoral; after that, back to the streets

Share

In other energy and climate news:

+Speaking of Mayor Mamdani, Ayana Johnson, with a bit of help from me, has an excellent chat with Luise Yeung, the mayor’s chief climate officer. The city—even without the federal dollars that would let scaling be much easier—is doing an enormous amount of interesting stuff. Battery-powered food carts! Also my rapper name revealed.

+A call from Katherine Hayhoe and Dana Fisher for bipartisan conversation on climate

We know that climate shocks, like the ones we’ve experienced this summer, open windows of opportunity: people who live through climate change-exacerbated extreme events are more supportive of climate science and climate action and are more civically and politically engaged. On this warming planet, we all need to learn from what the few who are talking about climate change are already doing. Research has shown that friends and family are trusted messengers who can initiate a pro-climate conversation loop. We all need to become climate communicators and stop letting those who want to delay climate action as long as possible polarize it and silence us.

+Big win in the EU, as Brussels confirmed—against Norwegian pressure—its ban on Arctic oil drilling. As Marta Pacheco reports

Norway has described gas exploration in the Arctic as insurance for the EU as the bloc grapples with rising energy prices. Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron is calling a G7 meeting on energy, where a second release of emergency oil stocks could be discussed.

Pressuring the EU to reconsider its position, Minister Aasland recently said that “continued activity in the Barents Sea serves both Norwegian and European interests”, citing disruption to global energy markets following the war in the Middle East. He also said Norway would continue drilling in the Arctic regardless of the EU’s position.

The issue is particularly sensitive for Brussels because Norway is deeply embedded in the EU’s energy security architecture. Recent shocks, including a damaged pipeline in Saudi Arabia, have highlighted how quickly Europe can be exposed when supplies from other producing regions are disrupted.

With Russian pipeline gas largely pushed out of the European market, Norway has become the EU’s largest LNG supplier, accounting for 54.4% of total EU imports between January and June, up from 52.1% in 2025, according to EU data.

Environmental activists, however, argue that Norwegian Arctic gas accounts for just 1.4% of EU gas imports and is unlikely to make a significant difference to near-term energy security. Gas from the New Barents Sea would not come online until 2045, too late to address the EU’s immediate needs, according to a new WWF-Norway analysis.

+Photographers: apply for the first James Balog Vision Award—top prize is $40,000. Balog, of course, is the great chronicler of climate change, above all its disappearing ice, and he wants the work to continue.

The Awards are intended to recognize the winning artists’ direct engagement with the world around us. Images may be literal and documentary or symbolic and interpretive. They may be of impacts that are positive and inspiring, or negative and distressing, or both.

+Under Keir Starmer, the UK’s Labour government refused to release a report from the country’s intelligence agencies detailing the danger of climate change to food security in particular. Now that Ed Miliband is the foreign secretary in the new government, the wraps have come off, and we’re seeing the kind of transparency we’re going to need in a fast-heating world

The UK has warned countries around the world that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their national security and defence, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of a report suppressed under Keir Starmer.

Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, made a presentation to the foreign ministers of the EU as well as Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, based on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages.

+The ever-active Charles Komanoff offers an essay on why he’s hoping for hundreds of nuclear power plants around the US. A longtime advocate of carbon taxes, Komanoff insists that reactor prices will be coming down. He couples it with a little jabbing at “mediocre” renewable energy. His thesis will get all the boost it could hope for from the Trump administration, which has been banning sun and wind even while bankrolling huge subsidies for nuclear. Yesterday the head of TerraPower told a Climate Week audience that their first plant, backed by Bill Gates and billionaire friends, might come online by 2031

+A federal judge has restored $7 billion in Solar for All funding that the Trump administration had confiscated. As Ethan Howland reports

“When an agency acts outside the bounds of its statutory authority, it violates the [Administrative Procedure Act],” Judge Mary McElroy, a Trump-appointed judge with the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island, wrote in her ruling.

She said that contrary to the government’s argument, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law July 4, 2025, did not convert Solar for All funding into “a lump-sum amount subject to EPA’s discretion.”…

“For more than a year, families and communities have seen higher energy bills while billions of dollars intended to lower electricity costs sat out of reach. Today’s decision makes clear that EPA unlawfully terminated the Solar for All Program,” Jillian Blanchard, senior vice president of climate change and environmental justice at Lawyers for Good Government, said in a statement.

+The network of Green Banks across the country receive less attention than they should—but a new report makes clear their growing importance

As electricity prices surge and power grids face unprecedented strain, green banking plays a critical role in filling gaps in clean energy funding. Green Banks are mission-driven lenders and community partners that provide capital and technical assistance to unlock clean energy projects that traditional lenders and investors often ignore because they are too small or unconventional.

Green Banks close the capital gap and get clean energy to underserved communities quickly — lowering household energy bills, addressing rapid data center and commercial load growth, and catalyzing equitable, place-based economic development in low-income and disadvantaged communities. The GB 50’s new Impact Report shows that Green Banks are having a significant impact across the country. Since their inception, GB 50’s member Green Banks have supported nearly $30 billion in total project investment nationwide, deploying more than $5.16 billion of their own capital and mobilizing nearly $25 billion in private capital across more than 180,000 projects in dozens of states.

It also includes this pretty shocking statistic, which should help you understand American politics circa 2026:

Over the past three years, U.S. residential electricity prices rose by about 14%, leaving 1 in 4 households behind on utility bills.

+From Jan Rosenow, a very fine account of the solar wave in the developing world, and the strains that develop as more and more people figure out how to leave the grid

Pakistan is probably the most dramatic and well-known case of a bottom-up solar revolution, but it is not unique, and versions of the same story are unfolding across the world right now: Countries with hot climates, fast-growing economies, expensive energy, and fragile grids are increasingly turning to solar. Not because of policy, but because individuals are voting with their wallets. In six developing nations — Pakistan, Nigeria, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Zambia, and Yemen — recorded solar generation has grown more than sixfold since 2019. Solar’s share of the electricity mix has risen sharply in each of them, in some cases by an order of magnitude.

But while Pakistan’s rapid, bottom-up solar shift offers a hopeful model for ramping up clean energy, it also offers a warning. The proliferation of household solar in Pakistan has led to an exodus from the national grid, rattling the network while saddling the poorest ratepayers — who cannot afford solar panels — with higher bills. Similar dynamics are now at play in Nigeria and Zambia. These countries are facing a boom and a crisis at the same time.

As Rosenow points out, the answer is not to slow down the solar boom. Instead:

An important task for governments and international agencies is to bring distributed solar into official energy statistics, using import data, registrations, and, where necessary, satellite monitoring. Think tanks such as Ember in the U.K. and Renewables First in Pakistan are already piecing this picture together from customs data. Governments need to use that data for planning. With a clearer picture of what is happening on the ground, officials can begin to integrate fast-growing solar capacity into the power system and do it in a way that strengthens the grid rather than undermines it. That means installing batteries that can store cheap solar during the day for use in the evening. It means building more flexible transmission networks that can move surplus rooftop power to where it is needed instead of wasting it. And it means offering targeted support for low-income households to make solar affordable for more people.

+Zoe Wood with an interesting and important new finding—though it comes from Britain, I’m willing to bet it’s universal:

Motorists buying a secondhand car with a lot of miles on the clock are likely to find an electric vehicle (EV) ultimately more reliable than a petrol vehicle, according to a study.

An analysis of 47.4m MOT tests found that after cars were driven 90,000 to 120,000 miles, EVs were about 25% less likely to fail than petrol models of the same age (based on a failure rate of 16.5% versus 22.1%).

Beyond 120,000 miles, 16% of EVs failed, compared with 23.5% of petrol cars.

+From Mark Hertsgaard and Covering Climate Now, an interview with California governor Gavin Newsom, which gives a heads-up that the “climate-hushing” era among Democrats is coming to an end. Newsom is just the latest Dem to say something like this:

“People say, ‘Why are you talking about climate change? You should be talking about kitchen table [issues],’ Newsom said. “I say, ‘I am. You haven’t connected the droughts to the cost of beef, to the cost of coffee? You have to connect climate risk with financial risk, with our trade policy. These are kitchen table issues.”

Extra bonus content:

Newsom “totally rejected” criticisms by Bill McKibben and other climate activists that his administration has slowed expansion of rooftop solar in California by lowering net metering payments to homeowners with rooftop solar. Those payments, Newsom argued, “were subsidizing Wall Street hedge funds” and boosting electricity costs for Californians who “can least afford it.” The solar industry, he added, is now “a mature industry that needs to start to stand on its own,” without subsidies.

Kind of sad that he unmasked my hedge fund commitments, but hey, you can’t become a billionaire writing free newsletters!

+Check this out: a 30-seat electric plane just flew a half hour route in upstate New York…on five bucks worth of electricity.

The aircraft reached 1,100 feet with one pilot aboard and no passengers. The flight marked the first time the company had put the X1 in the air.

The 30-seat plane is 76 feet long and has a 106-foot wingspan. It weighs more than 25,000 pounds. Heart says it is the largest fully battery-powered aircraft yet flown. “With the first flight of X1, Heart Aerospace has demonstrated electric flight at the scale of a commercial airliner,” Heart Founder and CEO Anders Forslund said in a statement.

Meanwhile, commercial utilization of sails to power cargo ships is quickly moving past the pilot phase.

One of the biggest came this month from Maersk. The company plans to install a 35-meter rotor sail on one of its 8,700-TEU containerships, with testing expected to begin in 2027 on regular Atlantic services.

The project is expected to mark the first rotor sail installation on a containership.

Rotor sails look more like giant vertical cylinders than traditional sails. They spin as wind passes around them, creating aerodynamic lift through the Magnus effect and generating thrust that reduces the load on the ship’s engines.

The concept is more than a century old, but modern controls and materials are making it practical on ships of a scale that would once have been difficult to imagine.

title: Exclusive-BP eyes Devon Energy asset amid renewed US M&A ambitions, sources say | live
description:

text:
By David French and Arathy Somasekhar

NEW YORK/HOUSTON, Sept 24 (Reuters) - BP is weighing a potential acquisition of Devon Energy's operations in South Texas as part of renewed efforts by the British supermajor to grow its shale asset base in the US, people familiar with the matter said.

After years of prioritizing investments in renewable energy and leadership churn that included five chief executives since 2020, London-headquartered BP has reverted to a strategy that places its traditional oil and gas business at its heart.

Since Meg O'Neill joined as CEO in April, BP has entered the data room on a small number of shale assets placed for sale by their owners, allowing the company access to confidential information provided to prospective buyers so they can evaluate the merits of a deal, according to six sources.

BP has targeted predominantly oil-producing assets with valuations of between $2 billion and $5 billion, three of the sources said.

This includes Devon Energy's Eagle Ford asset, which opened its data room in late August, said three of the sources. Analysts at TPH Research said in a note on Wednesday the asset could be worth around $4.5 billion.

The sources cautioned that entering a data room does not guarantee that BP will formally bid on an asset. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations.

Shares in Devon extended gains in the wake of the Reuters report, and closed 1.8% higher on Thursday. Devon has risen around 34% this year, per LSEG data.

BP declined comment. Devon did not respond to a comment request.

BPX ENERGY

BP's US shale operations are held within its BPX Energy unit, with assets in the Eagle Ford, Permian and Haynesville basins spanning Texas and Louisiana. Production in the second quarter was around 545,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd), of which its existing Eagle Ford was approximately 205,000 boepd, according to an August presentation.

The company is targeting over 650,000 boepd from BPX by 2030, according to BP's website.

Despite its strategic pivot back to oil and gas, previously overseen by Albert Manifold before he was fired as chair and replaced on a permanent basis earlier this month by Ian Tyler, BP has spent the last 18 months focused on reducing debt and hitting a $20 billion divestment target.

While it has engaged in some acquisition activity in that time, including showing interest in buying a majority stake in the Shenandoah field in the US Gulf, BP had been largely absent from shale data rooms, making its re-emergence in recent weeks as a potential buyer notable, three of the sources said.

Buying assets near its existing footprint would be logical, four of the sources said, given the potential for cost savings and BP's familiarity with local geology.

Part of Devon's Eagle Ford asset was held in a joint venture between the company and BP until the partnership's dissolution in 2025.

DEVON DIVESTMENT

Devon is marketing for sale both its Eagle Ford and Powder River basin acreage in Wyoming, the sources said, as part of a portfolio review undertaken following its $58 billion merger with Coterra Energy. The Eagle Ford asset consists of around 90,000 net acres, and produced around 77,000 boepd in the second quarter, per Devon's website.

The effort comes as U.S. energy assets have increased allure to buyers, as they can operate even as Middle Eastern conflict shakes global oil markets. The tension pushed crude back above $100 per barrel last week, with higher prices of benefit to sellers.

Conversely, market volatility makes it harder for buyers and sellers to agree on valuations, as buyers want to avoid the perception of paying an inflated price. Dealmaking involving US production assets has slumped in recent months as a result.

This uncertainty is reflected in potential valuations for Devon's Eagle Ford. The TPH Research analysts marked it at $4.5 billion, but the sources pointed to a range between $3.5 billion and roughly $4 billion.

Devon is also facing pressure from activist shareholders TOMS Capital and Kimmeridge Energy Management to improve performance and shed assets.

(Reporting by David French in New York and Arathy Somasekhar in Houston; Additional Reporting by Stephanie Kelly in London, editing by Colin Barr, Nick Zieminski and David Gregorio)

name: Congress
title: ICYMI: American Businesses Aren't Allowed to Build. It's Time Congress Helped Them.
description:
This inability to build harms every American industry and every American job.
American businesses aren’t allowed to build.
This inability to build harms every American industry and every American job.
Among the various federal permitting barriers, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) stands as the most egregious.
Yet these and many other strange bedfellows have come together this year to fix a profoundly broken statute and allow America to build again.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – America’s share of global manufacturing output has fallen from 25% in 1997 to 15% today. Absent intervention, it could reach 11% by 2030.

Those numbers get thrown around a lot. What is said less is what they mean for Americans: the United States is losing its ability to produce the things it needs to defend itself, to power its economy, and to care for its people. This failure is not because we lack talent, capital, or technology. It is because regulations have made it nearly impossible to build anything in the United States.

This inability to build harms every American industry and every American job. Whether it is semiconductor fabricators, munitions or battery factories, rare earth production facilities, natural gas pipelines, oil refineries or medical manufacturing centers, all hit the same regulatory barrier: federal permitting law.

As the Senate embarks on negotiations for permitting reform, U.S. Senator Kevin Cramer (R-ND), chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Subcommittee on Transportation and Infrastructure, teamed up with Katherine Boyle, General Partner at Andreesen Horowitz, for an op-ed on fixing the federal permitting process so America can build once again.

American businesses aren’t allowed to build. It’s time Congress helped them.

FOX News – September 24, 2026

America’s share of global manufacturing output has fallen from 25% in 1997 to 15% today. Absent intervention, it could reach 11% by 2030.

Those numbers get thrown around a lot. What is said less is what they mean for Americans: the United States is losing its ability to produce the things it needs to defend itself, to power its economy and to care for its people. This failure is not because we lack talent, capital or technology. It is because we have made it nearly impossible to build anything here.

This inability to build harms every American industry and every American job. Whether it is semiconductor fabricators, munitions or battery factories, rare earth production facilities, natural gas pipelines, oil refineries or medical manufacturing centers, all hit the same regulatory barrier: federal permitting law.

Among the various federal permitting barriers, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) stands as the most egregious. Unlike substantive environmental protections found in statutes like the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act, NEPA’s central function is procedural, requiring analysis and disclosure of environmental impacts before major federal actions.

Over time, regulatory layering and aggressive legal interpretation transformed this reasonable “look before you leap” statute into a roadblock for projects with any sort of federal connection.

This regulatory accretion has turned NEPA into a tool to stop nearly any meaningful project — across every state and political spectrum. It is not every day renewable energy advocates and oil and gas executives work together to reform a statute. Yet these and many other strange bedfellows have come together this year to fix a profoundly broken statute and allow America to build again.

The numbers explain why. The median NEPA review in 2024 ran 26 months. The statute’s more demanding environmental impact statements averaged 3.8 years. Environmental assessments, the so-called fast track, routinely average a year or more. None of those timelines are legally required. They are what happens when bureaucratic caution and unlimited litigation combine in the absence of any countervailing pressure.

And then there is the cost. DOE data showed mean environmental assessment preparation costs were over $300,000 while environmental impact statement costs averaged $6.6 million. Those figures exclude legal fees, staff time, and the cost of litigation. These millions add to the bottom line of every potential domestic manufacturing project.

For a major company, these delays and costs are annoying. For a small business seeking to open a factory or a startup raising its first manufacturing round, they are often a company-ending event. These are the types of businesses America most needs right now–the 50-person drone manufacturer, the battery startup and the defense tech company that won a Pentagon contract and needs to be in production before its runway expires are exactly the companies the current NEPA regime destroys. These are also the jobs Americans need.

This regulatory Sisyphean task doesn’t improve outcomes, it materially delays or even kills meritorious projects. Investors cannot deploy capital if regulatory uncertainty clouds a project.

While the Supreme Court’s “Seven County” decision and recent executive actions have helped, only Congress can enact durable statutory reforms needed to restore NEPA to its intended procedural role. Here are some basic fixes.

Enforce the deadlines and limit endless litigation. Agencies need to enforce permitting deadlines. Aspirational goals do not motivate federal bureaucrats, but neither does the prospect of getting dragged into court. Both extremes perpetuate analysis paralysis. Get the permits done and when they’re complete, there should be finality, providing certainty for manufacturers, the capital backing them and the federal agency granting the permit. Revocations should be permitted only when there is an imminent, irreparable and specifically documented harm.

Cut the red tape for companies which can least afford it. Agencies which finance or permit manufacturing already have categorical exclusions, pre-cleared categories of routine actions normally not requiring a full Environmental Assessment or Environmental Impact Statement. Most have never shared those categories with each other, despite a 2023 law explicitly allowing them to do so. Congress should require agencies which finance or permit manufacturing to adopt a curated list of relevant categorical exclusions from other agencies. This one reform alone would dramatically increase regulatory speed and certainty.

None of this dismantles environmental protection. Clean air, clean water and endangered species protections all remain fully intact. What these reforms remove is the accumulated procedural weight which has nothing to do with those protections and everything to do with a system no one has been accountable for fixing.

The opportunity to build in America is now. Nobody left, right, or center wants this to be an era of managed decline. We want growth, security, and innovation. That is why political polar opposites are making great strides to reach a deal, like Chairmen Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.V., Environment and Public Works, and Mike Lee, R-Ut., Energy and Natural Resources, and Ranking Members Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Environment and Public Works, and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., Energy and Natural Resources. The American people will benefit from the good jobs and the supply security these reforms create. It’s time to meet the moment and get America building again.

text:
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández is calling for a pause on new data center development in New Mexico until companies meet standards she says would protect water supplies, electric customers and local communities.

Leger Fernández, a Democrat who represents New Mexico’s 3rd Congressional District, unveiled what she called her “No Blank Checks for Data Centers Principles” on Wednesday.

The six principles call for data centers to pay for their own electricity and infrastructure without raising residential utility bills, avoid harming local water resources, use renewable or zero-carbon energy, create union jobs, obtain community approval before construction and avoid taxpayer subsidies while providing community benefits.

“Data centers want our water, our land, and our power,” Leger Fernández said in a statement. “But we will not give them a blank check.”

She said she would support projects only if they protect water, create good-paying union jobs, use clean energy and have backing from the communities where they are proposed.

New Mexico has at least 17 publicly mapped data center facilities, largely clustered in Albuquerque and Los Lunas, though industry estimates put the statewide total higher.

RELATED | City of Clovis rejects data center moratorium

Leger Fernández also called on Congress to establish a national regulatory framework for artificial intelligence and data centers, including civil and criminal liability standards.

“Communities must know how much water and electricity these projects will use, who will pay for them, and what residents will receive in return,” she said. “If a project cannot answer those questions, it should not move forward.”

Her announcement comes as data center proposals across the Southwest have prompted concerns about electricity demand, water use, tax incentives and the effect on nearby rural communities.

title: Green-energy revolution needs a cleaner supply chain | The Express Tribune
description:
Today, much of the world's clean-energy supply chain runs through China.
China now dominates much of the clean-energy supply chain, from solar manufacturing to battery production.
Yet the cobalt supply chain is plagued by violations related to labour rights and environmental standards.
The green transition risks losing credibility if consumers celebrate cleaner technologies while pollution and environmental damage are shifted elsewhere.
The real issue is that the clean-energy revolution cannot be considered a success if its environmental and social costs are simply displaced farther up the supply chain.
text:
For years, Western politicians talked about turning the fight against climate change into an economic opportunity. China didn't just talk about it, it built an economic powerhouse around it.

Today, much of the world's clean-energy supply chain runs through China. The country produces roughly 86% of global solar panels and dominates the manufacturing of batteries, electric vehicles, and many of the materials that make them possible. It helped drive down the cost of solar power to levels that once seemed unimaginable, making clean energy more affordable and accessible for countries around the world. China did not merely join the green transition, it has become its leading force.

China's success in the green transformation is no accident. While many governments treated climate policy primarily as an environmental issue, Beijing saw it as an opportunity to invest in industries of the future. The results are difficult to ignore. China now dominates much of the clean-energy supply chain, from solar manufacturing to battery production.

Western governments, meanwhile, are trying to rebuild their own industrial capacity. The US has used the Inflation Reduction Act to incentivise domestic clean-energy investment. The EU has pursued a similar objective through its Net-Zero Industry Act, seeking to expand European manufacturing and reduce strategic dependencies. These efforts indicate that the green transition is no longer just about reducing carbon emissions, it is increasingly being viewed by major powers as a race for technological leadership and more secure control of the supply chains that will power the twenty-first century.

Thus far, China's lead in vital areas of the green economy is undisputed. But now comes the trickier part.

The world should be wary of replacing one form of dependency with another. Dependence on fossil fuels created decades of geopolitical tussles, in addition to their enormous environmental toll. Building a clean-energy future that relies heavily on concentrated and contested supply chains could create a new set of risks.

Consider cobalt, a critical ingredient in many batteries. The Democratic Republic of Congo produces roughly two-thirds of the world's mined cobalt, while China accounts for around three-quarters of global cobalt refining. Yet the cobalt supply chain is plagued by violations related to labour rights and environmental standards.

Indonesia's nickel industry offers a similar warning. Nickel is increasingly important to battery production, yet much of its processing remains heavily dependent on coal-fired power. The green transition risks losing credibility if consumers celebrate cleaner technologies while pollution and environmental damage are shifted elsewhere.

For much of the world, which is not competing with China for clean-technology dominance, the problem is not that China has become a clean-energy powerhouse. The real issue is that the clean-energy revolution cannot be considered a success if its environmental and social costs are simply displaced farther up the supply chain. A solar panel, electric vehicle or battery may produce fewer emissions in use, but that does not make the technology inherently clean if the minerals needed to produce it are extracted through exploitative practices. A sustainable green transition must account for the full life cycle of clean technologies, from mining and refining to manufacturing and, ultimately, the disposal of the products which use renewable energy.

This is what the next phase of the global energy transition must address. Countries and companies that can build not only more diversified and resilient supply chains but also uphold higher standards of transparency, environmental responsibility and labour protection will help define the next phase of the green energy transition.

text:
DTE Energy says its proposed long-term energy plan, not yet filed with utility regulators, will keep electricity reliable and bills as low as possible.

The utility said the plan, known as an Integrated Resource Plan, or IRP, anticipates much higher electricity demand in the future — which it will meet with an "all of the above," resource mix, including updating its Fermi II nuclear power plant, dramatically increasing solar and long term storage, and constructing two new natural gas plants.

Despite the two new plants, DTE said it will remain on track to meet Michigan's 2040 energy goal of net zero carbon emissions.

But critics said there's something very risky built into the plan: data centers.

Bryan Smigielski is with Sierra Club of Michigan. He said the planned power plants will likely serve the electricity requirements of power-hungry, financially risky data centers.

Smigielski said his group will ask the Michigan Public Service Commission, which oversees utilities in the state, to require DTE to make that connection transparent, by modeling future energy needs with no data centers in their analysis, and comparing that to future energy needs including data centers.

"We just want to see them be very transparent about who's causing the need for additional generation in our state or in our region. And we all know it's data centers," Smigielski said. "I think if we can get this clear modeling done, it'll say that pretty clearly."

He said residential customers could be left paying the entire bill for an unneeded natural gas plant, if some data centers are unable to make a profit and go bankrupt.

For example, Smigielski said, Oracle, one of the companies building a mega data center in Saline Township, is rated BBB-, just above junk bonds.

"Why are we taking on those risks when a bank likely would not even take on those risks," Smigielski asked. "If they do go belly up, then we have a big gas plant with billions of dollars to pay, and that's enough of a financial burden that it could profoundly impact our economy."

DTE president and CEO Joi Harris said the plan would be $3.5 billion less expensive than the company’s previous IRP from 2022, after accounting for changed laws and other factors since then.

"We're building a stronger tomorrow for Michigan's children and grandchildren," she said.

"We listened closely to our customers throughout this process, and this plan reflects what they told us matters most to them: reliable power, affordable bills and a practical path to a cleaner energy future. It balances those priorities while ensuring Michigan has the energy it needs to continue growing for decades to come."

name: Clean Energy
title: The Energy Trust Gap Is Crashing Our Grid - Heatmap News
description:
Over the past four years, this has created what I’m calling the Energy Trust Gap.
But the Energy Trust Gap has not been created by Republicans alone.
Let me be clear: The Energy Trust Gap will cost Democrats elections.
Policymakers, clean energy and climate advocates, and industry cannot fix the issues plaguing our energy system without regaining some credibility.
This is the uncomfortable but necessary path to closing the Energy Trust Gap.
text:
In September 2024, then-presidential candidate Donald Trump told a crowd in Wilmington: “We will cut your energy prices in half … Mark it down, and you can get very angry at me if we don't do it.” He gave himself one year from when he’d take office.

Two years later, rates are up. And we’re angry.

Utilities requested $18.6 billion in rate increases in the first half of 2026, including a record $9.2 billion in the second quarter alone. Gas prices are hovering close to $4.50 a gallon, almost a full dollar more than this time last year. Diesel prices are even worse, recently passing $6.50 a gallon, up by over 50% from one year ago.

In the past two years, electricity prices have increased by over 10%. In the past five years, it’s over 36%.

President Trump’s failure to lower costs has tanked his approval ratings, currently just 34% overall and 33% on his handling of the economy. But he’s not alone. Incumbent politicians across the country — along with utilities, energy-intensive businesses, and tech companies — have found themselves swept up in the backlash.

Those feelings of blame and distrust have emanated throughout our democracy. Just 27% of Americans trust national institutions, according to a June Gallup poll, a single point above the all-time low. Just 17% trust the federal government to do what's right. Nearly seven in 10 people fear that institutional leaders are deliberately misleading them.

Looking at our energy infrastructure, I understand the feeling. Government and industry have chronically neglected our electricity delivery system, offering impossible-to-fulfill slogans rather than real solutions.

Over the past four years, this has created what I’m calling the Energy Trust Gap. It results from the toxic collision of an aging, neglected, and overstressed grid; rising prices; and voter frustration with policymakers, regulators, and industries that overpromise and underdeliver.

This is not merely a Trump problem, though it is true that the president’s chaotic tariff strategy, his impossibly stupid war in Iran, and his senseless energy obstruction have dramatically widened this rift.

Instead of deploying more energy to the grid, the Trump administration has blocked renewables when Americans need them most. It paid TotalEnergies $928 million and Invenergy $765 million to abandon offshore wind leases — $1.7 billion of public money not to build power. Through the Pentagon, it has halted over 28 gigawatts of onshore wind projects in 21 states, and attempted to suspend five fully permitted projects already under construction. Thankfully, all five won injunctions and resumed development by February. Still, the industry's trade association estimated that the cancellations and delays would add $45 billion in East Coast energy costs over a decade.

Though a federal appeals court recently ruled against it, the administration was also using emergency authority to keep 11 fossil units at seven plants running at a cost of roughly $1.5 million per day. The evidence is quite weak that these units are necessary to maintain grid stability or meet unexpected demand. Some are producing substantially less power than they can, or have even been taken offline.

But the Energy Trust Gap has not been created by Republicans alone. Here is the part my side needs to sit with.

In 2022, then-President Biden promised that the Inflation Reduction Act would “bring down family energy bills by an average of $500 a year.” The White House projected that, alongside the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the IRA would cut electricity rates by up to 9% by 2030. Advocates promised the law would create “more than 9 million good jobs.”

The Trump administration undid some of the efforts to fulfill these promises before they could bear fruit. But others were flimsy from the start.

An accompanying report on the 9 million jobs figure acknowledged, in a footnote, that “not all of the jobs created will be net new employment,” but rather would constitute workers hired away from elsewhere to remedy a tight labor market. It also clarified that “job” was less accurate than “job-year equivalent,” a technical measure of labor volume rather than individual people holding durable positions.

These caveats never made it into the president’s public comments, including at events I helped host.

We expected the government to spur private sector demand and create jobs across the country. We assumed the public would see the benefits and credit our clean energy policies. But voters didn’t see an IRA-driven jobs boom in their communities, didn’t feel its impact in reducing costs amid a crisis, and didn’t see it improving their lives.

Yes, there were jobs. But in an economy as large as the United States, the public simply doesn’t distinguish “clean energy jobs” from other sectors.

The promise of a national electric charging network to enable EV ownership didn’t pan out, either. Congress made $4.4 billion available for chargers in 2022; four years later, states had opened only around 150 public charging stations, a flop for a program designed to fund about 1,600 stations on the path to phasing out gas vehicles. Same story with home heating. The American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy found that in all four high-electricity-price states it modeled, the average gas household's bills increased after electrification.

When heating homes already accounts for more than 40% of residential energy consumption, you cannot credibly advocate for more expensive options.

These functional failures were also messaging failures. By 2024, 40% of registered voters hadn’t heard anything about the IRA. Governors got more credit for new renewable energy and green manufacturing facilities than President Biden did, according to a post-mortem on the law led by the University of Michigan’s Alexander Gazmararian. The Biden administration placed a big political bet on actions that were misbranded, inadequately promoted, and ultimately undeliverable before November 2024 — the only timeframe that mattered.

Let me be clear: The Energy Trust Gap will cost Democrats elections.

As policymakers head into November’s midterm elections, they are being called upon to answer for the proliferation of data centers and the skyrocketing cost of electricity. In this moment, Democrats could seize momentum from Republicans. But many are still ignoring the lessons of the past four years.

A large number of voters believe clean energy advocates are exaggerating the affordability of renewable energy. If candidates argue that the transition to clean energy is a guaranteed outcome, and that Biden’s climate law worked, they will lose.

Reality is breaking through in some places: Officials are concerned about the cost-of-living crisis, explicitly acknowledging the trade-offs that come with climate policy and prioritizing affordability for ratepayers above all else. In March, for example, Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey signed an executive order to bring more energy and energy storage to the Bay State, calling for an “all-of-the-above approach to energy, including “solar, wind, gas, nuclear and hydro.” In New York, Governor Kathy Hochul has been honest that the state cannot meet its 2030 climate targets “without imposing new and additional crushing costs,” citing state estimates of more than $4,000 a year for upstate households burning oil and gas.

“Something has to give,” she said.

That honesty is critical. Policymakers, clean energy and climate advocates, and industry cannot fix the issues plaguing our energy system without regaining some credibility.

Here’s where I would start:

We need to ban the bans on energy development, including those on renewables and on necessary natural gas expansions. We cannot ask consumers to give up gas-powered vehicles and HVAC systems in favor of more expensive alternatives. If we promise jobs, we need to deliver jobs and stay engaged with the communities meant to benefit.

We must make electricity more affordable by adding transmission lines and investing in factories that produce turbines and transformers. Doing that means resolving the intense, bureaucratic permitting burden that so often gets in the way. We need to broaden who pays for the grid, including hyperscalers, so the burden does not fall on ratepayers. Short-term cost relief is a must, as is long-term reform of the rate-and-return structure.

Finally, clean energy advocates — including us at Third Way — need to defend these tough, realistic decisions against purist crowds on the left.

This is the uncomfortable but necessary path to closing the Energy Trust Gap. The alternative is more broken promises and putting our ambitions for energy, the economy, national security, and climate completely out of reach.

If policymakers can’t be straightforward about the trade-offs and deliver on their solutions, we’ll doom ourselves to policy whipsawing and another energy crisis.

Then another. Then another. Then another.

title: Energy efficiency 'hits the road' - Environment America
description:
What does California’s tire efficiency standard do?
The California Energy Commission approved the Replacement Tire Efficiency Program (RTEP) in August 2026.
Historically smart public policy, from the ENERGY STAR program to appliance efficiency standards have helped spur efficiency advancements.
Driving a new age of efficiency While controversial in some corners, California’s replacement tire efficiency standard is an important step towards reducing the state’s transportation pollution.
California continues to lead on energy efficiency as the first state in the nation to enact these standards.
text:
The cleanest and cheapest energy is the energy we never need to use. The same is true whether you’re lighting your home, heating your office, and even when you drive. With gas prices on the rise, many Americans are looking to reduce their gasoline use. California regulators are making strides in vehicle mileage with tire efficiency standards.

Efficiency standards are nothing new; we have them for refrigerators, home appliances, and commercial equipment. But our cars can also be more efficient – starting with the tires we drive on. Tires provide the only point of contact between our cars and the road; that makes them critical to the vehicle efficiency equation.

Not all tires are the same

Some tires minimize energy loss as you drive by creating less rolling resistance – which determines the amount of force (and energy) you need to get your car moving. Lower rolling resistance means your car gets more miles to the gallon – saving you and the planet on gas and vehicle emissions.

New cars often come with low-rolling resistance tires, but replacement tires are often less efficient than your car’s original tires. That means you use more gas to get from point A to point B when you replace your car’s original tires. But this doesn’t have to be the case.

In other regions (such as the European Union) where tire efficiency standards are the norm, lawmakers have set out a grading system for consumers to know how efficient the tires they buy are. The EU also sets minimum efficiency standards tires must meet.

The United States Congress, for its part, passed the FAST Act in 2015 which required the Department of Transportation to regulate fuel efficiency for tires. Unfortunately, the Department of Transportation never actually put those regulations in place. In the absence of federal regulations, California has taken action of its own to bring more energy efficient tires to its roadways.

What does California’s tire efficiency standard do?

The California Energy Commission approved the Replacement Tire Efficiency Program (RTEP) in August 2026. The program’s first phase takes effect in 2029, giving manufacturers time to provide sufficiently efficient tires. Starting January 1, 2029, tire manufacturers may only sell replacement tires that meet the state’s minimum efficiency requirements.

The next phase, taking effect on January 1, 2033, increases the minimum efficiency requirements and would apply to tires manufactured or sold in 2033 and beyond. Already, about 30% of existing tires meet the higher standard.

The state expects California’s Replacement Tire Efficiency Program to curtail gasoline demand by 141 million gallons while cutting global warming pollution by 2 million metric tons every year. Both of these benefits stand to benefit both environmental and human health. Once enacted, this program’s impacts would be equivalent to taking 400,000 gasoline-powered cars off the roads.

On top of the environmental benefits, the program would also reduce electricity demand on California’s electric grid by nearly 1 TWh every year – that’s enough energy to power 100,000 homes for an entire year – while saving Californians nearly $1 billion on gas and electricity costs. The policy’s benefits abound, but the program still has its detractors.

Where the rubber meets the road: Opposition to California’s standard

Some critics of California’s tire efficiency standards have raised concerns about consumer choice – namely that Californians should have the opportunity to purchase worse, less efficient, and more expensive tires (when accounting for lifetime costs and savings).

Historically smart public policy, from the ENERGY STAR program to appliance efficiency standards have helped spur efficiency advancements. Similarly, California’s move to set a higher standard for tires promises to help our environment and consumers alike.

Driving a new age of efficiency

While controversial in some corners, California’s replacement tire efficiency standard is an important step towards reducing the state’s transportation pollution. California continues to lead on energy efficiency as the first state in the nation to enact these standards. By elevating more efficient tire models, California is saving energy and money while improving Californians’ health.

text:
Mark Levine, the new New York City Comptroller, used his first New York Climate Week in the new role to propose that the City’s public pension funds expand their allocations to climate solutions.

Speaking during the annual climate gathering in New York, Levine recommended that three of the City’s five public pension funds expand their private market allocations by a combined $5bn.

NZI Transition and Climate Investment Conference | 22 October | London | Register here

The move, which would involve New York City Teachers’ Retirement System (TRS), Employees’ Retirement System (NYCERS) and Board of Education Retirement System (BERS), could see the three funds expand their investments in a broad array of climate solutions. This could range from areas including renewable power generation, grid modernization, energy efficiency and storage, clean transportation, and building decarbonization, as well as technologies that can reduce pollution, strengthen energy and water security, and improve resilience to extreme weather, comptroller Levine said.

The move is driven by a desire to play into clean energy as a global investment trend whilst contributing to a more resilient energy sector and lower prices for consumers, he explained. “As the climate crisis places a growing strain on our infrastructure and the broader economy, investing in cleaner, more reliable and resilient energy that can lower costs and reduce emissions at the same time is an essential part of our prudent long-term investment strategy.”

He also accused the Trump administration of “a lack of leadership” on climate, highlighting that 223 ⁠manufacturing and clean ⁠energy projects, representing $82.9 billion in investment and 111,765 jobs had stalled or been cancelled across the US during the current federal administration.

Levine’s recommendation means that a range of investment opportunities in the sector will be presented to each pension board for consideration and approval, subject to each of the three Systems’ independent due-diligence and fiduciary review processes.

The new allocations would sit within the Systems’ existing net zero plan, which includes a goal to invest $37.8bn in the transition by 2035.

Earlier this year, NYCERS, TRS, and BERS committed $116m to the Sandbrook Climate Infrastructure Fund II, marking the first private markets climate-focused investment during Comptroller Levine’s term.

EL PASO—While Texas officials have hit pause on data center permitting, one project is still moving ahead: Meta’s $10 billion, 1-gigawatt data center in northeast El Paso.

Meta had already signed tax abatement agreements with El Paso, jumped through regulatory hoops and started construction before Texas officials tapped the brakes on data center development this year.

But one hurdle the project must still clear is securing approval for El Paso Electric’s application to the Public Utilities Commission of Texas to build a 366-megawatt natural gas facility, using modular generators, to power the data center. Once operational, Meta’s data center would be the utility’s largest electric customer. The City of El Paso intervened in the application, and a hearing was held in July.

Administrative law judges for the commission released their proposed decision Wednesday. They found that El Paso Electric failed to adequately consider alternatives to the gas plant, called the McCloud facility and failed to issue a request for proposals to contractors. The judges recommended that the Public Utilities Commission only approve the application on the condition that El Paso Electric does not pass capital and operating costs on to its ratepayers. Without this condition, the judges recommend the application be denied.

The ultimate decision lies with the five PUCT commissioners. The application has not yet been scheduled for a vote.

“We’re disappointed,” said Verónica Carbajal, an organizer with the Sembrando Esperanza Coalition in El Paso, which submitted comments of over 1,000 people protesting the application. “If the state was really serious about this, the commission would be denying everything related to data centers.”

El Paso Electric did not respond to a request for comment.

El Paso Electric officials initially claimed that solar power would supply the Meta data center. However, in December the utility applied to build a power plant made up of 813 modular natural gas generators, supplied by the contractor Enchanted Rock. Each modular generator has a capacity of 450 kilowatts. The total estimated cost of the McCloud facility is $499 million.

The gas plant would exclusively supply Meta for the first five years and then connect to the broader transmission system. Meta would assume the costs for the first five years, after which ratepayers could be asked to shoulder the cost.

El Paso residents have raised concerns that power generation for the data center will increase air pollution, strain water resources and could increase electric rates. Oracle’s Project Jupiter hyperscale data center is also under construction in neighboring Doña Ana County, New Mexico.

El Paso Electric proposed contracting with Enchanted Rock after Meta recommended the company. The utility did not consider other contractors, according to administrative law judges. El Paso Electric did not conduct a cost-benefit analysis to determine whether the proposed gas plant is a cost-effective option for ratepayers. The utility did not consider alternatives like purchasing capacity or investing in existing generation.

The administrative law judges wrote that Wurldwide, a Meta subsidiary named in the application, drove the process.

“The selection of the Project was driven by Wurldwide’s prescribed timeline and preferences—and its agreement to pay the capital and operating costs,” they wrote.

“The overall lack of analysis regarding options is also concerning,” the judges wrote, because the utility left open the possibility that ratepayers will someday have to pay for the power plant. For those reasons, the judges recommended approval of the application only on the condition that ratepayers not be held responsible for the cost.

Far West Texas, including El Paso, is one of the few regions of the state that isn’t part of the Electricity Reliability Council of Texas grid. Utilities are barred from owning power plants in ERCOT, but the rules are different outside of the grid’s territory, which is why El Paso Electric could make its proposal.

Krysti Shallenberger, a research and communications manager at the Energy & Policy Institute, said that the application is notable because El Paso Electric is a privately-held, monopoly utility seeking to build a power plant solely for a data center.

“What we’re seeing with El Paso Electric, we haven’t necessarily seen in the competitive market,” Shallenberger said. “Which is the utility proposing to build an expensive gas plant [for a data center] that it will rate base. It can make a profit off this.”

Rate base is the value of assets a utility holds to provide service. It forms the basis for calculating how much utilities can charge their customers.

After previously championing the industry, Gov. Greg Abbott has taken steps to slow or limit data center development in Texas. But these measures have largely not affected the Meta data center in El Paso.

The audit of data centers in the ERCOT interconnection process, announced in August, does not impact Meta because El Paso is on the Western Interconnection grid.

Earlier this week, Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to pause issuing permits for data center projects. However, El Paso Electric has already obtained a TCEQ air permit for the McCloud facility

It is unclear whether other permits for the data center are still in process and could be impacted by the pause. In response to questions from Inside Climate News, TCEQ director of external relations Ryan Vise said the agency “will provide a full update on compliance to the Governor’s Office by October 19, 2026.”

Carbajal said the current regulatory landscape leaves El Pasoans in limbo.

“There are some communities that are benefiting from the pauses. There are others where data centers are already operating,” she said. “But we’re in the middle because Meta is under construction but not operational.”

text:
By Emma Haidar

The US Energy Department plans to provide $1.9 billion to help fund 31 grid improvement projects across 26 states as part of a Trump administration’s push to fortify the US power networks.

The funding is intended to be used help replace or rebuild more than 1,500 miles (2,400 km) of transmission lines and put in place technologies to improve grid reliability across nearly 21,000 miles, the Energy Department said Thursday in a statement. The projects would get an additional $3.35 billion through recipient cost-share funding, according to the release.

The funding is part of an Energy Department initiative to upgrade infrastructure across America’s aging electricity networks. The nation’s grids have become strained by soaring demand, notably by data centers feeding the artificial intelligence boom, and vulnerable to extreme weather.

The efforts could make more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity available, according to the statement. A gigawatt is the equivalent capacity of one large nuclear reactor and enough to power as many as 1 million US homes.

As a member of the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Chair of the New Democrat Coalition’s Climate Change and Clean Energy Task Force, Rep. Peters has some of the largest bipartisan efforts in Congress to streamline the federal permitting process for energy and infrastructure projects.

Last year, he unveiled the SPEED and Reliability Act, which significantly streamlines the siting and permitting of critical national interest electric transmission lines. Faster approvals to build more electrical lines would lower costs for consumers and prevent blackouts.

He also reintroduced the Fix Our Forests Act, his landmark forestry bill, which would reduce bureaucratic delays to streamline environmental reviews for fuel reduction projects. This ensures energy projects move forward quickly and stops Administrations from cancelling permits that were already approved legally. His bill has been supported by almost 40 organizations, made up of the people who build, power, and maintain America's infrastructure.

text:
High gas prices are causing drivers to consider more fuel-efficient vehicles like hybrids and EVs.

Electric vehicle sales have declined, partly due to the end of the federal EV tax credit in late 2025.

Hybrid vehicle sales are increasing because they are affordable, fuel-efficient and often offer more features than gas-only models.

Gas prices are causing many drivers to consider hybrid and electric vehicle ownership because refueling costs have spiked. Hybrid sales have picked up year-over-year, but EV sales are slumping according to sales data from automotive news site Motor1.com.

Here's why hybrid sales are through the roof and EV sales are on the decline.

Why EV sales are down in 2026 despite high gas prices

Internal combustion engine vehicles may be less efficient than battery electric vehicles but the former still outsell EVs by a large margin. Though there are a few attractive electric car and SUV options on the market, there are several reasons why electric vehicle registrations dropped 31% in July.

One of the main reasons fewer drivers are purchasing electric vehicles in 2026 is the absence of the federal electric vehicle tax incentive. This incentive allowed eligible drivers to claim a tax credit of up to $7,500, reducing the total cost of their EV purchases.

An uptick in 2025 electric vehicle sales is largely due to drivers taking advantage of the tax credit while it was still available. The tax credit was officially eliminated on Sept. 30.

Without the tax incentive, most EVs are more expensive than their gas and hybrid counterparts, which makes them unattractive options for budget-focused consumers. Additionally, many drivers find electric vehicle charging to be inconvenient compared to gas and hybrid vehicle refueling.

Why hybrid car sales are climbing in 2026

Hybrid vehicle sales are climbing in 2026 because many hybrid models like the Toyota Camry and Honda Civic Hybrid are affordable and efficient. Vehicles with hybrid powertrains can achieve exceptional fuel economy, which is helpful as gas prices rise to historic heights.

"Toyota and other hybrid-focused rivals keep adding inventory that many dealers say they could sell twice over" according to Motor1.com. Hybrid vehicle sales are on the rise in 2026 because many hybrids come with more standard features than their traditional relatives. Additionally, hybrid powertrains also add horsepower to many nameplates, making the hybrid iterations more enjoyable to drive.

Automakers like Toyota produce several standard hybrid nameplates (Camry, Sequoia, Sienna, RAV4) since they can sell just as well as gas models and can offer even more value to consumers as daily drivers.

The best hybrid car segment for budget-oriented drivers

If you're looking for an affordable hybrid car, hybrid compact cars like the Corolla Hybrid and Elantra Hybrid are the best options. The 2026 Toyota Corolla Hybrid starts at $24,975 and achieves 50 miles per gallon combined.

Hyundai's Elantra Hybrid starts at just $25,650 and earns 54 miles per gallon combined. If you're in the market for an affordable new hybrid that achieves stellar gas mileage, there are plenty of great compact hybrid sedan options with starting prices under $30,000.

They may be slightly more expensive than their combustion engine counterparts, but hybrid cars can save drivers thousands of dollars in refueling costs over the course of ownership.

text:
WASHINGTON — Senate negotiators are trying to complete work by the end of this week on a major overhaul of the federal environmental permitting system.

They are considering revisions to the National Environmental Policy Act to speed the approval process for major infrastructure and energy projects.

The proposed permitting changes could affect projects like oil refineries, pipelines and wind farms.

Senate negotiators hope to adjourn this week as they turn their attention to midterm election campaigns. They say they are close to an agreement on the final wording but still are trying to work out compromises on a few details.

“I think the moment can be met this week and that’s what I’m looking forward to,” said Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va.

The National Environmental Policy Act at the center of the negotiations requires federal agencies to evaluate environmental infrastructure projects before a decision can be made on whether to approve them.

The reviews are sometimes blamed for dragging out the timeline for new projects. They also can lead to years of litigation under the 1970 law’s provisions allowing private citizens to challenge projects with environmental implications.

Supporters of the revisions say lengthy and unpredictable permitting reviews increase project costs and discourage investment. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups also have complained about duplication of regulations under NEPA, the Clean Water Act and other federal laws.

Environmental advocates argue that expedited reviews and restrictions on litigation could weaken protections against pollution and health hazards.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said Wednesday that disagreements over “permitting reform” were making an agreement elusive for the senators.

“That’s something that has economic consequences,” Thune said. “It’s very hard in this country to get energy projects permitted and ready to roll, and so we would like to see action on that.”

Any legislation that might emerge from the negotiations is taking on urgency as lawmakers confront public outrage over rising electricity demand from data centers and advanced manufacturing facilities.

The proposed legislation, titled the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act, was cosponsored by Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas.

“As energy use rises, we must remove unnecessary barriers holding us back from building reliable infrastructure that can keep up with demand,” Cornyn said in a statement.

The House already has passed the SPEED Act, a permitting overhaul that would revise NEPA and alter environmental reviews before federal approvals. The measure passed 221-196 in December, with 11 Democrats joining Republicans.

The Senate proposal for companion legislation would go beyond the House bill in trying to streamline the permitting procedures by setting limits on court interventions.

Cornyn’s statement said the Senate proposal seeks to establish “meaningful judicial review standards to ensure NEPA cannot be misused to stall critical infrastructure projects.”

A failure to finalize an agreement by Friday could mean the Senate will need to wait until next year to try again.

text:
Order would effectively exempt data center power generation from Commission oversight

COLUMBIA, S.C. — Today, the Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, requested that the South Carolina Public Service Commission reconsider its order deciding that the 460-megawatt power plant at the Valara data center is not subject to the South Carolina Utility Facility and Environmental Protection Act.

In June, SELC petitioned the Commission to declare that the Siting Act, and its open, public review of environmental and community impacts, apply to the Valara data center and its 460-megawatt gas power plant. The Act provides that “any person” constructing a power plant exceeding 75 megawatts of electric generation must first receive Commission review and approval. However, on September 14, the Commission issued a final order finding that the gas power plant at the Valara data center is not subject to the Act because the gas plant will be used to power the private data center rather than producing electricity for public use.

“We believe the Commission’s order is contrary to the plain and unambiguous language of the Siting Act,” said Kate Mixson, SELC Senior Attorney. “The decision would mean that future private power plants of any size, like the one proposed by Valara, could be built without oversight from the Commission. That isn’t what the law requires, and it is especially concerning as we see an influx of data center proposals flocking to South Carolina.”

“The potential biggest polluter in Spartanburg County should not get a pass from siting and environmental oversight requirements that have been in place since 1971,” said Eddy Moore, SACE Decarbonization Director.

The Commission must decide on the petition within 30 days.
