text:
How vehicle lifetimes, cross-border sales and second-life storage could shape Europe’s supply of recycled battery materials

Paper: Assessing recycling potential of critical materials in European electric vehicle fleet. AI-generated abstract conceptual image created using ChatGPT/OpenAI

A recent study published in the Journal of Cleaner Production finds that its high-reuse scenario reduces the cumulative availability of recycled material by about 20%–25% through 2045. Cobalt shows the largest projected shortfall against EU recycled-content targets.

It also develops a material flow analysis (MFA) model to estimate the theoretical recovery of critical materials from end-of-life (EoL) light-duty electric vehicle (EV) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) batteries through 2045.

The researchers combine EV adoption projections, vehicle survival patterns, cross-border flows, and changes in battery chemistry. They also incorporate material intensities (the amount of each material per unit of battery capacity), second-life use, and recycling efficiencies to track future battery stocks and material flows.

Linking EV Growth With Future Material Recovery

Europe’s transition to electric mobility will increase demand for battery materials while creating a growing source of secondary raw materials. Yet the materials in newly sold EVs are not immediately available for recycling.

Battery packs remain in vehicles for several years, and used vehicles can also move between countries before reaching EoL. These factors make it difficult to estimate when and where recyclable materials will become available.

The study addresses this gap with an MFA model that connects EV deployment with battery retirement and material recovery. It covers passenger cars and light commercial vehicles in the EU-27, the UK, Norway, Iceland, Switzerland, Turkey, and Liechtenstein. Medium- and heavy-duty vehicles are excluded. The model uses EV and PHEV sales from 2011 to 2024 and projects adoption through 2045.

The analysis focuses on lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese, as these materials are strategically important in battery manufacturing and recycling. It also examines how second-life applications could alter the timing of material recovery.

Modeling Vehicle Stocks, Battery Materials and Recycling

The researchers construct a cohort-based stock-flow model to follow EVs through their operational lifetimes. It uses country-specific logistic growth calibrated to historical sales and 2035 penetration targets aligned with the International Energy Agency’s Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) and Net Zero Emissions (NZE) Scenario. APS reflects announced policy pledges. NZE assumes a faster path to net-zero emissions.

The model separates technical degradation from behavioral turnover. This distinction allows young vehicles leaving one national fleet to enter another through exports rather than immediately becoming EoL vehicles.

The analysis translates vehicle stocks into battery stocks using data on battery capacity, chemistry, energy density, and material intensity. It also incorporates changes in battery chemistry, including the growing role of nickel-rich NMC and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) systems.

Researchers model direct recycling and second-life use in stationary storage. Reuse begins in 2025 and rises from 0% to 25% by 2045 in the low-reuse scenario or 50% in the high-reuse scenario. Only batteries from vehicles older than five years that leave service through behavioral turnover qualify for reuse. A reused battery remains in second-life use for 10 years.

Recycling calculations apply material- and chemistry-specific recovery efficiencies. The infrastructure model groups countries into 10 regional clusters and tests plant capacities of 10,000, 50,000, or 100,000 tonnes per year as EoL flows increase. The calculation assumes unrestricted battery availability within each region and omits logistics costs and cross-border constraints.

Recoverable Materials Rise as Battery Cohorts Reach EoL

The results show that EV adoption will develop unevenly across Europe. Norway is already approaching market saturation, while Turkey and Poland are emerging as important late-stage growth markets. The NZE pathway results in faster stock accumulation than the APS pathway, thereby increasing the volume of batteries entering the EoL stream.

Under NZE in 2045, Germany will have about three times the Balkan region’s cumulative EV sales and will require roughly five times its recycling capacity, reflecting faster vehicle turnover.

Cross-border vehicle movement further alters the geographic distribution of recyclable batteries. In a stylized allocation based on historical trade shares, Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, and the UK emerge as important exporters, reflecting high vehicle turnover. Balkan and Baltic countries are projected to rely more on imported used vehicles.

Recycling demand will depend on EV sales, vehicle lifetimes, and second-hand market conditions. These projections indicate structural trade effects. Exact bilateral flows fall outside the model, which omits prices, policy changes, and market frictions.

Battery chemistry strongly influences the composition of future recyclable material. Embedded cobalt mass grows more slowly as the modeled chemistry mix shifts toward cobalt-free or low-cobalt chemistries. Nickel continues to accumulate, with nickel-rich NMC batteries remaining important in the modeled fleet.

Lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese together account for 10%–12% of total battery mass under the assumed chemistry mix and material intensities. The study identifies a sharp rise in recoverable material from the late 2020s, as larger EV cohorts begin to reach EoL. Second-life deployment changes this trajectory.

The reduction in recyclable material appears under both APS and NZE, with reuse postponing recycling. Under the NZE–High Reuse scenario, modeled second-life storage capacity reaches 15.7 GWh by 2030. This equals about 5% of the lower bound of the projected range for 2030 EU storage needs, 300 GWh. By 2045, the same scenario reaches 2.58 TWh of second-life storage capacity. Sensitivity cases that start reuse at 10% or 25% increase the 2030 estimate to 27.6 GWh or 45.1 GWh, respectively.

Under NZE–Low Reuse in 2045, Germany, France, Belgium, and the UK show high recovery yields, while countries with slower EV development show lower yields. Luxembourg exceeds 100% for all four materials because its high turnover produces large EoL flows relative to annual new-vehicle demand. The yield is the ratio of material recovered that year to material in domestic new-EV sales, excluding imports. This flow ratio differs from recycling-process efficiency.

The values are theoretical upper bounds because the model assumes all EoL batteries are collected. It also assumes fixed recovery efficiencies and does not assess economic feasibility or material purity.

The PHEV contribution remains small: under the modeled phase-out to zero PHEV sales by 2035, PHEVs supply about 3% of the cumulative recycled critical materials used by BEVs and do not affect the compliance result.

Toward More Sustainable Battery Recycling

The study shows that Europe’s battery-recycling challenge depends on capacity and timing. EV sales are growing rapidly, but batteries remain in vehicles for several years, and cross-border movements and second-life use delay recovery. Under the study’s assumptions on adoption, lifetime, collection, and annual matching, this timing gap could complicate compliance with recycled-content targets.

Second-life use can extend battery service life and support stationary energy storage, but it also delays recycling. The authors call for joint reuse and recycling plans, faster collection, incentives for domestic capacity, battery traceability, strategic stockpiling, and cross-border coordination. The compliance comparison matches recovery with demand one year at a time. Carrying material forward could improve the result but would require additional assumptions about stockpiling, traceability, and timing.

The findings support coordinated planning for EV adoption, battery chemistry, and reuse and recycling capacity. Future work should add probabilistic uncertainty analysis for adoption, battery lifetimes, chemistry, and recovery.

text:
From solving climate challenges through research to preparing the next climate leaders, George Mason University is applying science, policy, and innovation to safeguard communities and ecosystems. And that commitment includes developing leadership and talent to produce solutions for our global community.

These interdisciplinary summer programs are helping the next generation of conservationists, environmentalists, and sustainability experts develop the critical skills needed to help build a climate-resilient society and a more resilient future.

Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation

In Front Royal, Virginia, the Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation (SMSC) opened its doors over the summer for high school students to gain college credit while exploring conservation through different but complementary perspectives: CONS 100 Introduction to Field Conservation Ecology and CONS 110 Natural History Illustration.

Students in CONS 100 participated in field investigations, testing research questions in a guided pilot study. In CONS 110, an online course, students learned to accurately observe and document the natural world through scientific illustration, with sketching practice, anatomical study, and lessons in different artistic mediums. Through both courses, students engaged in immersive, hands-on learning experiences that emphasize scientific inquiry, conservation, and observation.

“Whether they’re collecting field data or illustrating flora and fauna, we want the students to realize that observation is a powerful scientific skill,” said Robert Barrett, assistant director of recruitment and outreach for SMSC. “If they remember that conservation begins with paying close attention and that they have the ability to contribute through critical thinking and creativity, then they’ll carry something valuable with them long after the course ends.”

Together, these programs prepare the next generation of conservation leaders by teaching them the power of combining arts and sciences in observation, documentation, communication, and research to help communities adapt to environmental change and protect biodiversity. “By empowering students to translate observation into action, these courses contribute to the university's goal of building a more sustainable and climate-resilient society,” said Barrett.

Constellation Small Modular Reactor Summer Academy

Moving east from the mountains to Arlington, the inaugural Constellation Small Modular Reactor (SMR) Summer Academy at Fuse at Mason Square tackled questions of climate resilience through sustainable energy.

“The academy directly explores the challenge of providing reliable, resilient, and low-carbon electricity as demand continues to grow,” explained Liling Huang. During the week-long program, students participated in hands-on activities involving the NuScale SMR simulator at George Mason’s E2 Center, built Lego-based SMR applications, and took virtual reality tours of a nuclear power plant and renewable energy facilities. The camp concluded with a poster presentation competition attended by industry professionals.

“We want students to see the breadth of educational and career opportunities available in the energy industry,” said Huang.

By exploring potential solutions to the challenges of providing reliable, resilient, and low-carbon electricity, students began to develop the necessary skills to create a more resilient energy future.

“They can be a part of solving some of the most important energy challenges facing society,” said Huang. “They do not have to wait until they graduate from college to start thinking creatively, conducting research, and contributing ideas.”

Washington Youth Summit on the Environment

Across the Potomac River, the Washington Youth Summit on the Environment (WYSE) immersed students in the world of environmental conservation and sustainability. Over the course of one week, rising juniors and seniors in high school explored careers and developed the skillsets required to create actionable solutions, foster resilient communities, and ensure a sustainable future.

Led by faculty with expertise in environmental science, conservation, policy, law, and engineering, the youth delegates met with states’ U.S. Congressional Representatives and Senators; explored national and state parks, caverns, and waterways; toured the Smithsonian National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute; and heard from industry professionals such as conservation photographers, environmental project managers, animal keepers, marine biologists, and many more.

A tentpole of the youth delegate experience was roleplaying exercises, such as an intensive problem-solving water quality simulation. These sessions allow students to apply what they’ve learned to real-world problems and develop solutions.

“These high school students learn tangible skills and connect on a human level, with a goal of being impactful, empowered, and trustworthy citizens at home and abroad,” said Dawn Aponte.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced Thursday that Ohio will receive more than $100 million from the federal government to improve the state's electrical grid, targeting upgrades to existing transmission lines.

The federal government announced at an event in Columbus that it will invest $130 million to upgrade existing transmission lines, matched with the same amount of private investment from companies like First Energy and American Electric Power. This is part of a wider $1.9 billion investment in 26 states announced Thursday to rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission lines and deploy what the DOE calls "Grid-Enhancing Technologies" across nearly 21,000 miles.

The upgrades will mean more power will be able to flow through the lines at one time. The federal government project narrative said this will improve reliability, reduce congestion, accelerate interconnection of new load and generation, and enhance operational flexibility.

Officials stress the need for the grid to keep up with rapid growth in artificial intelligence technology and manufacturing. Central Ohio is a hub for data centers, but also new technology projects with the Intel semiconductor plant in New Albany and Anduril military drone factory in Pickaway County.

U.S. Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly said the funds will incentivize development for new technologies, but the government wants to also make energy more affordable.

"We are on the cusp of an absolutely extraordinary expansion of both technology and manufacturing in the United States, all of which requires this predicate basis of energy beforehand," Danly said.

New transmission lines have largely been the cause of increasing electric bills in Ohio. Danly said the U.S. won't be competitive if the existing grid isn't upgraded as well, allowing new energy capacity to power technology projects.

Danly said nuclear modules, revitalized nuclear power plants and natural gas plants are how the U.S. will achieve a goal of President Donald Trump's administration to create 400 gigawatts of new power by 2050. Currently, the U.S. electric grid has more than one terawatt of power capacity, or more than 1,000 gigawatts.

When asked by reporters, Danly didn't put an exact figure to potential reductions to utility bills. He said it will be difficult to predict exactly what rate impacts are going to be, but the aim is to make costs affordable for ratepayers.

"There is no doubt though that all things being equal, the more efficient the conductor is used, the less the cost of your transmission bill is going to be," Danly said.

Danly tried to frame the increasing demand for electricity as a good thing, because it is an indicator of economic growth. Many in central Ohio have told state utility regulators to reign in higher electric bills due to the increased demand.

"If you have a location in which nobody wants electricity, that's a place where nobody's trying to do anything. So the sign of a healthy economy is one in which you are constantly trying to meet demand that's rising, because that demand is the sign of all of those activities that require electricity," Danly said.

Public Utilities Commission of Ohio Chair Jennifer French, the chief utility regulator for the Buckeye State, said these advanced transmission technologies can provide additional capacity to the system without requiring new construction. She said this ensures the state responsibly and affordably enhances the grid.

"As we work collectively to meet the moment, the funding announced today will play an important role in the deployment of advanced transmission technologies across the country," French said.

The buildout is expected to take 48 months.

text:
Indiana has won $175 million in federal funding to upgrade a critical “choke point” between two regional electricity grid operators, officials announced Thursday.

“The challenge isn’t simply generating more electricity,” U.S. Department of Energy General Counsel Jonathan Brightbill said. “It’s making the grid so that it can move power where it is needed quickly, affordably, and reliably across one of the most important regional seams in the country — and that comes and lands right here in Indiana.”

The “seam” is where the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s service territory meets that of the PJM Interconnection. The border between the two regional transmission organizations runs through Illinois, Indiana, Michigan and Kentucky.

Brightbill said the project will unlock 2,000 to 4,000 megawatts of transfer capacity for an interconnection in the Hoosier state that Gov. Mike Braun dubbed a “pinch point” and a “choke point” in comments to reporters.

The work is expected to save ratepayers in and outside of Indiana between $50 million and $150 million annually by relieving congestion at that interconnection point.

“Congestion, that may cut off access to generation that’s available,” Brightbill said. “The way the bulk power system works, you end up with pockets. And then with dynamic pricing … you can end up with prices spiking in localized areas that then will cost those local ratepayers a lot of money.”

The four-year project will include:

Replacing old power lines with new ones with materials that carry electricity more efficiently.

Implementing dynamic assessment of the lines, allowing them to carry more electricity under ideal weather conditions. Static lines are set more conservatively, for the worst-case scenario.

Adding topographic software so grid operators can direct electricity from cheaper sources along more efficient routes to where it’s needed.

The project’s sponsors will put up an additional $150 million for a total price tag of $325 million.

Brightbill was in Indiana to announce the selection of 31 projects nationwide worth more than $5 billion. The $1.9 billion in federal investments are set to leverage an additional nearly $3.4 billion.

“Selected projects will reconduct or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission infrastructure. They will deploy cutting-edge, grid-enhancing technologies across nearly 21,000 miles of transmission lines,” Brightbill said. “And, together, we are expected to unlock more than 23 gigawatts of additional grid capacity. That’s a lot.”

Money for the initiative was authorized under the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law during former President Joe Biden’s administration.

Originally called Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships, President Donald Trump’s administration has renamed the program to SPARK, which stands for Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades.

Nuclear regulation deal inked

Also on Thursday, Indiana became the 41st state to take over responsibility of non-energy nuclear and radioactive materials used in medical, industrial, academic and fusion technologies from the federal government.

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission can hand down oversight under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. Kentucky became the first “agreement state” in 1962. Dozens of states have followed in its stead, with Indiana the latest.

The announcement has been in the works for years. Then-Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2021 submitted a letter of intent to pursue a deal.

“Agreement state status gives us better customer service, faster permit review times — which was always an issue — faster incident responses, and lower regulatory fees,” Braun said.

The Indiana Department of Homeland Security will manage the program.

Spokeswoman Ashley Morgan said the agency will have five health physicists responsible for handling licensing and inspections.

The work will be largely funded by licensing fees. An eight-page fee schedule shows costs, mostly in the thousands, for each type of license.

The state Department of Homeland Security also houses a dedicated radiation team managing nuclear emergency response and risk, and works with communities exploring nuclear — in collaboration with the Indiana Office of Energy Development.

“Making more licensing and permitting decisions here in Indiana rather than in Washington means Hoosiers have more control over Indiana’s energy future,” Braun said, calling the deal a “necessary step for Indiana to meet our nuclear energy generation goals.”

Federal officials, however, maintain regulatory authority over all commercial nuclear power reactors, research reactors and nuclear fuel cycle facilities, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s website.

Indiana currently has no nuclear plants in operation. But Braun and other state leaders hope to “lead” the nation in nuclear energy.

Commission Chair Ho Nieh said permissions for nuclear-fueled energy production will come faster under Trump’s “new NRC.”

“If Indiana and companies in Indiana want to pursue nuclear energy, I can assure you that the NRC will not be an impediment,” he said. “We will perform our safety responsibilities with efficiency, with credibility, and predictability … There’s a new NRC that has been created here, one that is going to safely enable and accelerate the deployment of nuclear technologies in America.”

The federal agency plans to approve applications for first-of-its-kind reactors in 18 months or less, and repeat reactor types in a year or less, Nieh said.

title: Debunking the Top 5 Renewable Energy Myths - MCE Blog
description:
Renewable energy is becoming a bigger part of how we power our homes, businesses, and communities, but misconceptions still create confusion.
Myth 1: Renewable energy is unreliable Fact: Wind and solar output varies with the weather, but the power grid is designed to balance many energy sources.
Myth 2: Renewable energy is too expensive Fact: The cost of renewable technologies has fallen significantly over time.
Myth 4: Renewable energy is just as polluting as fossil fuels Fact: Every energy technology has a lifecycle footprint, including manufacturing and construction.
Myth 5: Renewable energy requires too much land Fact: Energy projects of every kind use land.
text:
Renewable energy is becoming a bigger part of how we power our homes, businesses, and communities, but misconceptions still create confusion. Let’s take a closer look at five common myths and the facts behind them.

Myth 1: Renewable energy is unreliable

Fact: Wind and solar output varies with the weather, but the power grid is designed to balance many energy sources. A diverse mix of renewables, energy storage, flexible demand, and stronger transmission helps keep electricity dependable around the clock.

Myth 2: Renewable energy is too expensive

Fact: The cost of renewable technologies has fallen significantly over time. Wind and solar also use free fuel which can help reduce exposure to changing fossil-fuel prices.

Myth 3: Renewable energy does not help when the sun is not shining or the wind is not blowing

Fact: Electricity can come from a balanced portfolio that includes solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal energy, and other resources. Batteries can save energy for later, while smart energy use can shift some demand to times when more clean power is available.

Myth 4: Renewable energy is just as polluting as fossil fuels

Fact: Every energy technology has a lifecycle footprint, including manufacturing and construction. But renewable resources such as wind and solar produce electricity without burning fuel, resulting in far lower emissions over their lifetimes than fossil-fuel generation.

Myth 5: Renewable energy requires too much land

Fact: Energy projects of every kind use land. Thoughtful planning can place renewable energy on rooftops, parking lots, brownfields, agricultural land with compatible uses, and other suitable locations while protecting communities and sensitive habitats.

The bottom line

Renewable energy is not a single technology or a one-size-fits-all solution. It is a growing set of resources that can work together to deliver cleaner, more resilient electricity. Understanding the facts helps all of us make informed choices about our energy future.

text:
A state representative has accused the Electric Reliability Council of Texas of financial malfeasance in its dealings with the ongoing 765-kV transmission line projects and asked the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture to intervene.

State Rep. Brad Buckley (R–Salado) asked Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins to oppose the projects in a post to X Wednesday, calling them “the Green New Deal’s best friend.”

His request was made in response to a post from Rollins addressing a recent siting permit upset that stopped production of a major solar project in upstate New York.

Rollins called it a win for local residents, stating that the U.S. Department of Agriculture will “continue standing with American farmers, protecting the land that feeds our nation, and ensuring rural communities have a voice when their future is on the line.”

“America should never be forced to sacrifice its most productive farmland to satisfy a radical energy agenda,” wrote Rollins.

Buckley responded to Rollins by lambasting the 765-kV transmission projects in Texas, writing that the projects “will further our dependence on unreliable wind and solar generation.”

This is about the 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (STEP), a key part of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP). It currently has two stages. Stage one consists of the three STEP-Permian transmission lines spanning more than 1,200 miles to move power from East Texas to the natural gas-rich Permian Basin.

The next stage consists of the more than $9 billion STEP Western and STEP Eastern lines that together span roughly 1,200 miles.

PUCT has approved the southern and northern STEP-Permian lines, while the central line remains under consideration.

“ERCOT cooked the books to make it so, tried to make Pablo the $6M man, [Public Utility Commission of Texas] rubber stamps the deal and hard-working Texans pay the bill,” wrote Buckley.

Buckley was referencing a recent decision by ERCOT to grant a roughly $6 million contract extension to ERCOT CEO Pablo Vegas. The decision was reversed after Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick pushed back, writing that “this is not the time to give the CEO of ERCOT a multi-million-dollar pay raise on the backs of ratepayers.”

Buckley is not the first to criticize the connection between the transmission line project and unreliable energy dependence.

State Sen. Kevin Sparks (R–Midland) expressed concern in late July that wind and solar would flood the new 765-kV lines. The concern is backed by an analysis from Brent Bennett of the Texas Public Policy Foundation.

“In the absence of market reform that would better value reliability and stop overpaying wind and solar, the 765-kV [Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan] will primarily be used to move wind and solar around the state, responding to the huge temporal and geographic swings in their output,” Bennett told Texas Scorecard.

Private landowners have also recently filed a forensic audit request with PUCT to examine ERCOT’s dealings with the transmission projects, specifically comparing ERCOT’s 2024 Permian Basin model with its Regional Transmission Plan.

“We’re not accusing ERCOT of ‘cooking the books,’” one landowner said. “We’re saying the difference in the models [is] too significant, and they must be investigated.”

Buckley asked Rollins to oppose the project and “call for a pause until the people’s representatives take this up in the 90th [legislative session].”

Texas’ next legislative session is scheduled to begin on January 12.

ERCOT has not responded to a request for comment.

title: Super El Niño and Climate Change: What is the connection? - Frontier Group
description:
Scientists are warning that there is a high likelihood that, from October through December, El Niño will break current records, surpassing the strength of all previously recorded El Niño events.
If this happens, it will likely make it not just a “very strong” El Niño but the strongest El Niño ever recorded.
Because El Niño events transfer heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, El Niño years already experience higher-than-average surface temperatures.
Another challenge has been the dearth of long-term data on El Niño events, as detailed historical records of El Niño events began only in 1950 — too short a period for scientists to be able to accurately identify any clear trends.
Other scientists maintain that current evidence does not definitively prove that climate change is linked to worsening El Niño episodes.
text:
The forecast is in: El Niño continues to strengthen and is likely to evolve into what the National Weather Service terms “a very strong event,” or in common parlance, a “super El Niño,” this fall and winter. Scientists are warning that there is a high likelihood that, from October through December, El Niño will break current records, surpassing the strength of all previously recorded El Niño events.

El Niño is one of the most powerful drivers of extreme weather changes. Water in the Central and Eastern Pacific warms substantially, causing major shifts in atmospheric circulation, air temperature and precipitation patterns.

The wild weather accompanying this year’s super El Niño is just the latest in a series of extreme weather events around the world in the last year. Many types of extreme weather events are becoming more frequent and/or more extreme due to human-caused global warming.

But is the super El Niño one of them? And, when it comes to our response to climate change, how much does it matter?

This year’s El Niño: What can we expect?

El Niño itself is not unusual. A natural climate cycle, recurring every two to seven years, an El Niño is characterized as the warming of sea surface temperatures by +0.5° Celsius above normal levels. A “super” or “very strong” El Niño is defined as warming of +2° Celsius above normal. The National Weather Service is forecasting a greater-than-90% chance that the current El Niño will intensify into a super El Niño this year, and that, between October and December 2026, there is a 75% chance that surface temperature will rise to +2.5° Celsius above normal. If this happens, it will likely make it not just a “very strong” El Niño but the strongest El Niño ever recorded.

El Niño, even at its mildest, has a profound impact on countless lives and livelihoods. Here in the U.S., El Niño creates conditions for warmer winters in the north and wetter, cooler winters in the south, heightening the risk of flash floods. During the summer months, El Niño climate patterns amplify hurricane activity in the Central and Eastern Pacific.

Because El Niño events transfer heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, El Niño years already experience higher-than-average surface temperatures. A rise in ocean surface temperature of the magnitude currently being forecast for this year makes it increasingly likely that 2027 will become the hottest year on record, with some forecasters projecting that global average temperatures could reach 1.7 or 1.8° Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Already, August 2026 was the warmest August on record.

A super El Niño of the scale predicted for this year is projected to cause failed harvests; destruction of roads, electricity grids and other key infrastructure from flooding, with total financial losses of upwards of a trillion dollars; as well as increased disease burden.

El Niño and climate change: What do we know?

After a summer of wildfires, drought, flash flooding, extreme heat and other weather disasters — both in the U.S. and around the world — the looming super El Niño feels like a continuation of climate-change fueled weather events. But is it?

That is a question not so easily answered.

El Niño is an extremely complex phenomenon, subtly shaped by interactions between winds, ocean currents and fluctuations in sea-surface temperatures. These interconnected processes make it difficult for climate models to simulate the effects of global warming on El Niño. Another challenge has been the dearth of long-term data on El Niño events, as detailed historical records of El Niño events began only in 1950 — too short a period for scientists to be able to accurately identify any clear trends.

Both of these factors have made it difficult for the scientific community to establish a clear relationship between climate change and El Niño intensity. This lack of consensus was reflected in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) most recent assessment report, released in 2023, which abstained from commenting on its confidence regarding the effect of climate change on the El Niño phenomenon.

However, recent research suggests that El Niño events may be growing stronger in parallel with rising global temperatures caused mainly by the burning of fossil fuels. A study published in Science in August 2026 attempts to overcome the lack of long-term data about El Niño events using cores from fossil corals in the Galápagos Islands to estimate historical seawater temperatures and unlock a 1,000-year-long dataset capturing the intensity of El Niño events.

With this new trove of evidence, the researchers arrived at the conclusion that global warming has likely exacerbated the strength of El Niño episodes. Fossil coral core samples revealed that El Niño cycles were relatively stable from 1000 to 1850 — before the onset of human industrial activity. With the introduction of the unprecedented release of greenhouse gases beginning in 1850 and continuing into the 1980s, sea surface temperatures showed an increase in variation that the researchers claimed could not be explained by natural variability. The study identified that swings in temperature during El Niño events have intensified by over 36% since before the industrial era and jumped by 16% in just the last four decades, suggesting that this intensification may continue to accelerate.

Some researchers believe that the new findings are bringing science closer to a consensus that climate change is leading to stronger El Niño events. Kim Cobb, a scientist who worked on the IPCC’s 2023 report, recently remarked that “We are edging close to saying climate change has already had a considerable impact on the strength of El Niño” in anticipation of the next IPCC report, slated for release in 2029.

The issue is far from settled, however. Other scientists maintain that current evidence does not definitively prove that climate change is linked to worsening El Niño episodes. University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann points to “a substantial decline” in El Niño temperature variations in recent decades. John Bruno, a marine scientist at the University of North Carolina, contends that the observations collected with the coral fossils could be mostly the result of greenhouse gas-related warming, not variations in El Niño strength.

If these scientists are correct, their findings are no cause for comfort, since they reinforce that the effects of human-induced ocean warming are real and profound. Even if climate change doesn’t bring with it more extreme El Niño variations like the one we’re experiencing this year, it is still causing dramatic changes that could bring more severe impacts and unpleasant surprises in the years and decades to come.

Getting a clearer sense of whether and how climate change is affecting El Niño is important to help us prepare for the impacts. But it doesn’t change the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. And by reminding us of the damage that extreme weather events can do, this year’s El Niño should remind us why doing so is more urgent than ever.

text:
ALLENTOWN, Pa. -- The Energy Department announced on Thursday that it will spend almost $2 billion to try to squeeze more electricity out of the nation's aging and stressed power grid, as President Donald Trump's administration steps up efforts to avoid blackouts amid skyrocketing energy demand spurred by artificial intelligence.

The money will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity - enough to power 16 million homes. The projects will use new technologies such as sensors and other devices to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested or overloaded paths, the department said.

The upgrades could improve power reliability and lower electricity costs for about 100 million Americans, officials said.

"These investments will get more out of the infrastructure we already have, move more electricity across the grid, and help deliver affordable, reliable and secure power that will fuel American prosperity for decades to come," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement.

Wright was set to promote the grant program Thursday at a PPL Corp. facility in Allentown. The utility says two data centers in its territory came online this year and six more are under construction.

The announcement comes amid warnings that AI's voracious demand for power is threatening to overwhelm U.S. power supplies, as massive new data centers come online faster than new power plants can be built. It also comes as electricity bills rise faster than inflation in many parts of the U.S., blamed in some areas on demand from data centers.

The snowballing opposition to data centers in communities across the country has thrown a wrench into the plans of the world's richest companies and transformed the midterm election landscape.

Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both major political parties criticize them and many communities try to block them. Trump, a Republican, said last month that U.S. communities that don't have data centers will "end up being backwards and poor."

In the meantime, Congress and some states are trying to push regulators to require utilities to use technology and new components to make grids more efficient and better able to serve new customers without additional power sources.

Utilities - which have seen rising profits and share prices during the data center-fueled energy boom - tend to stay away from such efficiencies because they make more money from building new power plants and grid infrastructure projects that are more expensive and take longer to complete, utility critics say.

Projects being announced Thursday will involve component enhancements on more than 1,500 miles (2,400 kilometers) of transmission lines and technological enhancements across nearly 21,000 miles (34,000 kilometers), the department said.

Projects were prioritized based on those that can be put into operation quickly, officials said. Money for the grants comes from the bipartisan infrastructure law enacted by Congress under then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat. The government's $1.9 billion in funding will be matched by $3.35 billion in cost-share funding from the recipients, the Energy Department said.

Trump has vowed to "unleash" the nation's energy sector in his second term, aiming to drive up record-setting domestic oil and gas production, strip away pollution restrictions on power plants and keep expensive coal-fired power plants operating past their retirement dates.

His administration has pushed to help tech giants build and connect data centers to power plants and high-voltage power lines and convert Cold War-era uranium enrichment plants into data center and power plant complexes.

Trump's Environmental Protection Agency this summer issued a plan that would make it harder for the public to learn about and comment on proposed AI data centers.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced Thursday that Ohio will receive more than $100 million from the federal government to improve the state's electrical grid, targeting upgrades to existing transmission lines.

The federal government announced at an event in Columbus that it will invest $130 million to upgrade existing transmission lines, matched with the same amount of private investment from companies like First Energy and American Electric Power. This is part of a wider $1.9 billion investment in 26 states announced Thursday to rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission lines and deploy what the DOE calls "Grid-Enhancing Technologies" across nearly 21,000 miles.

The upgrades will mean more power will be able to flow through the lines at one time. The federal government project narrative said this will improve reliability, reduce congestion, accelerate interconnection of new load and generation, and enhance operational flexibility.

Officials stress the need for the grid to keep up with rapid growth in artificial intelligence technology and manufacturing. Central Ohio is a hub for data centers, but also new technology projects with the Intel semiconductor plant in New Albany and Anduril military drone factory in Pickaway County.

U.S. Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly said the funds will incentivize development for new technologies, but the government wants to also make energy more affordable.

"We are on the cusp of an absolutely extraordinary expansion of both technology and manufacturing in the United States, all of which requires this predicate basis of energy beforehand," Danly said.

New transmission lines have largely been the cause of increasing electric bills in Ohio. Danly said the U.S. won't be competitive if the existing grid isn't upgraded as well, allowing new energy capacity to power technology projects.

Danly said nuclear modules, revitalized nuclear power plants and natural gas plants are how the U.S. will achieve a goal of President Donald Trump's administration to create 400 gigawatts of new power by 2050. Currently, the U.S. electric grid has more than one terawatt of power capacity, or more than 1,000 gigawatts.

When asked by reporters, Danly didn't put an exact figure to potential reductions to utility bills. He said it will be difficult to predict exactly what rate impacts are going to be, but the aim is to make costs affordable for ratepayers.

"There is no doubt though that all things being equal, the more efficient the conductor is used, the less the cost of your transmission bill is going to be," Danly said.

Danly tried to frame the increasing demand for electricity as a good thing, because it is an indicator of economic growth. Many in central Ohio have told state utility regulators to reign in higher electric bills due to the increased demand.

"If you have a location in which nobody wants electricity, that's a place where nobody's trying to do anything. So the sign of a healthy economy is one in which you are constantly trying to meet demand that's rising, because that demand is the sign of all of those activities that require electricity," Danly said.

Public Utilities Commission of Ohio Chair Jennifer French, the chief utility regulator for the Buckeye State, said these advanced transmission technologies can provide additional capacity to the system without requiring new construction. She said this ensures the state responsibly and affordably enhances the grid.

"As we work collectively to meet the moment, the funding announced today will play an important role in the deployment of advanced transmission technologies across the country," French said.

The buildout is expected to take 48 months.

text:
Honda is looking to build another assembly plant in Ohio, according to a report by Automotive News.

The new plant, which would be Honda's eighth in North America, would focus on hybrid-vehicle assembly and could cost up to $2.5 billion to build.

The plant would likely be operational by 2030 and might produce the proposed three-row "Acura XL" and Honda "Pilot XXL," if the transaction is finalized.

Honda has hit a bit of a rough patch. Earlier this year, it canceled the development of three EVs that were slated to be built in the United States and projected a massive financial hit for 2026, citing the volatile U.S. EV market, tariffs, and changing vehicle tastes in China.

But Honda has big plans to bounce back within the next few years, and a potential eighth North American assembly plant might make the company's ambitious production goals more attainable.

The Japanese automaker currently has seven assembly plants in North America. Four of those are located in the U.S., with two plants in Ohio, one in Indiana, and one in Alabama. If the transaction gets completed, it looks like an eighth plant would add another tally to Ohio.

Honda CEO Toshihiro Mibe first mentioned the brand was weighing another plant in July. Now, a new Automotive News report claims Honda is currently in the final stages of negotiations, and Ohio is the brand's top contender. If an agreement is made, the new plant could begin vehicle production by 2030.

The proposed third Ohio plant would specialize in hybrid vehicles, and Honda has more than enough in the pipeline to keep the factory busy. In May, the automaker announced a plan to introduce 15 models globally by 2030 and placed a heavy emphasis on its next-generation hybrid system.

Most of these new models will be aimed at North America, which is Honda's most profitable market. We've already seen a few reports of Honda's future plans, with an "Acura XL" SUV expected to begin production in 2029 and a Honda "Pilot XXL" tentatively scheduled for 2032. The automaker has also shown prototypes of a Honda hybrid sedan and an Acura hybrid SUV, and it's reportedly considering building a lifted Accord SUV.

These new vehicles are projected to run on Honda's next-gen hybrid system, which the automaker says will increase fuel efficiency by 10 percent and cut costs by 30 percent. Honda is reportedly hoping to cut costs across the board, as it recently met with suppliers and asked for price reductions that would save the company $9.4 billion by 2030.

However, if Honda wants to fulfill its 15-model plan, it'll have to invest in more space. Honda's North American assembly plants are already running at about 90 percent capacity and produce some of Honda's most profitable models, including the CR-V, Accord, Civic, Odyssey, and Pilot. Another plant would give the company room for growth, especially since it would allow more vehicles to be built and sold without import tariffs.

Honda expects to spend up to $2.5 billion on the proposed Ohio plant, according to the AN report. And the hybrid-focused plant could reportedly manufacture the aforementioned large SUVs.

text:
A project to wring more capacity out of existing power lines will help suppliers like PPL Electric Utilities improve reliability and affordability for customers, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Thursday.

As the energy industry scrambles to meet surging electricity demand, largely from AI data centers, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) is poised to spend nearly $2 billion to help fund 31 grid improvement projects in 26 states.

“Energy is life,” Wright said in a news conference near Allentown, where he met with Lehigh Valley leaders. “Get energy policy right, and you create a community with tremendous opportunity, affordability. You attract businesses, which bid up wages. You create a stronger, more thriving community.”

That philosophy guides the DOE in the Trump administration, he said.

“Every project is evaluated in economics — Is that going to increase energy supply, drive down energy prices, and increase energy security? Because that’s how America thrives,” Wright said.

The program, in partnership with utilities that will contribute $3.4 billion, will rebuild or modernize 1,500 miles of transmission lines and deploy grid-enhancing technologies over 21,000 miles, increasing capacity nationally by 23 gigawatts.

Allentown-based PPL is slated to get up to $71.5 million to rebuild about 30 miles of high-voltage transmission lines to improve resilience, increase capacity and replace aging support structures. It will benefit the company’s customers in the Susquehanna Valley, Greater Lehigh Valley and Northeast Pennsylvania, the company said in a news release.

“By modernizing critical infrastructure with advanced technologies, we’re strengthening a key transmission corridor and nearly tripling its grid capacity while improving our ability to monitor system performance,” PPL President Christine Martin said at the event with Wright.

The technologies employed in PPL’s Montour Grid project will include advanced conductors that can carry more electricity and a fiber optic system that will allow the company to monitor strain in the wires and other environmental conditions.

Earlier this year, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed legislation as part of the state budget that would require utilities to assess whether the technologies could save ratepayers money before applying for approval to build new power lines.

Facing voters in the midterm elections this fall, elected leaders and candidates across the country have been straining to answer concerns about soaring electricity prices, as data center proposals drive demand forecasts to unprecedented levels.

Wright said the recipients of grants under the DOE’s SPARK Initiative were chosen because of their willingness to invest their own money in the technology.

“PPL won an award two months ago because they focus on their ratepayers, they focus on their communities to build smart, thriving communities,” Wright said, adding that the project is in line with the Trump administration’s prioritization of the economy in its energy policy.

Since taking office in his second term, President Donald Trump has ended support for renewable energy resources such as wind and solar in favor of fossil fuels and nuclear energy. The DOE has also ordered owners of coal, oil and natural gas fired power plants that were slated to close to keep them on standby for spikes in electricity use.

“We lost our way, and we started to spend money only based on decarbonization goals, forgetting American people, forgetting taxpayers, forgetting jobs and opportunity,” Wright said.

The funds for the SPARK initiative come from the bipartisan infrastructure law that former President Joe Biden signed into law.

“We are reallocating funds that were already dedicated towards the United States electricity grid, but just driving them towards reliability and affordability instead of making things more expensive for political posturing,” Wright said.

Wright added that new demand for electricity can result in lower costs for retail ratepayers but it depends on suppliers negotiating the right deal with large users. In March, the Trump administration announced it had reached an accord with hyperscale data center and AI companies to carry the costs of their energy consumption.

Under the pledge, AI and data center developers would be required to, “build, bring, or buy all of the energy needed for building and operating data centers, paying the full cost of their energy and infrastructure, no matter what.”

A bill with similar intentions passed the U.S. House in August. The Ratepayer Protection Act would require state utility regulators to explore strategies to make data centers pay their own way.

Martin, PPL’s president, said the commonwealth has seen “a lot of data center interest” particularly in the utility’s service area. A major data center campus is under construction in Salem Township, Luzerne County, adjacent to the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station nuclear plant.

PPL also announced last year it had formed a joint venture with Blackstone Infrastructure to build, own and operate new gas-fired power plants to supply AI data centers under long-term energy service contracts.

“As we see this new large load entering our system over the next few years, those customers will be paying for a much more significant portion of our transmission system,” Martin said, noting that it expects its service agreements to grow from 11 gigawatts to 30 gigawatts.

“That is a huge amount of load over which to spread the cost of a fixed asset. So we will see costs for all other customers coming down,” she said, adding that PPL is the only utility in the commonwealth to have a large-load rate structure that requires those customers to pay for growth.

About Good Jobs Western North Carolina Good Jobs Western North Carolina brings together 11 community colleges, employers, philanthropy and regional partners across 23 counties to expand pathways to good jobs and strengthen the region’s workforce.
text:
The Rockefeller Foundation becomes the first national philanthropy to commit to this regional initiative, triggering a matching commitment from the John M. Belk Endowment.

$3.2 million in previously raised funds awarded to 11 community colleges in the region to train and place 1,200 people into good jobs, promising jobs, and work-based learning in health care, skilled trades, and manufacturing.

ASHEVILLE, N.C. | September 24, 2026 — America Achieves today announced $3.3 million in new philanthropic commitments to Good Jobs Western North Carolina, a regional effort to help residents of 23 counties land good jobs and to build the talent systems that will keep that work going. The New York-based Rockefeller Foundation is committing $1 million over two years — the first national philanthropy to invest in this effort — triggering a matching two-year $2 million investment from John M. Belk Endowment. The North Carolina GlaxoSmithKline Foundation also recently announced it is joining the Good Jobs WNC funding coalition, adding an in-state partner with deep roots in apprenticeship and work-based learning. Good Jobs WNC is a large-scale rural regional talent system intervention, and its built-in learning loop will surface the specific barriers that keep people from reaching good jobs, giving policymakers, policy shapers, college and K-12 leaders, and philanthropists a clear picture of what needs to change in policy, funding, and institutional practice to scale and sustain this work.

MC Belk Pilon, President and Board Chair of the John M. Belk Endowment, and Jon Schnur, CEO of America Achieves, made the announcements at the Good Jobs Western North Carolina Summit, which brought together hundreds of employers, education and workforce leaders, policymakers, local funders, and 11 national foundations to advance the region’s work and consider what it means for communities nationwide. The Summit is co-hosted by the John M. Belk Endowment, America Achieves, AMY Wellness Foundation, Dogwood Health Trust, The Leon Levine Foundation, and WNC Bridge Foundation, several of which have been engaged in Western North Carolina’s recovery since the earliest days after the storm.

That work is the backdrop for this week’s announcements, which come two years after Hurricane Helene struck the region. The recovery that followed has been extraordinary in its scope and its persistence: rebuilding roads, homes, water systems, and businesses, and sustaining families and communities through a long and difficult stretch. Many of the philanthropies now backing Good Jobs Western North Carolina funded immediate relief and then the slower, less visible work of rebuilding. As the region moved from response to recovery, its community colleges and local partners began asking what their role should be in rebuilding the regional economy for the long term, and how to connect residents to good jobs. Good Jobs Western North Carolina emerged from that locally led effort.

The Rockefeller Foundation’s commitment will support its Big Bet on Good Jobs for America, a three-year, $100 million strategy launched in April 2026. The strategy supports locally driven approaches that connect people, particularly in distressed and underserved communities, to good jobs, while spreading effective practices to expand economic opportunity in communities across the country.

The Good Jobs Western North Carolina Steering Committee also announced today $3.2 million from the Good Jobs Program Fund to help all 11 community colleges in the region train and place 1,200 people into good jobs, promising jobs, and work-based learning in the region’s 23 counties. The funding will help colleges expand and redesign training with local employers so more residents can access jobs with good pay, benefits and opportunities to advance.

“This funding will provide western North Carolinians new opportunities to build careers in the communities they call home,” said Governor Josh Stein. “This initiative is preparing people for good jobs, supporting businesses’ searches for skilled workers, and strengthening the region’s economic recovery for years to come.”

“Good Jobs Western North Carolina is a model for how to help people get and keep good jobs at a time of profound transformation in the labor market,” said Dr. Rajiv J. Shah, President of The Rockefeller Foundation. “This effort stood out to us because it brings together employers, educators, and the public sector to train people for the work employers need and help them get hired. The Rockefeller Foundation is proud to be the first national philanthropy to join this initiative as part of our $100 million Big Bet to connect Americans to the dignity of work in a changing economy.”

The Good Jobs Framework, developed by America Achieves, guides the initiative’s work across 11 community colleges and 23 counties to expand education, training and employment access for low-income residents of Western North Carolina. The goal is twofold: prepare and place more residents into good jobs in Western North Carolina, and translate that experience and lessons learned to build evidence, tools, and recommendations to improve education and workforce policy at large scale at the state and national levels.

“This work began with listening to the people who know Western North Carolina best: its community college leaders, employers, and residents,” said MC Belk Pilon, President and Board Chair of the John M. Belk Endowment. “Their leadership has brought us to this point. We are thrilled that national philanthropy will build on local communities to help make sure that this region not only delivers strong local programs but develops lessons learned and tools to take lasting pathways to economic mobility to a much larger scale.”

“Western North Carolina’s colleges and employers are working together to build scalable models to help people get good jobs that employers need to fill,” said Jon Schnur, CEO of America Achieves. “This initiative and the Good Jobs Framework guide and support that programming — and will inform the design of a system enabling this type of work statewide for the long-term. Philanthropy is intended here to finance the transition, not permanently subsidize the system.”

The initiative will share tools, labor-market findings, playbooks, and policy recommendations gained from implementation so other communities and states can adapt the approach.

The initiative builds on bipartisan National Governors Association (NGA) calls for states to take action. Good Jobs Western North Carolina was introduced publicly in April as part of America Achieves’ broader Good Jobs Economy national work that was first announced by then-NGA Chair Oklahoma Governor Stitt and current NGA Chair Maryland Governor Wes Moore at the NGA summer meeting in 2025. At the time, Governor Stitt called on governors to “build strong bridges between millions of Americans seeking good jobs and the employers eager to hire them” — including by establishing a “Good Jobs Fund that supports scalable, high-impact workforce solutions.”

At the summit, Governor Stein’s Senior Advisor Sharon Decker described the just-released Western North Carolina Economic Recovery Plan to continue the region’s recovery and rebuilding post Hurricane Helene. The plan calls for $20 million to support Good Jobs WNC — and highlighted Good Jobs WNC as one of the core current priorities for the region.

Investments in 11 Community Colleges across Western North Carolina

These investments will help local residents attain good-paying jobs, address labor market shortages in health care, advanced manufacturing and skilled trades, and support the region’s recovery from Hurricane Helene. Programs range from expanded nursing education and paid manufacturing training to shorter skilled-trades certificates and class schedules that better accommodate working adults.

The initiative builds on early support from North Carolina philanthropy, including the John M. Belk Endowment and The Leon Levine Foundation — and then an expansion of that support from NCCCS Foundation, SECU Foundation, AMY Wellness Foundation, WNC Bridge Foundation, C.D. Spangler Foundation, Cannon Foundation, Dogwood Health Trust, Pisgah Health Foundation, and NC GSK Foundation.

Through its Good Jobs Program Fund, the initiative pairs flexible funding with hands-on support to help colleges redesign programs around employer demand and track whether participants move into better-paying work. America Achieves provides technical assistance in partnership with the John M. Belk Endowment and regional funder leaders.

Today’s grants build on an initial planning phase that brought all 11 colleges together to examine labor market data, identify priority occupations and develop programs with employers. Colleges used a regional labor market analysis from Strada Education Foundation and the Good Jobs Western North Carolina Data Hub, powered by Julius Education and co-developed with America Achieves.

The resulting portfolio involves 48 employer partners engaged in activities that include curriculum development, hiring and financial or other contributions. Partnerships connect classroom learning with opportunities such as paid work experience, clinical training and guaranteed interviews.

Current college plans project approximately 1,200 participants during the first two years — about 900 in job placements and about 300 in work-based learning such as internships, clinical rotations and apprenticeships. The projections include new program completers, existing students and workers pursuing advancement. Colleges will track credential completion, job placement, wages and retention. Investments in instructors, equipment and employer partnerships build capacity to serve additional students each academic year.

“The education we provide must reflect the skills and expectations of today’s employers, and the best way to ensure that alignment is to design programs with employers at the table from the very beginning,” said Dr. Mark Poarch, President of Caldwell Community College and Technical Institute. “For working learners, access is equally important. Programs must fit the realities of their lives through flexible scheduling, relevant instruction, comprehensive support services, and clear pathways to employment. This funding gives us the opportunity to bring those elements together at scale alongside partners who share our commitment to student success and regional economic growth. Together, we are creating stronger pathways to Good Jobs for more residents while helping employers build the skilled workforce they need to thrive.”

These grants will support:

Asheville-Buncombe Technical Community College: Expanded electrical, plumbing and HVAC pathways, with multiple entry points for students and workers.

Blue Ridge Community College: Engineering and advanced manufacturing pathways, including new introductory academies that lead toward further credentials.

Caldwell Community College & Technical Institute: Expanded nursing capacity through additional instructional and simulation support.

Haywood Community College: Expanded commercial driver training, including a daytime option.

Isothermal Community College: Short-term certificates in HVAC, construction trades and electrical systems that students can build on over time.

Mayland Community College: Expanded registered nursing education, with additional instruction, clinical coordination and student support.

McDowell Technical Community College: M3 Manufacturing Momentum, connecting foundational manufacturing training with further education and guaranteed interviews with participating employers.

Southwestern Community College: Two programs: a 14-week HVAC certificate with workplace learning and an evening practical nursing track.

Tri-County Community College: A new practical nursing program developed with regional healthcare employers.

Western Piedmont Community College: Strengthened mechatronics, machining and welding pathways, including opportunities for apprenticeships and internships.

Wilkes Community College: Paid Work & Learn opportunities in advanced manufacturing, alongside career exploration and training for current workers across manufacturing, health care and skilled trades.

Employer partnerships are already taking shape including:

At McDowell Technical Community College, Baxter Healthcare, Smurfit WestRock and Columbia Forest Products have committed to interviewing graduates of the college’s manufacturing training program and referring job candidates to the program.

At Western Piedmont Community College, agreements with AUMOVIO, Leviton and Case Farms identify hiring needs and support curriculum development and work-based learning.

At Southwestern Community College, the college is working with Ward Plumbing, Heating and Air on a paid learning opportunity tied to a specified minimum starting wage.

At Caldwell Community College and Technical Institute, partnerships with Bernhardt, Fairfield Chair, McCreary Modern and Lectra helped launch the college’s Furniture Factory Lab, providing hands-on training in upholstery and industrial sewing in a simulated factory environment.

Building a lasting Good Jobs Talent System

The colleges’ experience is intended to build evidence for a Good Jobs Talent System: a statewide strategy that aligns colleges, employers, K–12 education, workforce boards and government around measurable goals. Lessons from the regional work can help identify changes in policy, funding and institutional practices needed to connect more people to good jobs.

In 2027 and 2028, the Good Jobs Program Fund will support additional programming across the 11 colleges as they launch second and third pathways in regional priority sectors, including health care, advanced manufacturing, and the skilled trades. Building on these investments in individual programs, subsequent rounds will pair pathway expansion with continued technical assistance to support college-wide implementation. The goal is to embed a consistent approach across priority sectors: using local labor market data, validating demand directly with employers, designing programs around hiring commitments, and tracking whether graduates secure good jobs.

This expansion coincides with North Carolina’s implementation of Propel NC, a new funding formula that prioritizes high-wage, high-demand sectors and establishes funding parity between workforce continuing education and curriculum programs. This creates a stronger foundation for sustaining the work: philanthropy can cover the upfront costs of developing pathways, while enrollment-based state funding helps support ongoing instruction as successive cohorts enroll.

A Focus on Rural Healthcare Delivery The North Carolina program centers on healthcare access, particularly for communities located far from major medical hubs.

text:
BETA Technologies has commenced electric aircraft operations in North Carolina, marking a significant step in efforts to modernize rural healthcare logistics through zero-emission aviation. The Vermont-based manufacturer is deploying its ALIA CTOL conventional takeoff and landing aircraft as part of the Federal Aviation Administration's Electric Aircraft Integration Pilot Program (eIPP).

The initiative positions North Carolina as one of the earliest testing grounds for integrating electric fixed-wing aircraft into everyday commercial and public service operations. For aviation enthusiasts tracking the maturation of advanced air mobility, the launch represents a tangible move from demonstration flights to sustained operational use.

A Focus on Rural Healthcare Delivery

The North Carolina program centers on healthcare access, particularly for communities located far from major medical hubs. BETA is working alongside state partners to explore how quiet, low-emission aircraft can shorten transit times for medical cargo, patient services, and clinical support in areas where ground transportation is slow or unreliable.

Rural healthcare logistics have long presented challenges for providers operating across dispersed geographies. Electric aircraft, with lower operating costs than conventional turbine platforms and reduced noise footprints, offer a path to expanding the range of services that can be delivered by air without the infrastructure burden traditionally associated with fixed-wing operations.

The ALIA CTOL Aircraft

BETA's ALIA CTOL is a fixed-wing, all-electric aircraft designed for regional missions. The company has been progressing the platform through FAA certification while simultaneously flying it in real-world settings under special authorizations. The CTOL variant complements BETA's eVTOL development track and is intended to serve routes currently operated by small piston and turboprop aircraft.

By deploying the CTOL model in North Carolina, BETA can operate from existing general aviation airports without requiring the vertiport infrastructure associated with eVTOL platforms. That practical advantage has made the CTOL an early candidate for near-term commercial deployment.

The FAA Electric Aircraft Integration Pilot Program

The eIPP was established to accelerate the safe integration of electric aircraft into the National Airspace System. The program pairs manufacturers with state and local partners to identify use cases, develop operational procedures, and generate data that can inform future regulatory frameworks.

North Carolina's participation reflects a broader state-level push to attract advanced aviation activity. State officials have positioned the region as a hub for aerospace innovation, and the addition of electric aircraft operations extends that strategy into the emerging clean aviation sector.

Company Statements

Kyle Clark, BETA's founder and chief executive officer, has said,

"Supporting North Carolina's world-class healthcare systems by using cost-effective, electric flight to overcome the distance that can make it difficult to get critical supplies, specialists, and care where they need to go."

BETA has been steadily expanding its footprint across the United States, with charging infrastructure and flight operations already established in multiple states along the East Coast. North Carolina joins a growing network of regions where the company is testing the economics and practicality of electric flight in real service conditions.

Charging Infrastructure and Ground Support

Central to BETA's operational model is the buildout of its proprietary charging network. The company has deployed charging systems at airports across the country, designed to service both its own aircraft and third-party electric platforms that adopt compatible standards. The infrastructure question remains one of the most important variables in determining how quickly electric aviation can scale.

For the North Carolina operations, charging availability at supporting airfields will determine mission range and turnaround times. BETA has indicated that its infrastructure investments are intended to support not just its own operations but the broader ecosystem of electric aircraft operators expected to enter service in the coming years.

Implications for Advanced Air Mobility

The North Carolina eIPP launch signals a shift in how electric aviation is being introduced to the public. Rather than waiting for full type certification of novel eVTOL platforms, BETA and the FAA are using conventional fixed-wing electric aircraft to establish operational patterns, gather safety data, and build public familiarity with the technology.

Healthcare logistics offers a particularly compelling proving ground. The missions are typically well-defined, the value of speed is measurable, and the beneficiaries are communities that stand to gain immediately from improved connectivity. If the North Carolina program demonstrates measurable benefits, it could serve as a template for similar deployments in other states.

For enthusiasts following the electric aviation sector, the launch marks a meaningful milestone. The industry has spent years discussing potential use cases and projected capabilities. With BETA now flying in North Carolina in support of healthcare operations, the conversation is shifting toward what electric aircraft are actually doing today.

Specific fleet size, flight frequency, and financial terms of the North Carolina program have not been publicly disclosed by BETA at this stage.

title: No Blank Checks for Data Centers/AI | Congresswoman Teresa Leger Fernández
description:
Congress must act to regulate data centers with these principles in mind.
We cannot let AI and data centers regulate themselves Our water.
No Blank Checks for Data Centers Principles Don’t hike up electric bills.
Data centers must pay for their own electricity and infrastructure without passing their costs on to New Mexico families.
We cannot just let AI and data centers regulate themselves or depend on their goodwill to lower utility costs and limit the most destructive possibilities inherent in this rapidly evolving technology.
text:
What I Believe

The role of government is to protect us from greedy corporations. Data centers want our water, our land, and our power. Communities may want the jobs they could bring to New Mexico. But we will not give them a blank check. I will only support data centers that pay their own way, protect our precious water, create good-paying union jobs, use clean energy, and earn the support of the communities where they want to build. Data centers must work for New Mexico, not the other way around. Communities must know how much water and electricity these projects will use, who will pay for them, and what residents will receive in return. If a project cannot answer those questions, it should not move forward. Congress must act to regulate data centers with these principles in mind. We cannot let AI and data centers regulate themselves

Our water. Our land. Our power. Our say. Those are New Mexico’s terms.

No Blank Checks for Data Centers Principles

Don’t hike up electric bills. Data centers must pay for their own electricity and infrastructure without passing their costs on to New Mexico families.

Don’t negatively impact water resources in the area.

Use energy sources that meet New Mexico’s renewable energy and zero-carbon requirements.

Create good-paying union jobs.

Get community approval and do consultation before permitting and building.

No taxpayer subsidies, projects must provide community benefits.

AI Safety

Trump called AI concerns “a HOAX.” He said opponents of data centers “want to end up being backwards and poor.” No, Mr. President, Americans want Congress and you to do your job protecting humanity, protecting our utility bills, and protecting us from out-of-control, corrupt greed.

A principal role of government is to protect the American people. Safety must always be our first mandate. It is also the government’s job to protect the American people from unmitigated greed. The billionaires that you are listening to now would prefer the government stay on the sidelines. But the U.S. government knows how to regulate corporate greed and how to address new technologies that could destroy our world.

What we do now will matter. We cannot just let AI and data centers regulate themselves or depend on their goodwill to lower utility costs and limit the most destructive possibilities inherent in this rapidly evolving technology. We must let local communities have a say in what is built in their neighborhoods so they can protect their water, environment, and cost burdens.

But Congress must act. There must be a strong, enforceable national regulatory framework. We must have civil and criminal liability. We must protect the local and national financial interests of working families.

It is not a hoax, Mr. President. And we have a job to do.

title: Indiana receives $175 million for energy growth from DOE SPARK program
description:
On Thursday, during a news conference, Jaworowski said a new partnership between Indiana and the U.S. Department of Energy will continue to facilitate energy growth statewide.
Indiana will participate in the “Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades,” also known as SPARK, program in the DOE’s office of electricity.
According to the DOE website, the program will help fund 31 grid improvement projects across 26 states.
Through the SPARK program, Indiana will receive $175 million to expand the transfer capacity between PJM and MISO interconnection.
