description:
Maxvolt Energy has announced its upcoming battery plant in Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh.
The company has announced an investment of ₹700 crore into the battery facility with a planned capacity of 12.5 GWh.
The facility will be developed in two phases of 5 GWh each, taking the planned annual manufacturing capacity to 10 GWh.
The project is positioned as the largest upcoming battery manufacturing project in Uttar Pradesh and among the significant upcoming battery manufacturing projects in India.
At full capacity, Maxvolt Energy says the upcoming battery manufacturing plant will have an annual turnover of over ₹6,800 crore.
text:
Maxvolt Energy has announced its upcoming battery plant in Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh. The company has announced an investment of ₹700 crore into the battery facility with a planned capacity of 12.5 GWh. With the new facility, Maxvolt is expanding its portfolio into four-wheeler electric vehicle batteries, and will also scale manufacturing across electric mobility, energy storage, telecom and power backup.

The company completed the foundation ceremony at the site, which is spread over six acres. The facility will be developed in two phases of 5 GWh each, taking the planned annual manufacturing capacity to 10 GWh. The combined capacity across the two sites will reach 12.5 GWh annually. The project is positioned as the largest upcoming battery manufacturing project in Uttar Pradesh and among the significant upcoming battery manufacturing projects in India.

Speaking about the foundation ceremony, Satendra Shukla, Co-Founder & CEO, Maxvolt Energy, said, “India's battery demand is not arriving through one door. E-rickshaw fleets, solar installers, telecom operators, hospitals and households are all moving to lithium at the same time, and every one of them wants a different pack. Aligarh is built for that reality. We are not adding capacity for a single segment, we are scaling a platform that already serves several, and four-wheeler EV batteries are the next application we take on rather than the reason we are building. Dedicated OEM lines let us build to a customer's specification at volume, which is the difference between being a supplier and being a manufacturing partner.”

Mukesh Gupta, Co-Founder & CMO, Maxvolt Energy, said, “The Aligarh facility is an important milestone in Maxvolt Energy’s journey from expanding capacity to building a broader manufacturing ecosystem. The focus is not only on producing more batteries, but on creating the capabilities to serve different applications, from electric mobility and energy storage to telecom, power backup and OEM requirements. With dedicated production lines and the planned expansion into four-wheeler EV batteries, we are building greater flexibility into our manufacturing platform while creating opportunities for customers and partners across the value chain.”

The upcoming facility will manufacture battery solutions ranging from 1 kW to 5 MW. It will have BMS capabilities for slow charging as well as L3 and L5 fast-charging applications. Dedicated OEM production lines will enable the company to manufacture batteries according to individual customer specifications. At present, the company produces batteries for electric two-wheeler and three-wheeler offerings.

At full capacity, Maxvolt Energy says the upcoming battery manufacturing plant will have an annual turnover of over ₹6,800 crore. The company claims the facility will generate 1,500–2,000 direct jobs and 7,500–10,000 indirect employment opportunities across manufacturing, engineering, quality control, logistics and the wider supply chain. The firm expects India’s battery demand to rise from 3 GWh in 2022 to 54 GWh by 2027 and 127 GWh by 2030. The upcoming plant will address multiple battery requirements across mobility, storage, and OEM-specific requirements.

title: Fossil-fuel firms in line for billions in benefits after answering Trump's donation call
description:
It also highlighted that the Trump administration repealed federal vehicle greenhouse gas standards and moved to roll back emissions rules for power plants and oil and gas facilities.
Separately, the EPA estimated that the repeal would result in at least $580bn in additional fuel costs over the next three decades.

text:
The fossil fuel industry secured an estimated $190bn in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade after responding to Donald Trump’s pre-election call for major campaign donations, leaving American taxpayers to shoulder higher bills and public health costs associated with pollution, according to a new report.

Released on Thursday by Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate environment and public works committee, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, the report details what the senators describe as the fossil fuel industry’s expansive influence over the Trump administration.

Pointing to Trump’s April 2024 fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago, Florida where he reportedly asked industry executives for $1bn in campaign contributions, in exchange for tax breaks and deregulations, the report said: “Big oil delivered in the hundreds of millions.”

The senators said: “The Trump administration has delivered right back, handing polluters benefits worth hundreds of billions of dollars. That bargain came at a price, and American families are the ones paying it: higher energy bills and higher costs associated with increased damages from climate change and air and water pollution.”

The senators also cited the Trump administration’s “near-total refusal to cooperate with legitimate congressional oversight”, saying it “complicated” their investigation.

The estimate of $190bn savings for industry is calculated from existing tax breaks and subsidies over the next 10 years plus new benefits delivered by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to an analysis by Senator Bernie Sanders for legislation he proposed with Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to eliminate “handouts” for industry.

In addition to an estimated $201m investment in Trump’s re-election campaign, industry executives contributed $19m to his inaugural fund, which the report described as “the largest political investment the industry has ever made”.

In exchange, the report said Trump appointed 26 senior officials – all of whom had previously worked for fossil fuel, chemical, or other polluting industries – across various government agencies including the Environmental Protection Agency, as well as the energy and interior departments.

The report also noted that the fossil-fuel industry secured various policies that would curb competition from clean energy, increase gas and coal consumption and “force Americans to spend at least $580bn in added fuel costs alone over the next three decades”.

As part of Trump’s “big, beautiful” domestic spending bill, signed last July, the government created a $1bn direct subsidy fund for fossil fuels, using the Defense Production Act authority to “funnel taxpayer money into propping up fossil fuel projects” considered economically risky by private capital markets.

The act also provides a permanent 20% business income deduction for oil and gas companies, which the report said would cost the government an estimated $737bn overall.

The report further accuses the Trump administration of exempting companies from pollution controls, saying Trump “abused” the Clean Air Act by exempting more than 180 polluting facilities. The senators noted that “the rules at issue were designed to limit emissions of known neurotoxin and carcinogens”.

It also highlighted that the Trump administration repealed federal vehicle greenhouse gas standards and moved to roll back emissions rules for power plants and oil and gas facilities.

While the Trump administration estimated the changes would save Americans $1.3tn, the report cites an EPA estimate of $1.5tn in additional fuel, repair and maintenance costs for consumers. Separately, the EPA estimated that the repeal would result in at least $580bn in additional fuel costs over the next three decades. The report describes the policy as potentially the “single largest payback” the Trump administration has provided the fossil fuel industry.

Moreover, the report found that the Trump administration’s attacks on fossil fuel competitors include paying companies $1.8bn in taxpayer funds to cancel wind projects across the country. As of May, more than 160 projects – all proposed on private land – had been frozen.

According to the report, the stalled projects represent approximately 30 gigawatts of generating capacity, $54bn in capital investment, and enough electricity to power more than 8.5m homes. The report also pointed to Trump’s own pledge earlier this year: “My goal is to not let any windmill be built.”

The report said: “The buyouts follow the same structure: taxpayer money is used to buy off fossil fuel’s low-cost clean energy competition – a double hit, first to the public treasury, then to the electric rates.”

In the second Trump administration, environmental enforcement has also weakened. The report found that the justice department has brought 76% fewer civil environmental enforcement cases than during Joe Biden’s first year in office, and 81% fewer than during Trump’s first term.

Highlighting the impact of the fossil fuel industry’s influence on Trump and its consequences for the American public, the report stated that Trump’s “polluter-first agenda exposed Americans to price shocks on fossil fuels, heating, food production, and electricity; increased the cost of trucking food to grocery stores; and raised fertilizer prices for farmers”.

One modeling estimate cited in the report found that average household energy bills could be $78 to $192 higher per year by 2035. Industrial energy costs, meanwhile, are projected to rise by between $7bn and $11bn over the same period.

In response to the report, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told the Guardian: “These Democrat senators should do some self-reflection on their ties to the so-called ‘green’ energy industry. They wasted billions of American taxpayer dollars in the name of the Green New Scam.

“While they are focused on a useless partisan report, the Trump administration is actively working to pass historic permitting reform to help improve energy infrastructure and lower costs.”

The administration has hailed its “energy dominance” agenda as delivering for industry, energy workers and saving the US public money in energy costs.

The report, however, said the sharpest increases could ironically fall on Republican-led states that lack state-level policies supporting renewable energy development.

In addition to rising energy costs, the report pointed to the public health costs associated with Trump’s policies, noting that fossil fuel-related air pollution and climate-related harms cost approximately $820bn annually, or roughly $2,500 per person in additional health costs each year.

“Even if Americans do not suffer from polluter-driven heart or respiratory disease, they pay more as health insurance companies spread around those costs,” the report said.

Homeowner insurance costs are also rising as climate-driven disasters become more frequent and severe. The report noted that the average American homeowner now pays “about $2,948 per year in insurance premiums, nearly 12% higher than just one year ago”.

The report also found that in 2025, fossil fuel companies paid more to shareholders than the direct damages attributable to extreme weather in the US, despite surges in hurricanes, wildfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts.

Several environmental advocacy organizations have criticized the Trump administration in response to the report.

Climate Power spokesperson Alex Glass told the Guardian: “This report lays it out in black and white. The Trump administration isn’t setting energy policy; the fossil fuel industry is writing it for them. Fossil fuel money bought access, and fossil fuel executives got the keys to the agencies meant to regulate.”

Similarly, Mahyar Sorour, the director of beyond fossil fuels policy at the Sierra Club, said: “This report elevates a troubling reality: while fossil fuel companies throw money at politicians to fulfill polluters’ wishlists, American families are left paying for an energy system that puts corporate profits ahead of public health.

“It’s time to make polluters pay.”

Meanwhile, David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s climate program, told the Guardian: “The campaign contributions to Donald Trump by big oil have paid dividends, and have allowed the fossil fuel industry to continue to pollute our communities … Every American family struggling with high costs is suffering because of the corrupt relationship between Donald Trump and the fossil fuel industry.”

title: Dirty tricks: Why is Congress voting to scrap California's clean air protections? - The Hill
authors: Dori Chandler, opinion contributor, Dori Chandler, opinion contributor
description:
The primary argument for taking away California’s waiver has been cost.
Taking away California’s waiver would therefore produce no meaningful savings for consumers.
But that leaves out a critical fact: California’s program does not require every ship to use shore power.
Goods continue moving through California’s ports without disruption.
Senators who claim to care about public health must reject this measure and preserve California’s waiver.
text:
Just last week, the U.S. House of Representatives voted to revoke a federal waiver that allows California to protect its residents from cancer-causing pollution released by ships, most of them foreign, docking at the state’s ports.

Americans should understand just how reckless this is — and why the consequences extend beyond California.

The waiver allows California to enforce its Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth Regulation. In plain terms, the program requires ships to stop pumping toxic diesel exhaust, proven to cause detrimental health outcomes, into the air while they are docked.

These shipping companies have valid solutions available. They can plug into shore power (the electric grid) and turn off their engines, or they can use technology that captures pollutants before they reach nearby communities.

Even when a ship is not moving, it typically keeps diesel-powered auxiliary engines running to supply electricity for lights, ventilation, pumps, refrigeration and other onboard systems. A vessel may remain at a port for hours or even days, releasing soot and smog-forming gases close to homes, schools and workplaces.

That pollution is not harmless. Diesel exhaust is known to the State of California to cause cancer, while exposure to air pollution is also linked to asthma, heart and lung disease, cognitive decline and premature death. The microscopic particles in diesel exhaust can travel deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

The health burden is especially severe in communities surrounding California’s busiest ports. In a 2022 survey of Wilmington residents, 54 percent reported black spots or oily residue around their homes, and 57 percent reported respiratory ailments in their households.

California created its at-berth program to stop this pollution before it reaches the air. And the program is working.

The original program achieved an 80 percent reduction in harmful emissions across more than 13,000 vessel visits beginning in 2014. California later expanded the program to cover additional vessels, including auto carriers and tankers — categories responsible for 56 percent of the fine-particle pollution produced by ocean-going vessels while docked at California ports.

The projected public health benefits of this program are substantial. Once fully implemented, California’s program is expected to reduce pollution from vessel visits by 90 percent and lower the potential cancer risk by 55 percent for communities near the ports of Los Angeles, Long Beach and Richmond. California estimates that it will deliver $2.31 billion in public health benefits.

The infrastructure has already been built. Ports, utilities and private businesses have invested. Shore-power connections and approved emissions capture systems are already operating, allowing ships to reduce their pollution without disrupting the movement of goods.

The primary argument for taking away California’s waiver has been cost. Opponents have cited large total figures to suggest the program places a significant burden on everyday Americans. But those numbers obscure what compliance actually costs when spread across the enormous quantities of goods these ships carry.

According to the federal government’s own analysis, the cost is approximately $1.14 for each shipping container, $7.66 for each automobile transported and less than 1 cent for each gallon of finished product carried by a tanker.

For context, a 20-foot shipping container holds goods worth approximately $54,500 on average. The $1.14 compliance cost amounts to roughly two-thousandths of a penny for every dollar of goods inside.

Taking away California’s waiver would therefore produce no meaningful savings for consumers. It would instead shift the far greater costs of pollution from international shipping and oil companies onto California families, workers and taxpayers through preventable illness, missed work and higher health care expenses.

On the House floor, lawmakers also argued that oil tankers cannot connect to shore power. But that leaves out a critical fact: California’s program does not require every ship to use shore power. When plugging in is not practical, vessels can use state-approved emissions capture and control technology instead. In fact, major oil companies are currently using the technology at California ports. Shell and Olympus Terminals are among the companies already being served in Southern California, while TransMontaigne has signed an agreement to use the technology at its Martinez and Richmond terminals.

The infrastructure exists. The technology works. Companies are using it. Goods continue moving through California’s ports without disruption. And the cost to consumers is negligible.

Now the decision falls to the Senate. Senators can defend a proven program that reduces cancer risk, protects communities and respects investments already made by California businesses, or they can make it easier for ships to keep pumping toxic exhaust into our air.

Californians should be watching. Senators who claim to care about public health must reject this measure and preserve California’s waiver.

Dori Chandler is a policy advocate with the Coalition for Clean Air working to protect communities from pollution caused by heavy-duty freight and shipping.

title: Data centre buildout uplifting US BESS market outlook, Wood Mackenzie says
description:
According to the latest edition of ESMO, Q2 2026 saw 6.7GW/20.2GWh of energy storage deployed across all market segments between March and the end of June.
This month, Massachusetts’ Department of Energy Resources (DOER) announced it was distributing approximately US$40 million in funding to 36 BESS projects through its Advancing Massachusetts Power Energy Storage Grant Programme.
Residential storage is forecast to decline 4% in 2026 before resuming growth from 2027 through 2031, averaging 9% annual expansion during that period.
In July, FranklinWH Energy Storage, a San Francisco Bay Area-based manufacturer of home energy management and BESS, announced it was selected to participate in two VPP programmes in Texas.
Market implications According to Wood Mackenzie’s report, data centre buildout uplifts the US storage outlook across all segments, noting that storage can provide needed capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone.
text:
The community-scale and commercial and industrial (CCI) segment deployed 48MW, reverting to typical installation volumes following what the firm noted as California’s exceptional Q1 performance tied to the net metering programme, NEM 2.0 grandfathering cutoff.

Residential installations recorded their third straight quarterly decline in Q2, dropping 15% to 676MW due to tax credit phase-outs, consumer uncertainty, and difficulties navigating the third-party-ownership (TPO) shift.

Wood Mackenzie’s total US Q2 installation numbers are a little lower than those reported a few weeks ago by the US Energy Storage Market Outlook (ESMO), a rival report from trade association Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) with research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. According to the latest edition of ESMO, Q2 2026 saw 6.7GW/20.2GWh of energy storage deployed across all market segments between March and the end of June.

Installation forecast

As previously noted, Wood Mackenzie said US BESS installations will grow over 50% in MW terms over the next five years as low costs propel storage into new regions and use cases.

Utility-scale storage is projected to expand at an 8% average annual rate over the next five years, driven by the need to balance increasing large loads and renewable generation.

Wood Mackenzie reported that project durations continued to increase in Q2 2026 with the deployment of a long-duration energy storage (LDES) project in California designed to meet state mandates and utility-contracted storage assets in Texas.

In June, REV Renewables and its parent company, US energy sector developer and investor company LS Power, commissioned the first 8-hour duration BESS in California, the Tumbleweed Energy Storage facility, installed in Kern County.

The CCI segment is expected to grow 27% between 2026 and 2031 as deployment spreads beyond California into emerging markets including Maryland and Texas.

CCI segment expansion in Hawaii, New Mexico, and Texas partially mitigated the overall decline, whilst New York and Massachusetts continued to rank among the segment’s top-performing markets.

This month, Massachusetts’ Department of Energy Resources (DOER) announced it was distributing approximately US$40 million in funding to 36 BESS projects through its Advancing Massachusetts Power Energy Storage Grant Programme.

Residential storage is forecast to decline 4% in 2026 before resuming growth from 2027 through 2031, averaging 9% annual expansion during that period.

The top five markets—California, Texas, Puerto Rico, Arizona, and Illinois—represented 88% of storage capacity installed in Q2, though all five markets experienced quarter-over-quarter declines. Notably, Puerto Rico saw the largest absolute contraction, dropping from 129MW in Q1 to 73MW in Q2.

Distributed energy resource (DER)-focused company Sunrun and Tesla recently announced that residential BESS in California discharged more than 580MW of peak power to the state’s grid on the evening of 9 September via a joint virtual power plant (VPP).

In July, FranklinWH Energy Storage, a San Francisco Bay Area-based manufacturer of home energy management and BESS, announced it was selected to participate in two VPP programmes in Texas.

In April, the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau (PREB) approved a motion from Tesla, Sunrun, and residential solar installer SunStrong Management to auto-enroll participants in an emergency capacity resource programme created by the Governing Board of the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA).

Residential energy storage startup Base Power, which in August announced a US$1 billion Series D financing at a US$13 billion post-money valuation, expanded to Illinois in June, installing BESS for customers of utility ComEd.

Market implications

According to Wood Mackenzie’s report, data centre buildout uplifts the US storage outlook across all segments, noting that storage can provide needed capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone.

The firm stated that as hyperscalers increasingly encounter grid-connection constraints, utility-scale storage will facilitate faster power access for data centres, either through on-site deployment to manage asset loads or at the system level to address evolving grid requirements.

The value proposition of distributed storage is expanding beyond customer-focused benefits to encompass grid services, as the industry positions VPPs as a “key enabler of load growth.”

Over 130GW/534GWh of utility-scale BESS will be deployed between 2026 and 2031. The utility-scale segment will experience stagnation in 2026 and 2027 as the industry adjusts to shifting supply chain dynamics. Wood Mackenzie forecast US cumulative installations to reach 207GW/715GWh by 2031, upping the firm’s previous estimates. Meanwhile, the authors of ESMO at SEIA and Benchmark predicted US cumulative installs will reach 683GWh by 2030.

Growth will resume in 2028, with the market expanding at an 11% average annual growth rate through 2031 as domestic cell manufacturing scales up. The recovery will be driven by storage deployed to manage large loads, accelerated renewable installations in advance of the 2030 production tax credit (PTC) expiration, and state-level incentives.

In August, Energy-Storage.news Premium spoke with Raafe Khan, energy storage and emerging markets head at the consultancy Camelot Energy Group, who stated around the convergence of BESS of data centres, “Even if data centres were to slow down for whatever reason, I don’t think BESS would be as disproportionately impacted as, let’s say, gas generation.”

title: Nearly 37,000 clean energy jobs lost in 2025, E2 reports - pv magazine USA
description:
The report finds that jobs were lost across all the largest sectors of the clean energy economy including energy efficiency, renewables and clean vehicles.
The U.S. energy economy employed 8.4 million workers in 2025 and lost 86,000 jobs, according to estimates by the Department of Energy (DOE).
With more than 3.5 million workers employed, the clean energy is the largest part of the U.S. energy industry, and the clean energy sector accounted for roughly 43% of all energy sector job losses, according to E2.
Florida led in clean energy job gains, with 3,800 workers added in 2025 or a gain of 2.1%.
According to E2’s Clean Economy Works project tracker, companies canceled or downsized 142 clean energy manufacturing, generation and storage projects in 2025, representing $57.8 billion in lost business investment.
text:
E2’s 2026 Clean Jobs Americareport arrives more than one year since passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) that cut incentives for clean energy manufacturing, generation and job creation.

This eleventh annual report from E2, a national, nonpartisan group, analyzes the clean energy economy nearly four years since it was boosted by the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean energy investments and six years after many industries were leveled by the Covid-19 pandemic. In the past two years, Congress and the current administration have incrementally withdrawn federal support for clean energy; a move reflected in the reported job losses.

The 36,949 jobs lost in 2025 reflect the first annual job loss in the U.S. clean economy since the economic crisis that followed the Covid-19 pandemic, ending four consecutive years of strong growth. Furthermore, it erases almost 40% of all new jobs created in 2024, the report says.

The report finds that jobs were lost across all the largest sectors of the clean energy economy including energy efficiency, renewables and clean vehicles. Only storage and grid and biofuels posting slight increases in new jobs last year.

Other energy sectors experienced a similar downturn, according to the report. The U.S. energy economy employed 8.4 million workers in 2025 and lost 86,000 jobs, according to estimates by the Department of Energy (DOE). With more than 3.5 million workers employed, the clean energy is the largest part of the U.S. energy industry, and the clean energy sector accounted for roughly 43% of all energy sector job losses, according to E2.

Clean energy employment fell in 35 states, with California experiencing the greatest loss (21,000 jobs). Florida led in clean energy job gains, with 3,800 workers added in 2025 or a gain of 2.1%.

The report notes that the national loss was concentrated in the largest job markets. As shown in the chart below, the five states with the largest drops accounted for roughly 82% of the national net job loss, including four of the top 10 states with the largest clean energy workforces.

One caveat to the job losses is that the U.S. experienced several years of momentum when 100,000 new jobs or more were added each year, and the 2025 numbers are 16% higher than 2020 levels. The report states that “long-term gains remain, but momentum has stopped.”

E2 notes that the job losses reflect a reversal and not slower growth in the clean energy industry.

“The combination of job losses and unprecedented project cancellations shows that the Trump administration’s energy policy shift beginning in 2025 is imposing measurable economic costs on businesses and workers.”

Job losses go hand in hand with project cancellations. According to E2’s Clean Economy Works project tracker, companies canceled or downsized 142 clean energy manufacturing, generation and storage projects in 2025, representing $57.8 billion in lost business investment. In the first five months of 2025, E2 reported that the cancelations, which include solar module as well as battery and electric vehicle (EV) facilities, totaled $15.5 billion in investments and were expected to create 12,000 new jobs.

[Read The ongoing economic fallout of the OBBBA]

The cancellation or downsizing of clean energy projects were expected to create an additional 84,400 new jobs (positions not included in the DOE data or this analysis). E2 reports that, combined, the existing jobs cut last year and the announced jobs that were canceled add up to more than 120,000 positions.

BW Research Partnership, which performs the underlying survey and data collection for the DOE’s annual US Energy and Employment Report, produced the data analysis used in this report. E2 reports that employment figures are based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy’s 2026 U.S. Energy & Employment Report (USEER), with prior-year comparisons from E2’s Clean Jobs America 2025. This latest data coincides with employment estimates at the end of Q4 2025.

name: EVs
title: Automakers have finally run out of excuses for overpriced EVs | Dagens.com
description:
While automakers continue to push the price of a standard gas-powered commuter car higher into the stratosphere, the once-massive premium for an electric vehicle is rapidly shriveling up.
According to reporting by InsideEVs, the average new electric car in the United States now costs just 9.4 percent more than its combustion-engine equivalent.
Meanwhile, the average electric vehicle dropped nearly 3 percent down to $54,813.
It proves that average consumers will absolutely buy an electric vehicle if manufacturers simply stop treating the technology like a boutique lifestyle statement.
The era of the electric vehicle as a heavily subsidized, overpriced novelty is dead.
text:
For years, the legacy auto industry has leaned on a single, bulletproof excuse for why electric vehicles remained an exclusive luxury purchase: the underlying technology was simply too expensive to mass-produce without massive government subsidies. But according to the latest pricing data, that entire narrative is starting to collapse.

While automakers continue to push the price of a standard gas-powered commuter car higher into the stratosphere, the once-massive premium for an electric vehicle is rapidly shriveling up. According to reporting by InsideEVs, the average new electric car in the United States now costs just 9.4 percent more than its combustion-engine equivalent. A year ago, that gap was hovering at 16 percent.

The underlying math here exposes a brutal reality about how car companies are moving inventory. In August, the average transaction price for a traditional gas-powered car ticked up nearly 2 percent to cross the $50,000 mark. Meanwhile, the average electric vehicle dropped nearly 3 percent down to $54,813. The pricing parity that executives have been promising for the better part of a decade is finally showing up on dealership lots—not because of a sudden technological breakthrough, but because automakers are actively choosing to make their gas cars prohibitively expensive.

The death of the subsidy crutch

What makes this collapsing price gap so significant is that it is happening without the artificial sugar rush of desperate factory discounts.

For the last two years, the auto industry relied heavily on massive tax credits and subsidized lease deals to artificially lower the barrier to entry for battery-powered cars. But that crutch is actively being kicked away. According to Kelley Blue Book data cited by InsideEVs, the average EV incentive actually plummeted by 20 percent over the last year, dropping from roughly $8,200 down to $6,600 in August.

The industry is now staring down the barrel of a major holiday sales season entirely devoid of the massive federal tax credits that juiced previous quarters. The fact that EV prices are still dropping while manufacturer incentives dry up signals a massive shift: the electric vehicle market is finally being dictated by brutal, unromantic supply-and-demand fundamentals rather than policy-driven panic.

It isn’t just Elon Musk anymore

Historically, whenever the average cost of an electric car dropped, it was entirely because Tesla slashed prices and dragged the rest of the market down with it. While Tesla still exerts massive gravitational pull over the sector, the current price collapse is actually being driven by legacy brands finally doing their jobs.

Rather than relying entirely on bloated, $80,000 luxury SUVs, companies like Toyota, Chevrolet, and Hyundai are finally moving serious volume on affordable commuter models. Cars like the refreshed Chevy Bolt—which starts just under $29,000—and the Toyota bZ are actively pulling the industry average down. It proves that average consumers will absolutely buy an electric vehicle if manufacturers simply stop treating the technology like a boutique lifestyle statement.

We have officially crossed a psychological tipping point. The era of the electric vehicle as a heavily subsidized, overpriced novelty is dead. It is now just a car—and pretty soon, it might be the cheaper option on the lot.

text:
Researchers at University of Waterloo have created a 3D-printed electrode that could help make it easier and safer to store large amounts of renewable energy generated by wind and solar farms.

Led by Dr. Maxime van der Heijden, the research team drew inspiration from natural structures to redesign a key component of redox flow batteries (RFBs), a technology that can store electricity for later use. The new design helps battery liquid move more efficiently, allowing the chemical reactions that store and release energy to occur more effectively.

RFBs work differently from the Li-ion batteries commonly found in phones, electric vehicles, and many energy-storage systems.

These batteries use water-based electrolytes rather than the flammable materials found in Li-ion batteries, making them a potentially safer alternative for large-scale energy storage.

RFBs are a complementary technology to Li-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage applications. Their water-based electrolytes make them a safer option for storing renewable energy at the scale needed to supply, for example, communities and the electrical grid with continuous renewable energy.

“Instead of storing energy in solid materials, they store energy in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks,” said van der Heijden, Chemical Engineering Professor. “The amount of stored energy can be increased simply by using larger tanks, making them well-suited for large-scale renewable energy storage and grid applications.”

That flexibility could become increasingly important as more electricity comes from renewable sources. Wind and solar power are intermittent, as they do not always produce electricity when it is needed, creating a need for technologies that can store excess energy and return it to the grid later.

Researchers used 3D printing to create porous RFB electrodes, enabling precise control over their structure and fluid flow.

A key innovation was the use of triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) geometries, complex, repeating three-dimensional shapes that can resemble structures found in nature.

The researchers tested several TPMS designs and found that one known as the “diamond” geometry worked best, increasing performance by 52 percent.

They then used a digital light-processing 3D printer to produce the porous structures, which were heat-treated to form conductive carbon electrodes capable of carrying electricity.

The team successfully tested the electrodes in laboratory flow cell experiments and in a working vanadium RFB, demonstrating that the 3D-printed designs can function in an operating battery. The proof of concept could help pave the way for more efficient redox flow batteries designed for large-scale energy storage.

Future research will focus on increasing the electrodes’ surface area, improving manufacturing methods and exploring advanced design tools to create even more effective electrode structures.

Here is an exclusive Tech Briefs interview, edited for length and clarity, with van der Heijden.

Tech Briefs: What was the biggest technical challenge you faced while using 3D printing to create the porous RFB electrodes?

van der Heijden: One of the biggest challenges was developing a manufacturing process that could reliably produce complex porous carbon structures with the level of precision required for battery applications. The process starts with selecting a suitable resin (and its printing properties such as illumination time as the resin is polymerized by a light source in the technology that we used (called digital light processing)) that can survive carbonization, where the printed structure is heated to temperatures of around 1,000 °C in an oxygen-free environment. During this step, the material shrinks significantly, often by roughly a factor of two in each dimension, so careful optimization of this heating step is needed to ensure the final electrode retains its intended shape and mechanical stability.

Another challenge was balancing design complexity with the practical limitations of the printer. We want to create very small and highly detailed features to maximize performance, but every printer has a finite resolution. This requires considerable fine-tuning of both the printing parameters and the electrode geometry. What is exciting is that the technology has advanced rapidly. When I published my first work on 3D-printed carbon electrodes, we were limited to much larger and less detailed structures. For the study that was just published, we used a newer generation of printers, and today we have even more capable systems in the lab. These printers are inexpensive and are generally used by people in their homes, showing how quickly additive manufacturing is evolving.

Tech Briefs: What was the biggest technical challenge you faced while testing the electrodes in lab flow cell experiments and in a working vanadium RFB?

van der Heijden: One important lesson in flow battery research is that there is no universally optimal electrode. The electrode architecture and the electrolyte chemistry need to be matched carefully because different battery chemistries are limited by different processes.

Current 3D-printed electrodes generally have a lower surface area than commercial fibrous electrodes because of the resolution limits of today's printers and the relatively smooth surfaces they produce. As a result, these electrodes are particularly attractive for electrolyte systems where mass transport (flow of the liquid electrolyte through the porous electrode structure), rather than surface area, is the dominant limitation. Organic RFB electrolytes are a good example because they often exhibit fast electrochemical kinetics (which makes surface area less important) and lower electrolyte conductivity (how well ions are transported through the battery), making efficient transport through the porous structure especially important. For that reason, we first evaluated our designs using organic electrolytes, where the benefits of the improved transport pathways using these TPMS structures could be demonstrated most clearly.

At the same time, we wanted to show that these electrodes can also operate in the most established flow battery chemistry available today, namely vanadium RFBs. That is why the study concludes with a proof-of-concept full-cell demonstration using vanadium electrolytes. While the results were promising, there is still significant room for improvement in vanadium systems, particularly by increasing surface area and catalytic activity, which are active areas of research in our group.

Tech Briefs: Do you have any set plans for such further research/work/etc.?

van der Heijden: Absolutely. One of the major goals of our current research is to combine the excellent transport properties of these 3D-printed structures with higher electrochemically active surface areas. A Ph.D. student in my group, Muhammad Zain Qamar, is leading work in this direction by incorporating advanced two-dimensional materials into our printed electrodes. This approach aims to increase both the surface area and catalytic activity of the structures, particularly interesting for vanadium RFBs. The results are very encouraging, and we see significant performance improvements compared with the materials reported in this study. We also anticipate publishing these findings in the near future.

Beyond surface engineering, we are investigating new printable resin formulations that can produce electrodes with improved surface properties. At the same time, our group has a strong computational component, and we are exploring the use of machine learning and optimization algorithms to identify next-generation electrode architectures. By combining advanced manufacturing, materials development, and data-driven design, we hope to accelerate the discovery of electrode structures that would be difficult to develop through trial and error alone.

Tech Briefs: Is there anything else you’d like to add that I didn’t touch upon?

van der Heijden: I think it is important to place this work in the broader context of energy storage. RFBs are not intended to replace Li-ion batteries. Instead, they are designed to address a different challenge: large-scale, long-duration energy storage for the electrical grid. As renewable energy generation continues to expand, we need technologies that can store large amounts of energy for extended periods and help balance the intermittent nature of for example solar and wind power or balance the grid. Flow batteries offer several attractive features for these applications, including independent scaling of power and energy, long operational lifetimes, and enhanced safety. However, advancing a technology from the laboratory to widespread deployment requires more than scientific innovation alone. Continued investment in research, manufacturing, and supply chains is essential. Government support, industrial partnerships, and long-term policy commitments all play important roles in helping promising technologies reach commercialization.

There are also many exciting research opportunities still ahead, including the development of alternative redox chemistries, new reactor and electrode designs, and applications ranging from renewable energy integration to remote communities, data centers, and backup power systems. We will need a portfolio of energy storage technologies to support the energy transition, and RFBs have the potential to be an important part of that future.

Something I would like to highlight and share with the world is that solving the energy storage challenge will require both scientific innovation and long-term vision. Many of the technologies needed for a sustainable energy future already exist in some form today, but they still require research, investment, and public support to reach widespread deployment. RFBs are one example of a technology with tremendous potential for large-scale energy storage, and it is exciting to contribute to a field that could help enable a more resilient and sustainable energy system for future generations.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

An East Texas coal-fired power plant has been given another lease on life thanks to the Trump administration’s repeal of certain environmental regulations.

The Environmental Protection Agency is repealing regulations requiring coal-fired power plants to close if they don’t reduce greenhouse gas emissions within the coming years.

Agency leaders announced the changes Sept. 14 as part of President Donald Trump’s plan to “unleash American energy.” The agency also plans to eliminate all additional regulations aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the power sector, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said.

The regulatory rollbacks mean coal-fired power plants such as Martin Lake plant near Tatum won’t be forced to close or comply with certain costly emissions reduction measures within the next decade.

Leaders of the Sierra Club, a traditionally left-leaning environmental advocacy firm, said the rollback is a detriment to public health, as climate change, premature deaths and asthma cases are tied to higher emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from coal-fired and natural gas-fired power plants.

Trump administration officials and organizations on the political right, however, say the rollbacks don’t have a negative impact on human health, and their elimination will lower energy costs for everyday Americans. Leaders of the traditionally right-leaning Heartland Institute said that increased greenhouse gas emissions have positive impacts on vegetation worldwide.

Leaders of Vistra, the parent company of plant owner Luminant, did not respond to a request for comment.

‘More prosperous America’

The Obama and Biden administrations made greenhouse gas reductions core parts of the EPA’s plan to combat climate change. The Trump administration, however, has sought to deregulate the energy industry, with the president saying climate change is a “con job.”

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the rollback Sept. 14 in Houston, saying it will promote electric grid reliability by protecting coal-fired power generation. He also said it will save American electric customers and electric businesses $310 billion, though he didn’t give a timeline for those savings. Officials said they estimate coal production for use in the power sector to increase by 10 times.

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” Zeldin said in a statement. “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning. We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”

While Zeldin said the rollback will lower energy prices, Sierra Club leaders disagree. Studies show that green energy is cleaner, cheaper to produce and more reliable than coal-fired power generation.

“The coal industry cannot compete with solar – it’s being kept on life support by taxpayer subsidies and regulatory handouts, while ordinary families pay the price in higher electricity bills, dirtier air, and more extreme weather fueled by carbon pollution,” Sierra Club leaders said in a statement.

Public health concerns debated

Central to the debate over greenhouse gas emissions is whether they negatively impact human and environmental health.

Power generation facilities are the nation’s second-largest emitters of greenhouse gases, with transportation as the largest contributor, according to the EPA. Greenhouse gas emissions trap heat and make the plant warmer, the agency’s website states.

The U.S. is the world’s second-largest emitter of carbon dioxide. The largest producer, China, emits 13 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually, and the U.S. emits 4.6 billion tons.

Texas coal and natural gas plants emitted 190 million tons of carbon in 2025, according to EPA data.

Jaime Perkins, a campaign organizer with the Sierra Club, said greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide warm the planet and contribute to natural disasters, and they can contribute to health issues, such as asthma, heart attacks and lung issues.

Those assertions are affirmed by organizations such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

With the rollback, power plants are “left off the hook” from changes that would have prevented and reduced health issues in area residents, Perkins said.

The impact of the regulatory rollback extends beyond carbon reduction. Sierra Club leaders said the carbon reductions also would have reduced emissions of mercury, heavy metals, particulate matter, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide.

Martin Lake is one of the top four pollution-emitting power plants in Texas, Sierra Club officials have stated, based on publicly available pollution data.

The Clean Air Task Force, a global nonprofit that aims to eliminate carbon from the energy sector, estimates that pollution from Martin Lake contributes to dozens of premature deaths, heart attacks, asthma cases and more in people living near the plant.

Zeldin and other EPA officials disagree with concerns about greenhouse gases. In the Sept. 14 press release, Zeldin said the gases targeted by the regulations — and any public health concerns related to them — “are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the U.S. power sector.”

Leaders of the Heartland Institute also say they believe higher carbon dioxide emissions can yield benefits to the planet. Anthony Watts, a senior fellow at the institute, said Sept. 14 that rising levels of carbon dioxide have “well-documented benefits.” For example, they’ve contributed to higher plant growth and made crops more productive.

“If power-plant CO₂ emissions are supposedly destroying the planet, a greener Earth with enhanced plant growth is an inconvenient fact that deserves far more attention,” Watts said. “Any rational assessment of CO₂ regulation should consider these measurable benefits alongside its claimed costs.”

The EPA’s regulatory rollbacks are expected to face legal challenges.

title: The Heat Decision Hidden in Paving Specifications - Environment+Energy Leader
description:
The property that decides it Solar reflectance is the share of incoming sunlight a surface returns rather than absorbs, expressed from 0 to 1.

Four lines that cost nothing at tender Solar reflectance measured to ASTM C1549, reported for the material and finish actually being supplied.

text:
Paving is one of the few building materials still routinely chosen by eye. A sample board goes in front of a client, a colour is agreed, and a surface that will sit in full sun for thirty years is specified on how it looks indoors under a downlight.

That would matter less if the alternative were difficult. It is not. There is a measured property that predicts how hot a paved surface will get, a standard test method for obtaining it, a standard way of expressing it as a single comparable number, and a green building threshold that already references it. Almost none of that reaches a typical specification.

The property that decides it

Solar reflectance is the share of incoming sunlight a surface returns rather than absorbs, expressed from 0 to 1. The US Environmental Protection Agency identifies it as the primary determinant of a pavement’s maximum surface temperature, and records conventional asphalt and concrete peaking at 120 to 150 degrees Fahrenheit in summer.

The spread between materials is wide, and it is well documented. Work by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s Heat Island Group puts new asphalt at roughly 0.05 and aged asphalt at 0.10 to 0.20. Cement concrete comes in at 0.30 to 0.50 when new, falling to 0.20 to 0.35 as it ages and soils. White cement concrete reaches 0.70 to 0.80 new. The same body of measurement records a black-and-red granite at 0.19 and a dark red basalt at 0.17.

A surface at 0.19 is absorbing about four-fifths of the energy landing on it and re-emitting most of that as heat. A surface at 0.50 is absorbing half. The difference is not marginal, and it is fixed at the moment the material is chosen.

Why an energy manager should care about a paving choice

Three consequences follow, and only the first is widely discussed.

Ambient load. Hot hardscape warms the air above it, which raises the temperature of the air a building’s cooling plant is working against. A plaza, a car park and a service yard are all thermal inputs to the building they surround.

Occupant-facing surfaces. A burn-medicine team logged roughly 75,000 surface readings across six materials through a desert summer and recorded sunlit porous rock at 170 degrees Fahrenheit on one August afternoon, against 166 for asphalt, 152 for brick and 144 for concrete. Those are temperatures at which a surface stops being usable and starts being a liability.

Credit compliance, discovered late. Reflectance is not usually checked until a project is chasing a rating, by which point the paving is specified, sometimes ordered.

The threshold most projects meet by accident or not at all

LEED v4.1 asks non-roof hardscape to reach an initial solar reflectance of at least 0.33 to count toward its heat island reduction credit. Specifiers working from older habits should note that the three-year-aged alternative of 0.28, available under v4, was dropped for hardscape in v4.1. The initial value is now the test.

Set 0.33 against the material figures above and the position becomes clear. New cement concrete may clear it. Aged concrete frequently does not. Asphalt is nowhere near. A genuinely dark stone or paver, whatever its geological family, will not meet it, and no finish or sealer changes that enough to matter.

This is not an argument for pale paving everywhere. It is an argument for knowing the number before the drawing is issued rather than after.

What to ask for, in the words that will get an answer

Two standards do the work, and naming them changes the quality of the response a supplier gives.

Solar reflectance measured to ASTM C1549. This is the portable-reflectometer method used for the values quoted above. Asking for reflectance without naming a method invites a number from anywhere.

Solar Reflectance Index calculated to ASTM E1980. SRI converts reflectance and thermal emittance into one figure on a scale where a standard black surface is 0 and a standard white surface is 100. It is computed at fixed design conditions rather than at whatever the weather did during the test, which is precisely what makes it comparable between products.

One practical note on SRI for non-metallic, high-emissivity materials such as stone, concrete and brick: the wind-speed convention used in the calculation has little effect on the result, so the medium-wind figure is the one to work with.

What a real answer looks like

A supplier that has done the work can produce a value, a method and a laboratory. One that has not will offer an adjective.

Published manufacturer data with third-party calculation shows the shape of a genuine report. One North American producer publishes figures calculated by an independent laboratory to E1980: a grey granite at 0.44 reflectance and SRI 49, an Indiana limestone at 0.47 and SRI 54, and another granite at 0.29 and SRI 31.

That last figure is the useful one. It is a pale, unremarkable-looking stone that fails the LEED threshold. Anyone selecting by appearance would have assumed it passed. This is the entire case for asking, in one line: colour is a decent clue and a poor proxy, and the only way to tell the difference is a measurement.

The intervention that outperforms the specification

Having argued for the number, it is worth being honest about its limits.

The same desert study measured identical materials in sun and in shade simultaneously. Shaded surfaces held at 104 to 108 degrees Fahrenheit while sunlit ones ran 36 to 56 degrees hotter, with peaks arriving between two and four in the afternoon. Modelling of urban tree species for the Journal of Environmental Quality found tree shade reducing asphalt surface temperature by 13.8 to 22.8 degrees Celsius, though the World Resources Institute notes the effect on air temperature is far more modest at roughly 0.3 degrees Celsius per ten per cent of added canopy.

No reflectance decision available to a specifier recovers 36 to 56 degrees Fahrenheit. Shade does. And the EPA’s own compendium adds the intervention nobody has a product to sell for: reduce the paved area first, then treat what remains.

The sequence that follows from the evidence is therefore: pave less, shade what is paved, and specify by measured reflectance where sun still reaches the ground.

Four lines that cost nothing at tender

Solar reflectance measured to ASTM C1549, reported for the material and finish actually being supplied.

Solar Reflectance Index calculated to ASTM E1980, with the calculating laboratory named.

Confirmation of which value is initial and which, if any, is aged, since the applicable threshold now turns on the initial figure.

The finish the values apply to, because texture and gloss are part of what was measured.

None of this is exotic. It is the paperwork equivalent of asking a window manufacturer for a U-value. The difference is that nobody expects to be refused the U-value.

The gap worth closing

The standards exist. The test is inexpensive and quick. A rating system already names a threshold. What is missing is the habit of asking, and the consequence of not asking lands on whoever operates the building afterwards rather than on whoever specified it.

A surface chosen by eye is a thermal decision made without data, on an asset that will outlast the project team. It is one of the easier gaps in a specification to close, and one of the least often closed.

text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- Chicago leaders are weighing competing proposals to regulate data centers as the industry continues to expand across the city.

Chicago has at least 39 data centers of various sizes located in different parts of the city and continues to attract new developments.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

According to David Lampert, an associate professor of engineering at the Illinois Institute of Technology, several factors make Chicago attractive for data center projects.

"The climate being cooler here, electricity prices being cheaper ... the availability of large parcels of land where they can build these data centers. I think that's all the reasons that Chicago is seeing a lot of new data centers," Lampert said.

Mayor Brandon Johnson has introduced an ordinance that would impose a one-year moratorium on new data centers and on the expansion of existing facilities. Supporters say the pause would give city officials time to craft regulations for the growing industry.

"The moratorium will give all of us the time that's necessary to make sure that best practices can be established," Johnson said.

Ald. Maria Hadden, 49th Ward, co-sponsored the proposal.

"We need to make zoning rules. We need to think about energy regulations. It's going to be complicated, so the moratorium buys us time," Hadden said.

However, Ald. Bill Conway, 34th Ward, questions the legality of a moratorium and has introduced a competing proposal that would establish specific regulations. His ordinance would require data centers to be treated as planned developments subject to community review.

"Right now there are less regulation over a massive data center than there are opening a nail salon in Chicago, and that makes no sense at all," Conway said.

Data center advocates have warned against what they view as City Council overreach. In a statement, the Data Center Coalition said additional restrictions could "drive away the many union jobs that are responsible for building and maintaining data centers while sacrificing the significant clean energy investments that data centers drive."

Marc Poulos of Operating Engineers Local 150 said many concerns raised about data centers are already being addressed.

"A number of things that people have complained about - energy, water, all those things - they're already being regulated in the market, as it is. Are there more things we can do? Absolutely," Poulos said.

The competing ordinances could face delays after opposing aldermen sent them to the Rules Committee. The proposals follow an executive order issued by Johnson last month establishing a task force to recommend regulations for future data centers.

Brad Tietz, Director of State Government Affairs-Midwest at the Data Center Coalition, issued the following statement:

"As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment, create thousands of high-wage jobs, help fund schools, transportation, public safety, tax relief, and other local priorities, and drive significant clean energy investments - all of which help make life more affordable for Chicagoans.

"Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business, both for data centers and for other significant economic development projects. If adopted, it will cause Chicago to relinquish significant long-term economic investment, jobs, and tax revenue to neighboring areas and states.

"In particular, while the city claims to prioritize union labor and clean energy, a moratorium would actually drive away the many union jobs that are responsible for building and maintaining data centers, while sacrificing the significant clean energy investments that data centers drive.

"We strongly encourage Chicago leaders to work with the industry and all stakeholders to establish reasonable regulatory frameworks that meet local needs without deterring the industry and the benefits it can bring, to help ensure the City of Chicago remains competitive in the modern economy."

Other City Council business Wednesday

Also on Wednesday, the city of Chicago extended its ride with Divvy.

The city signed a deal with owner, Lyft, to keep its rentable bikes, e-bikes and scooters running through 2033.

Under the contract, Divvy will upgrade bikes and bring more scooters and e-bikes into the system. It also extends the price freeze on annual memberships, and brings discounted rentals on the South and West Sides.

text:
Government-led initiative builds on Mission 300 and a landmark Green Climate Fund project to mobilize investment for universal energy access, rural development and climate resilience.

NEW YORK, 23 September 2026 — The Government of Mozambique today announced its intention to establish a Strategic Funding Coalition for Off-Grid Electrification, bringing together development finance institutions, climate and energy funds, philanthropies and private investors to coordinate and mobilize financing to accelerate rural electrification.

Announced during a high-level roundtable convened by the Government of Mozambique on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly and Climate Week NYC, the proposed coalition, supported by the UN through Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) and Enabel, the Belgian Agency for International Cooperation, will help implement Mozambique’s ambition to achieve universal electricity access by 2030, using renewable energy to drive economic development, industrialization and greater climate resilience.

Mozambique has already more than doubled electricity access, from 31 percent in 2018 to nearly 65 percent today. Its National Energy Compact targets 100 percent access by 2030, requiring an additional 4.9 million connections and aiming to mobilize USD 18.6 billion across the energy sector, including about USD 8.7 billion from the private sector.

Off-grid solutions will be critical to reaching this ambitious target. Mozambique’s National Geospatial Least-Cost Electrification Pathway, developed with support from SEforALL, identifies 2.5 million off-grid connections, requiring an estimated USD 1.1 billion in investment. The proposed coalition will develop a coordinated financing architecture to support the full deployment life-cycle of off-grid technologies, blending public and concessional resources with guarantees, results-based financing and commercial capital to de-risk investment and expand private-sector participation.

H.E. Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique, said:

“Mozambique is putting energy at the heart of our development. Our goal is to ensure that energy creates opportunity — powering businesses, strengthening agriculture, supporting industry and improving essential services. Through this coalition, we want to bring government and our partners around a common financing framework that can turn our considerable renewable energy potential into jobs, growth and greater resilience for our people.”

The initiative builds on reforms already underway to strengthen the market for private investment, including improved planning, sectoral coordination platforms, updated regulatory frameworks, competitive off-grid electrification concession tenders and financing mechanisms designed to support renewable energy companies. The National Energy Compact explicitly prioritizes dedicated credit lines, guarantee schemes and other instruments to address barriers including limited local-currency financing.

It also builds on the Green Climate Fund-supported PURE Mozambique Rural Climate Project, jointly implemented by FUNAE, Enabel and Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL). The seven-year initiative will use solar-powered mini-grids and productive uses of renewable energy to benefit approximately 225,000 people, 52 percent of them women, strengthen rural livelihoods and avoid an estimated 399,131 tonnes of CO₂e emissions over its lifetime. The New York roundtable includes the signing of a Letter of Intent between FUNAE, Enabel and SEforALL to cooperate on delivery of the GCF-funded project.

Damilola Ogunbiyi, CEO and Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Sustainable Energy for All, said:

“Mozambique has made significant energy access progress, and the next chapter must be about using energy to power economic growth. Achieving that ambition will require financing at a much greater scale and strong coordination between government, investors and partners. SEforALL is proud to support Mozambique in turning its energy ambitions into the foundation for lasting economic transformation through data-backed strategies.”

Jean Van Wetter, CEO of Enabel, said:

“The PURE Mozambique project is already showing the direction of travel: rural electrification must go beyond connections to create productive economies and resilient communities. The proposed coalition allows us to take that approach to scale, combining climate and development finance with private investment to build a sustainable market for rural energy.”

As its first action, the proposed coalition will embark on a nine-month process to co-develop a National Off-Grid Financing Roadmap, identifying financing gaps, de-risking mechanisms and opportunities to mobilize greater public and private capital. The Government and its partners are targeting a public launch of the roadmap and associated funding announcements at COP32 in November 2027.

Mozambique’s broader energy ambition extends beyond universal access. Renewable energy currently accounts for 78.4 percent of the country’s generation mix, with the Government targeting 80.6 percent by 2032 and positioning Mozambique as a regional energy hub that can use its resources to support industrial growth, job creation and Southern Africa’s wider energy transition. The country also plans to extend clean cooking solutions to 54 percent of the population by 2030, up from approximately 17 percent today.

Notes to Editor:

text:
The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers.

There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city.

Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use.

What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents."

Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers.

"The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement.

Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews.

Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations.

At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction.

Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already paused new data center development or expansion.

The other side: "As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment," Data Center Coalition's Brad Tietz said in a statement.

"Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business."

Friction point: Communities across the country are pushing back against proposed data centers over concerns about electricity demand, water use, pollution and other impacts.

President Trump has criticized efforts to restrict them, writing on social media: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."

text:
The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) is initiating eight new bulk energy storage projects and 13 large-scale renewable energy projects in the state. Combined, these projects are expected to provide 1.7 GW of new large-scale energy resources, create more than 1,000 family-supporting jobs and generate over $3.7 billion in private investment.

“These newly-contracted large-scale energy projects not only further the growth of clean energy and more than double the utility-scale energy storage that exists currently statewide, but they contribute to New York’s comprehensive, all of the above energy strategy, said Doreen M. Harris, NYSERDA president and CEO. This will help reduce costs for New York ratepayers while continuing to improve the reliability of our state’s grid.”

These projects were submitted to NYSERDA’s Bulk Energy Storage solicitation and its 2025 Tier 1 Renewable Energy Standard solicitation. They’re expected to provide over $127 million in economic activity in disadvantaged communities, as defined by the Climate Justice Working Group.

Once operational, the eight contracted bulk energy storage projects will add 950 MW of new energy storage capacity. The projects represent a diverse portfolio ranging geographically from New York City and Long Island to Hudson Valley and western New York. They were selected through a process that included bid proposals from 46 projects totaling approximately 6 GW of capacity. The eight contracted projects range in duration from four to eight hours and will provide critical reliability benefits to the state’s electric grid.

In western New York are Lighthouse Energy Storage in Chautauqua County, Zenobe Burns in Allegany County. Eastwater Energy Storage will be in the Finger Lakes region. In Hudson Valley, KCE NY 5. For New York City, Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium storage, which will be be in Bronx County. And Holtsville and KCE NY 37 will be in Long Island .

Payments under these contracts will not commence until projects have begun commercial operation, after obtaining all permits and local approvals.

The contracted projects will use lithium-ion technology and, as with all NYSERDA-supported energy storage projects, are contractually required to meet the new storage safety codes that became effective Jan. 1, 2026. NYSERDA will issue the second annual Bulk Energy Storage Request for Proposals by year-end, with plans to procure 3 GW of energy storage projects over three solicitations.

The 13 contracted large-scale renewable energy projects will total more than 719 MW of renewable capacity – enough to power over 230,000 New York homes annually once completed.

The solar projects include Flint Mine Solar, Hecate Greene 1 and 2, Greens Corners Solar Park and Rich Road Solar Energy Center. All projects are expected to be placed in-service by the end of 2030 as required by the 2024 New York Public Service Commission’s Energy Storage Order.

text:
Maxvolt Energy Industries Ltd. has commenced work on a new ₹700-crore battery manufacturing facility in Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh, as part of its capacity expansion plans and entry into the four-wheeler EV battery segment. The project was formally inaugurated with a Bhoomi Pujan ceremony attended by senior Uttar Pradesh government officials, company executives and industry stakeholders.

Spread across nearly six acres, the upcoming facility will be developed in two phases, each with a planned capacity of 5 GWh annually. Once fully operational, the Aligarh plant will contribute 10 GWh of annual battery production capacity. Combined with Maxvolt's existing Duhai facility, the company expects its total planned manufacturing capacity to reach 12.5 GWh per year.

The new plant will manufacture battery packs for a broad range of applications including electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers, energy storage systems, telecom infrastructure and power backup solutions. Maxvolt said dedicated OEM production lines will also enable it to produce battery packs tailored to customer requirements.

ALSO READ - Maruti Suzuki Advances Green Hydrogen Push With 300 kW Facility In Manesar

According to the company, the facility will support battery solutions ranging from 1 kW to 5 MW and will feature battery management systems (BMS) compatible with slow-charging as well as L3 and L5 fast-charging applications. The expansion will also mark Maxvolt's entry into the four-wheeler EV battery space, complementing its existing portfolio of battery packs for two- and three-wheelers.

The Aligarh project represents one of the larger battery manufacturing investments announced in Uttar Pradesh. At full capacity, Maxvolt estimates the facility could generate annual revenues of more than ₹6,800 crore. The company expects the project to create between 1,500 and 2,000 direct jobs and up to 10,000 indirect employment opportunities across manufacturing, engineering, logistics and related industries.

Maxvolt said the new facility is being built to cater to rising demand from multiple sectors rather than a single vehicle category. The company cited growing battery requirements across electric mobility, stationary energy storage, telecom networks and backup power systems as key drivers behind the investment.

The expansion comes as India continues to increase domestic battery manufacturing capacity to support the growth of electric mobility and energy storage. Maxvolt currently operates through a network of more than 950 dealers across 22 states and partners with over 30 OEMs. The company also plans to strengthen its battery recycling operations through its recycling arm, ReEarth, which aims to recover up to 500,000 batteries annually by 2030 through a network of more than 100 collection centres.

Maxvolt said its battery packs are manufactured in compliance with AIS 156 safety requirements and are developed under an ISO 9001:2015-certified quality management system. The company is also working with auto-component partners to enhance battery safety and expand its research and development capabilities.
