Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry is joining Republican candidates who are calling for a ban on exports of diesel fuel. They say it’s a way to lower historically high prices but they are facing pushback from industry leaders who say that idea could actually drive prices up.

The Advocate reported that prices rose about.40 cents per gallon last week alone to a national price Monday of $6.51 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association. On this day last year, the average price nationally was $3.69 per gallon.

The reason for higher gasoline and diesel prices is caused by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Landry wrote on social media that he favored banning the export of diesel fuel for 90 days in order to build up reserves and bring down the price of the fuel that farmers, truckers and Northern homeowners rely on.

Landry said Monday on CNBC’s Squawk Box. “Right now a record amount of diesel is going to Europe and Americans are subsidizing Europe’s problems. Europe has done nothing to help America in either one of those two positions and yet they are sucking the energy out of America and making American citizens pay for it.”

As is his usual custom, Landry is echoing comments and views expressed by President Donald Trump.

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright during a Thursday interview with the Daily Caller, a right-wing news source, said a diesel export ban would force a reduction in refining, due to a lack of domestic pipeline activity and storage, and that would result in an increase in fuel prices.

Tommy Faucheux, the president of the Louisiana Mid-Continent Oil and Gas Association, also had a different view from Landry.

“Without available capacity to redirect supply, halting the export of American diesel would force refineries to reduce production, which would also decrease the production of gasoline,” Faucheux said Wednesday in a statement. “This is a misguided proposal that would cause more harm and increase, not decrease, costs for American families and businesses.”

In return, Landry said he had heard from Faucheux and big oil company executives.

“I get it. The majors out there, those that are exporting, are making record profits and I don’t have a problem with them making those particular profits. The American citizens should not be subsidizing Europe’s problems at a time when Europe refuses to help America.”

American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, a Washington-based trade association, also fretted that the ban wouldn’t work. AFP pointed out that U.S. refineries make about 5.3 million barrels of distillate fuel per day, of which Americans use about 3.6 million barrels per day.

“If exports are banned, refiners cannot simply stockpile unlimited diesel fuel. They would have to reduce production. Because gasoline and diesel are produced together, producing less diesel also means producing less gasoline.”

Politico, a political trade publication, said U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins told reporters that Trump had called her Monday to discuss diesel prices.

Trump may have some thoughts about a diesel export ban but the experts, by a wide margin, don’t think it’s a good idea.

SOUTH BURLINGTON, Vt. & RALEIGH, N.C., September 23, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--BETA Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: BETA) ("BETA"), an aerospace and defense company, today announced the launch of flight operations in North Carolina's eLIFT program under the U.S. Department of Transportation's ("U.S. DOT") and Federal Aviation Administration's ("FAA") eVTOL Integration Pilot Program ("eIPP"). Since September 17, BETA has conducted all-electric operations, including a historic flyover of the Wright Brothers National Memorial and simulated deliveries of essential healthcare cargo to rural medical access points, including a deployable medical field tent and supplies. The operations will demonstrate how lower-cost, all-electric aviation can reduce the time required to deliver critical supplies, strengthen the resilience of regional healthcare networks, and improve access to care across the state.

"Under President Trump, we are unlocking the future of flight, one test flight at a time," said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. "More than 120 years after the Wright Brothers took to the skies at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina is again leading the charge to transform how Americans move. Thanks to these tests, we are closer than ever to welcoming next-generation aircraft into our skies."

Working with the North Carolina Department of Transportation ("NCDOT"), Metro Aviation and healthcare partners across the state, including ECU Health and WakeMed, BETA designed the flight campaign to test how electric aviation could strengthen connections between regional medical centers and the rural and coastal communities they serve. The campaign covered more than 1,300 nautical miles and focused on future healthcare missions connecting the Research Triangle, including routes between Raleigh Executive Jetport and Pitt-Greenville Airport, with communities such as those served by Dare County Regional Airport.

"We are supporting North Carolina's world-class healthcare systems by using cost-effective, electric flight to overcome the distance that can make it difficult to get critical supplies, specialists, and care where they need to go," said Kyle Clark, founder and chief executive officer of BETA Technologies. "Medical applications have been part of BETA's DNA from the beginning, and the best way to prove our technology is to put it to work on real missions that deliver for the healthcare community. Alongside our customers and partners, we're flying and learning from every operation and showing how aviation can extend the reach of healthcare networks to rural and coastal communities across the state."

title: BMW 3 Series combines product sustainability and short distances within site cluster
description:
With the new BMW 3 Series Sedan, the BMW Group is systematically extending its holistic approach to sustainability to the fully-electric variant and combustion-engine model.
Landshut: Light metal and components expertise BMW Group Plant Landshut is the company’s largest component plant worldwide and a centre of in-house manufacturing expertise.
At the same time, close cooperation between the German pilot plants and series production facilities worldwide supports the global production network.
The BMW Group production network comprises over 30 production sites worldwide; the company has a global sales network in more than 140 countries.
In 2025, the BMW Group sold 2.46 million passenger vehicles and more than 202,500 motorcycles worldwide.
text:
Munich. With the new BMW 3 Series Sedan, the BMW Group is systematically extending its holistic approach to sustainability to the fully-electric variant and combustion-engine model. From the supply chain and production, through to the use phase and recycling, key levers have been optimised with the aim of reducing the CO₂e footprint throughout the vehicle lifecycle. The Bavarian production cluster plays an important role in this: Plants Dingolfing, Landshut, Irlbach-Straßkirchen and Munich bring together core expertise, reduce transport distances and efficiently integrate specialised production steps.

Focus on supply chain decarbonisation

The supply chain is a key lever for reducing CO2e emissions. In this area, the BMW Group relies, in particular, on renewable energy and higher secondary material content, as well as product and process innovations. The measures are systematically applied to all drive train variants of the new BMW 3 Series. Already during the product development phase, supply chain CO₂e emissions were reduced by around 37 percent for the BMW i3 and by around 30 percent[1] for the variant with an internal combustion engine. A particular focus is on battery cells and the use of aluminium.

The Gen6 battery cells for the BMW i3 rely on secondary materials for a portion of their cobalt, lithium and nickel. The BMW Group also uses renewable energy in the production of anode and cathode materials, as well as in cell manufacturing. In comparison with the Gen5 cell in the BMW i4, the CO2e footprint per watt-hour was reduced by approx. 33 percent.

Systematic use of secondary materials

Measures implemented in the supply chain and at the company’s own facilities enable a high secondary material content in the new BMW 3 Series – also for heavy-duty components. These include aluminium suspension components such as wheel rims, swivel bearings and wheel supports, which rely on electricity from renewable sources for both electrolysis and production. Secondary material is also used for the car body: The bonnet is made of approximately 70 percent recycled aluminium. In the battery-electric BMW i3 50 xDrive, around 31 percent of the total vehicle consists of secondary materials; in the BMW 3 Series with internal combustion engine, the share is around 25 percent[1].

BMW Group sites combine sustainability with specialisation

The Dingolfing, Landshut, Irlbach-Straßkirchen and Munich facilities pool core expertise within the Bavarian production cluster. Short transport distances and closely integrated processes unlock potential for reducing CO₂e emissions.

“The cluster approach to BMW production is directly linked to the concept of sustainability: Short distances and close proximity are key characteristics of a cluster, creating direct economic, environmental and social sustainability benefits through regional networking and concentration. A regional production cluster, like at BMW, creates added value for the economy, people, the environment and, of course, the region,” explains Prof Dr Rudolf Juchelka, Chair of Economic Geography, especially Transport and Logistics at the University of Duisburg-Essen.

Landshut: Light metal and components expertise

BMW Group Plant Landshut is the company’s largest component plant worldwide and a centre of in-house manufacturing expertise. The light metal foundry produces parts for electric drive trains, as well as engine components such as crankcases and cylinder heads. For the new BMW 3 Series, the facility is also manufacturing the e-drive housing for the rear axle of the fully-electric variant, alongside crankcases and cylinder heads for the combustion-engine model. The corresponding drive trains are produced at BMW Group Plant Steyr in Austria, which has been a source of drive train expertise within the production network for over 40 years.

The Landshut site combines long-standing aluminium and foundry know-how with specific sustainability measures, such as using aluminium from recycling loops and material produced in part with electricity from renewable sources. In-house component manufacturing strengthens material expertise, conserves resources and supports close integration of production processes.

Irlbach-Straßkirchen: “Local for local” high-voltage batteries

Construction of the new assembly site for sixth-generation high-voltage batteries at Plant Irlbach-Straßkirchen got underway in spring 2024. In line with the “local for local” principle, the plant will supply high-voltage batteries for the BMW i3 from October 2026. This strengthens regional structures, reduces transport distances and helps secure jobs. At the same time, close cooperation between the German pilot plants and series production facilities worldwide supports the global production network. Key components for the BMW i3 will be manufactured close to vehicle production and transported to Munich on electric trucks.

The plant requires no fossil fuels for regular operations. A photovoltaic system generates a share of the electricity required directly on site. All additional energy needed is supplied entirely from renewable sources. The process is designed so that no water is required for assembling the high-voltage batteries. In this way, the site is combining the industrialisation of electromobility with lower emissions and resource-efficient production.

Munich: Transformation towards the BMW iFACTORY

BMW Group Plant Munich produces vehicles for the Neue Klasse, following the principles of the BMW iFACTORY, with a focus on efficiency, digitalisation and sustainability. The site obtains all the external power it requires from renewable sources. The plant is also committed to responsible use of resources – for example, through the material loop in the press shop: Steel and aluminium scrap generated while punching body parts is collected and separated by material type, recycled and subsequently used to manufacture new coils.

Dingolfing: Renewable energy and process heat

BMW Group Plant Dingolfing combines efficient production processes with close integration with the surrounding component sites. All purchased electricity comes from renewable sources, with a portion generated directly on site. Since late 2025, a photovoltaic system on the plant's roof, with a capacity of just under 11 megawatt peak, has supplied electricity for the site.

A new biomass heating plant west of the vehicle plant also provides up to 100,000 megawatt hours of locally-produced heat from renewable energy sources. In this way, the facility can meet about half of its process heat requirements.

Efficiency during use phase

With its EfficientDynamics technology package, the BMW Group optimises vehicle efficiency across all relevant subsystems. This includes aerodynamics, lightweight construction, low rolling resistance tyres and overall energy management. EfficientDynamics has been used by the BMW Group across all drive technologies since 2007. The new fully-electric BMW i3 also features the “Heart of Joy”, with the fully in-house developed BMW Dynamic Performance Control Driving Stack. The system enables effortless and confident drivability, with highly controlled deceleration to a standstill. At the same time, it enhances efficiency: During deceleration, more energy is recovered through recuperation – in significantly more driving situations, right down to a standstill. Gen6 drive technology components are also systematically optimised for efficiency.

Using so-called SiC technology in the electric drive units, it was possible to reduce energy losses by up to 40 percent.

Transparency through TÜV-verified Product Carbon Footprint

The BMW Group will publish the Product Carbon Footprint for the BMW 3 Series, validated by the German Technical Inspection Association (TÜV), to coincide with the series launch. The report, including the underlying calculation methodology and methods, will be publicly available. In this way, the BMW Group creates transparency around the raw materials used and CO2e emissions throughout the vehicle’s entire lifecycle.

The Product Carbon Footprint for individual components and materials is calculated in accordance with the Catena-X rules. The data ecosystem enables standardised data exchange, with traceability of emissions data throughout the value chain – from the extraction of raw materials to the end product.

Transformer manufacturer Hammond Power Solutions Inc. (HPS) is increasing its North American production capacity after recently signing a long-term lease agreement for a new manufacturing facility in Fort Worth, Texas.

The Canada-based company projects that the $36 million (C$50 million) Fort Worth facility will expand its capacity by roughly $177.3 million annually once fully operational in Q1 2028. As a provider of magnetic and power electronic solutions, HPS produces integrated hardware systems that manage electrical energy efficiently through advanced magnetism and semiconductor circuits.

An example of this solution-oriented development is HPS’s smart transformer units, which integrate advanced automatic computing meters directly onto low-voltage and medium-voltage transformers. With this emerging tech integration, facilities can transition operations from reactive to predictive maintenance while eliminating the safety risks associated with manual, on-ground inspections in the process.

These solutions provide critical support for power-intensive industries, including mining, steel, commercial construction, wind power generation and data center infrastructure development. According to a company release, the planned facility will expand HPS’s ability to serve these U.S.-based customers, who require large standard and custom-engineered transformers for massive GW-scale projects.

HPS noted that Fort Worth's strategic location closer to key North American customers will improve its ability to deliver certain products at shorter distances compared to its operational hubs in Canada and Mexico.

“This new investment in a U.S. facility is about being closer to our customers and better positioned to support the long-term demand we are seeing for our products,” said HPS CEO Adrian Thomas in a statement. “Demand for transformers continues to increase, particularly from large projects tied to data centers, electrification and power infrastructure.”

Thomas added that the Fort Worth facility, which is expected to begin production in stages starting in Q4 2027, will not only improve HPS's U.S. delivery speeds but also establish a vital additional domestic manufacturing footprint. As part of these initial phases, HPS expects to invest $35 million to $36 million to equip and commission the initial production phase through a combination of existing liquidity reserves and pre-approved corporate borrowing agreements (credit facilities funding).

In June, global law firm Norton Rose Fulbright facilitated a $450 million credit agreement between HPS and financial investors J.P. Morgan Chase, National Bank of Canada and Royal Bank of Canada. Under the agreement, HPS had access to up to $300 million in term debt to acquire energy storage converter provider AEG Power Solutions for approximately $258 million. The agreement also included a $150 million revolving credit facility, which will expire in Q3 2030.

HPS states the Fort Worth site could potentially support a total annual manufacturing capacity of $283 million to $284 million, as scalability and market demand increase for key electrical infrastructure equipment.

"Over the past several years, we have made significant investments to enhance efficiency, throughput and capacity across our manufacturing operations in Canada and Mexico,” said HPS chief operations officer John Bailey.

The Fort Worth facility, Bailey added, provides HPS an opportunity to apply the manufacturing processes learned from those investments in a new U.S.-built environment designed to bolster future growth.

Because of these factors, battery testing often takes years to complete.

In addition to improving testing, BMW claims that the Insight project can also speed up the final approval step in the battery production process.
text:
Behind every new EV battery is a manufacturer that has spent years developing and refining its production process. The most costly step in that development cycle is testing. To validate real-world performance, battery engineers need to build new cells with real material and test them thoroughly over weeks or months. Engineers also need to hold onto valuable material and equipment throughout the testing process, which prevents them from developing other cell designs at the same time.

In the past, battery manufacturers could cover these high testing costs with higher prices. However, as average battery prices have steadily fallen in recent years, manufacturers have had to lower prices to remain competitive. All battery producers have therefore lost margins, some more than others. To recoup losses, companies are looking for ways to reduce testing costs because they have an outsized impact on overall product development costs.

A growing number of battery producers see AI as a promising solution. These companies envision engineers using AI models trained on production and test data to predict how a process change will affect the finished cell before they run a test. With AI tools, engineers could validate the same cell technology with fewer tests and less time than traditional testing.

In recent months, Battery Technology has covered AI use in battery production by startups including QuantumScape, SandboxAQ, and Xos as well as major research organizations such as Argonne and Honda R&D. In this piece, we'll explain how AI can help battery engineers and two European manufacturers, BMW Group and EAS Batteries, that are leading their own AI projects.

AI’s appeal for battery manufacturers

Before releasing a new battery to market, manufacturers must perfect their production process to create cells with the desired performance consistently. Ordinarily, battery engineers rely on trial and error to find the optimal production settings. They would tweak a setting, like electrode coating, build a real cell, and physically test it. By testing many settings, engineers can gradually identify which production process yields the best cells.

Unfortunately, this testing approach is very costly. Trial-and-error is inherently slower than more efficient methods like predictions or simulations. The production line has many settings, and each setting affects the others, so engineers must test every parameter combination separately. Each test can also involve charging and discharging a cell hundreds of times over months so engineers can determine when the cell degrades. Because of these factors, battery testing often takes years to complete.

To shorten the testing process, many battery engineers use design of experiments (DOE), which is a statistical method that identifies ideal combinations for testing. DOE helps engineers reduce the number of tests, but they still spend time and resources building and physically evaluating each remaining test combination.

AI is a much more promising solution. Manufacturers already have the data AI models need, including coating measurements, defect images, and charging curves for every cell produced. With this data, engineers can train a model and ask it to find and evaluate production setting combinations they have never considered before.

Today’s AI models are more than capable for this application, as evidenced by a 2019 study in which researchers used machine learning to predict LFP cell cycle life. The only remaining barrier is for battery producers to implement AI in real production environments.

Building a virtual cell at EAS Batteries

In July, a German consortium, led by EAS Batteries, launched a project to apply AI to battery production. Called KiBa-Pro, the project aims to combine the efforts of multiple partners to digitalize LFP cell production through June 2029. It’s received 2.4 million euros from the German Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space, and includes universities like Karlsruhe Institute of Technologie, and companies like Omron Europe.

KiBa-Pro targets LFP because the chemistry is used in more than half of EV batteries and over 90% of energy storage systems. The project aims to build a virtual LFP cell that battery manufacturers can use to simulate how different production settings affect the finished cell's properties. For example, an engineer can input coating thickness, porosity, throughput, and temperature data into the virtual cell and receive the expected service life and energy capacity.

According to EAS, KiBa-Pro will help manufacturers increase cell service life by at least 10% and production yield by at least 15%. If the project meets those targets, battery producers can significantly reduce wasted material from testing and speed up new cell development.

These benefits are far from a guarantee because the project just started. EAS and its consortium plan to spend the rest of the first year capturing the production process digitally and running reference batches for AI training. Next, they plan to build out the model and validate it in industrial production over two years.

Predicting cell performance at BMW Group

In 2024, BMW Group and the University of Zagreb in Croatia launched a joint project called Insight to apply AI across battery cell production. The partners work at BMW's Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich, where BMW Group develops cell chemistry and production processes. Since the project started, researchers at BCCC have been training an AI system on past test data and live production data to predict process parameters and cell performance.

With predictions from the AI systems, engineers can quickly decide whether to shorten a test series or drop it. BMW reports that teams using these predictions have cut material and time usage in individual process steps by more than 50%.

In addition to improving testing, BMW claims that the Insight project can also speed up the final approval step in the battery production process. Typically, after a cell is charged for the first time at the end of production, it needs to be stored at a set temperature for a period of time to allow defects to appear. The company says that because its AI systems can fully analyze the cells for defects in advance, it can eliminate the final storage step.

While the Insight project has yielded promising results, BMW has proven the benefits only in a prototype environment. As the company readies the AI systems for a live production environment, BMW says it will transfer testing to a near-production facility in Parsdorf, Germany.

The Promise of future savings

To date, BMW and its Insight project have reported positive prototype results and are working to scale them into a live production environment. Meanwhile, the EAS-led KiBa-Pro project is currently capturing production data and plans to deliver real results by 2029.

Despite their promise, neither project has shown benefits on a running production line. In addition, neither project was designed to work across multiple factories simultaneously. Because each model is trained on one factory’s equipment and materials, what works at one site may not necessarily work at another. Only when an AI system works universally for any battery producer can companies recover lost margin from falling battery prices and release better batteries sooner.

text:
23 September 2026 – Today, Germany is publishing its national roadmap to phase out coal, oil, and gas by 2045.

In response, Laurie Van Der Burg, Public Finance lead at Oil Change International, said:

“Germany deserves credit for publishing a national roadmap that commits to a fossil fuel phaseout. But Germany’s government’s efforts to play the role of climate leader are not commensurate with the reality of the crisis, or its responsibility as a wealthy, historic emitter.

“Germany’s 2045 phaseout date is far too late, and is an insult to equity when it comes to a fair global energy transition. Germany also has a track record of breaking international climate promises. Since joining the Clean Energy Transition Partnership to end international public finance for fossil fuels, Germany has approved $1.5 billion in fossil fuel finance, making it the second largest violator of the agreement behind Italy. Now, the government plans to further weaken its export finance policy, while other countries have successfully brought down international fossil fuel finance by 78%.

“If Germany is serious about economic prosperity, energy security and affordability it should end its fossil fuel finance, strengthen its national roadmap, and redirect public money toward a resilient and affordable renewable energy future.

“On the road to COP31, governments around the world must put forward stronger national roadmaps, with rich countries moving first and fastest, delivering the climate finance they owe to the Global South and supporting the financial system reform needed to enable the transition. Country leaders face a clear choice: plan for a fair fossil fuel phaseout now, or be trapped in an outdated, volatile and destructive energy system.”

text:
In South Carolina, where Samsung Electronics Home Appliances America has maintained a longstanding manufacturing presence in Newberry County, the company is partnering with The Longleaf Alliance to restore native forests that improve watershed health and strengthen ecological resilience. The investment builds on Samsung’s long-term commitment to South Carolina, where its Home Appliance Manufacturing Campus has been part of the state’s manufacturing community for nearly a decade.

“This partnership demonstrates how corporate sustainability investments can create meaningful environmental outcomes while supporting the communities where companies operate,” said Carol Denhof, President of The Longleaf Alliance. “By investing in longleaf pine restoration, Samsung is helping restore one of North America’s most significant ecosystems while generating measurable and lasting water, biodiversity, and climate benefits.”

The project will restore over 200 acres of unmanaged forestland to native longleaf pine habitat on privately owned forestland through ecological thinning, longleaf pine establishment, and prescribed fire. These restoration activities will improve forest health while increasing water yield by reducing evapotranspiration and restoring the open-canopy structure characteristic of healthy longleaf pine forests.

“Our collaboration with The Longleaf Alliance reflects Samsung’s commitment to advancing meaningful, science-based solutions that help protect South Carolina’s natural resources and the communities that depend on them,” said Cordell Hull, Executive Vice President and Head of U.S. Public Affairs at Samsung Electronics America. “South Carolina has been an important part of Samsung’s manufacturing story for nearly a decade, and we’re proud to build on that longstanding commitment through investments that strengthen the environment and support local communities.”

TLA collaborator Milliken Advisors will oversee the forest restoration implementation and forest inventory and monitoring throughout the project. For more than 75 years, landowners have trusted Milliken Advisors to guide them with the right tools and tailored, proven strategies to help them make the most of their land investments. In addition to measurements of forest structure, the project will also monitor biodiversity through forest assessments and acoustic recording technology to document improvements in wildlife habitat over time.

Private landowners play an essential role in conservation across the Southeast, where approximately 87 percent of South Carolina’s forests are privately owned. Through initiatives like this, The Longleaf Alliance is creating new opportunities for private investment to help landowners restore forests that provide clean water, wildlife habitat, climate resilience, and sustainable economic value.

About The Longleaf Alliance

The Longleaf Alliance works throughout the Southeastern United States to ensure the future of longleaf pine ecosystems through science-based management, outreach, partnership engagement, and on-the-ground conservation assistance. The Longleaf Alliance is the only nonprofit solely dedicated to conserving and restoring the longleaf pine ecosystem.

About Milliken Advisors

Milliken Advisors works with clients and collaborators to strategize, plan, and implement Nature-Based Solutions that balance commerce and conservation. Companies and NGOs engage Milliken to design, test, and prove sustainability projects – blending forestry, ecology, and technology to protect natural resources and meet business sustainability goals.

text:
BOSTON — The Healey-Driscoll Administration today announced that the Massachusetts Economic Assistance Coordinating Council (EACC) approved $11.5 million in tax credits for 10 business expansion projects expected to create 674 new jobs, retain 1,093 existing jobs and generate more than $339 million in private investment across Massachusetts.

The awards are made through the Economic Development Incentive Program (EDIP), which supports businesses that commit to creating jobs, retaining workers and making new investments in Massachusetts.

“Massachusetts businesses are growing, hiring and investing in communities across our state,” said Governor Maura Healey. “These awards will help create nearly 700 new jobs, retain more than 1,000 existing jobs and drive hundreds of millions of dollars in private investment. We are proud to support companies that are choosing Massachusetts to grow their businesses and create new opportunities for workers.”

“These investments are supporting businesses and creating jobs in communities across Massachusetts, from Orange and Sunderland to New Bedford, Taunton and Lowell,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “We’re partnering with companies that want to grow here, put people to work and strengthen local economies.”

“These companies are expanding the industries that will shape our economic future, including advanced manufacturing, robotics, defense, aerospace and critical materials,” said Economic Development Secretary Eric Paley. “Through EDIP, we are supporting ambitious projects that will build new facilities, expand production and create hundreds of jobs across Massachusetts.”

EDIP is administered by the Massachusetts Office of Business Development (MOBD) and designed to support business expansion and job creation by offering performance-based tax credits in exchange for commitments to create new jobs, retain existing employees, and invest capital. Nine of the projects approved are manufacturers and two are located in Gateway Cities.

The EDIP certified projects approved during today’s meeting include:

Rodney Hunt Inc. – Orange

Rodney Hunt Inc. plans to expand its water flow control equipment manufacturing by rehabilitating a 60,000-square-foot vacant facility and upgrading equipment to increase production capacity and meet growing demand. The company will also hire 20 new permanent fulltime employees. The EACC approved $200,000 in EDIP tax credits.

Reed Farm LLC – Sunderland

Reed Farm is a woman-led, vertically integrated poultry farm and processor that raises, processes, and distributes pasture-raised poultry while providing essential processing services to other Massachusetts producers. The farm is investing approximately $3.1 million to expand its poultry processing operations and create 10 new jobs. The EACC approved $100,000 in EDIP tax credits.

Foundation Alloy Technology Explorations Inc. - Woburn

Foundation Alloy is a manufacturing company that develops metal alloys and high-performance metal components for the automotive, tooling, and consumer goods sectors. Foundation Alloy plans to invest approximately $1.6 million in a new headquarters and manufacturing facility, creating 18 new full-time jobs by the end of 2027. The EACC approved $255,000 in EDIP tax credits.

WGI Inc. – Southwick

WGI, an 85-year-old family-owned aerospace company, will invest approximately $19 million in a new Southwick manufacturing and FAA-approved repair facility. The project will add specialized equipment, including a clean line, to expand production capacity and product offerings, and create 30 new jobs. The EACC approved $450,000 in EDIP tax credits.

Plumbers' Supply Company – New Bedford

Plumbers’ Supply is a plumbing, heating & HVAC distribution business that is expanding its New Bedford distribution center by approximately 155,000 square feet to support continued growth, creating at least 25 new jobs while retaining approximately 262 existing positions in Massachusetts. The EACC approved $312,500 in EDIP tax credits.

Prysmian Cables and Systems Usa LLC - Taunton

Prysmian is a leading player in the energy transition and digital transformation sectors. The company is considering a $16.7 million manufacturing expansion in Taunton to increase specialty cable production, creating 20 new jobs. The EACC approved $250,000 in EDIP tax credits.

CPS Technologies Corp - Attleborough

CPS Technologies designs and manufactures advanced metal matrix composites and hermetic packaging solutions for aerospace, defense, power electronics, and industrial markets. CPS Technologies plans to invest $15 million to relocate and expand its manufacturing operations from Norton to an 80,000-square-foot facility in Attleboro, creating at least 30 new jobs while retaining 112 employees. The EACC approved $325,000 in EDIP tax credits.

Kopin Corporation - Westborough

Kopin Corporation creates application-specific optical systems which include proprietary high-performance microdisplays and optics for cross-industry customers. Kopin plans to invest more than $80 million to onshore critical microdisplay manufacturing, expanding infrastructure and equipment and creating up to 80 new jobs over five years. The EACC approved $1,460,000 in EDIP tax credits.

GreenSight Inc. – Location to be determined

Boston-based GreenSight develops commercial and defense robotics, mostly unmanned arial vehicles or drones. GreenSight plans to establish a 150,000-square-foot advanced defense drone manufacturing facility in a location to be determined to produce drones and critical components, expanding its existing Massachusetts R&D operations and hiring 321 additional employees. The EACC approved $6,420,000 in EDIP tax credits.

Phoenix Tailings Inc. – Burlington

Phoenix Tailings, Inc. is a privately held, Massachusetts-founded U.S. advanced-materials manufacturer. Phoenix Tailings plans to invest approximately $16.7 million in its Burlington facility to expand rare-earth metal manufacturing capabilities for defense, aerospace, automotive, semiconductor, and clean-energy applications. The company will create 120 new jobs. The EACC approved $1,800,000 in EDIP tax credits.

About the Massachusetts Office of Business Development

The Massachusetts Office of Business Development (MOBD) within the Executive Office of Economic Development (EOED) assists businesses expanding in and relocating to Massachusetts, with specific attention paid to projects that create and retain jobs and invest capital. MOBD administers the Economic Development Incentive Program. The MOBD team provides a highly responsive, central point of contact that facilitates access to resources, expertise, and incentive programs for businesses. The MOBD team is part of EOED’s effort to connect businesses with resources through the Business Front Door at www.mass.gov/bfd.

text:
Buying your first electric vehicle can be intimidating and a little overwhelming. Besides the purchase itself, you need to think about recharging and possibly getting an electrician to come out to your home and install a charger.

Given that, it’s easy to see why a number of consumers forget to inquire about programs from their utility provider. GM is now streamlining things by announcing a new partnership with Pacific Gas and Electric [PG&E].

More: GM Wants Your Parked EV To Sell Power Back To The Grid, But There’s A $20,000 Catch

Dubbed the Smart Charge Bundle, the first-of-its-kind program “makes home charging part of the EV buying conversation from the start.” When at participating Cadillac, Chevrolet, or GMC dealerships, eligible customers can discuss their charging needs, explore charger options from GM Energy, and sign up for a program from PG&E.

While there’s a lot to take in, customers can get an Energy PowerShift or PowerUp 2 home charger at no cost. That’s a savings of up to $1,999, although installation, permitting, and any necessary electrical upgrades are the responsibility of the customer.

The PowerUp 2 charger typically costs $899 and is rated at 11.5 kW. However, the star of the show is the 19.2 kW PowerShift charger, which offers a bidirectional charging capability when paired with a V2H Enablement Kit. This allows your EV to act as a massive battery bank to power your home during outages.

While the free charger is certainly a bonus, the incentives don’t end there. Quite the opposite, as dealers can sign people up for PG&E’s EV Charge Manager program. According to the utility, it “schedules electric vehicle charging when electricity prices and demand are at their lowest.” You simply plug in your vehicle when you get home, and it will automatically begin charging at the proper time. It’s also worth noting you can override a “managed-charging session” whenever needed.

That’s oversimplifying things a bit, but customers could receive a $15 monthly bill credit. On top of that, owners could save up to $50 per month by charging when the electricity rate is low.

The incentive is available to eligible PG&E residential customers in Northern and Central California through February 2027, or until capacity in the program is reached. There are a few caveats – such as having to use GM Energy’s preferred installer network – but the Smart Charge Bundle sounds like a win-win.

GM Energy Vice President Wade Sheffer remarked, “GM Energy’s reason for being is to make EV ownership a leap forward in value and ease, from choosing the right vehicle to charging it at home. Our work with PG&E is the result of listening to owners, reducing steps, and doing the hard work in the background to make the customer experience really simple, with clear benefits.”

text:
WISCONSIN – Sierra Club has released its annual Dirty Truth Report. This year, We Energies’ score has plummeted to 4 out of 100 possible points– its worst score ever and 20 points lower than its first score when the Dirty Truth came out only six years ago. We Energies is spotlighted in a case study within the report. We Energies has earned its abysmal grade from delaying the retirement of the Oak Creek coal plant for the third time and planning to build 1.2 gigawatts of new gas power plant capacity by 2035– increasing its existing gas capacity by nearly 50 percent.

The surge in new gas largely comes from We Energies trying to incentivize Big Tech to come to Wisconsin to build massive AI data centers, opening the door to more profit at the expense of their ratepayers. This year, We Energies is proposing a 14% increase in utility bills without sufficient clarity on the actions the utility has taken to protect existing customers from costs attributable to data center load.

Over 1,800 public comments were submitted to the PSC, 91 percent of which opposed the rate increase. Of those in opposition, nearly 75 percent cited affordability as a primary concern, and nearly 42 percent called for a decrease to We Energies’ profits and CEO and Board of Directors payments. Other comments cited concerns about data centers, lack of clean energy investment, health concerns, and power shutoffs.

“This report and overwhelming public opposition to We Energies’ latest rate increase crystallize what Wisconsinites have known for years: We Energies’ bottom line has been maximizing executive and shareholder profit at the expense of the people they’re supposed to serve,” said Cassie Steiner, Senior Campaign Coordinator. “Rate increase after rate increase, the PSC has sat idly by and done little to nothing to protect Wisconsinites from skyrocketing utility bills. People are being priced out of their homes and neighborhoods, and are suffering health harms from fossil fuels, because of We Energies. We’re not going to sit back and let this happen again.”

“The Dirty Truth report has once again revealed utilities’ overwhelming failure to plan a phase-out of their expensive and dirty fossil fuel infrastructure, and transition to clean energy,” said Sierra Club Chief Program Officer Holly Bender. “Every year that utilities drag their feet on the clean energy transition is another year where families pay record bills for expensive fossil fuels, another year of extreme weather events, and another year of air and water pollution threatening our health. We cannot afford to wait any longer to bring our grid into the 21st century. As artificial intelligence data centers drive demand for energy, utility companies are rushing to expensive and dangerous fossil fuels, leading to soaring electricity prices and worsening air pollution. The time is now for these companies to transition to affordable, reliable, clean energy to build a healthier and more sustainable energy future. The Sierra Club will continue to push utilities to deploy more renewable energy and work to lower costs and emissions.”

Background on the Dirty Truth

The Dirty Truth Report grades utilities across the country based on how much coal they are retiring, how much gas they are planning, and how much renewable energy they are adding. Nationally, the 76 utilities scored 7 out of 100 in aggregate. This is eight points lower than last year’s report and the lowest score in the report’s history.

Renewable energy remains the cheapest way to generate electricity, while coal and fossil fuels remain expensive and extremely harmful to public health. Despite this, the Dirty Truth Report shows that We Energies is doubling down on dangerous, expensive fossil fuels. This means higher bills for families, more dangerous pollution, and less reliable energy.

The full report is available on the Dirty Truth website or here.

title: Chinese EVs Expand in Global South as Recalls Raise Risks
description:
In South America, more Chinese vehicle investment is heading to Brazil as Chinese EVs increasingly gain ground in the region’s ride-hailing market.
This week in the Chinese EV scene: Rwanda Edges Closer to Establishing a Chery EV Assembly Plant The Rwanda Cabinet approved a strategic investment agreement under which Chinese automaker Chery will establish a local EV assembly plant.
Ghana Inaugurates Phase Three of Chinese Vehicle Assembly Plant Ghana’s Chinese-owned Zonda Tec has expanded its vehicle assembly capabilities by commissioning its third assembly plant.
In addition to bringing more Chinese vehicles into the African market, investments like Zonda’s will catalyze growth across Ghana and its intermediary markets.
Why This Matters: Chinese EV battery tech is increasingly expanding beyond the country, closely following vehicle trends and shifting potential markets.
text:
This is a free preview of the upcoming Africa EVs Weekly Digest, part of the new CGSP Intelligence service.

Nobody wants to hear that their car has been recalled.

In the global energy transition, recall-driven safety concerns about EVs have proven a significant hurdle to EV adoption. In Global South countries, manufacturing defects raise further concerns about limited vehicle maintenance ecosystems.

While a recall is manageable for buyers who buy from dealerships, second-hand owners may not be as lucky—especially if the vehicles are not under warranty.

This is important because in many African countries, second-hand vehicles are a common choice due to their affordability. This week, BYD announced that it is recalling 183,211 Qin and Tang series vehicles produced between 2014 and 2022 due to a defect in a batch of brake pedal stopper pads, while another Chinese EV maker, Nio, is recalling some 686 of its Firefly-brand electric vehicles (EVs) over a steering system component manufacturing defect.

This recall news should create an urgency for localized EV solution centers to promptly address any issues that arise. Otherwise, African countries could become a dumping ground for technology that could quickly become obsolete.

Recalls aside, Chinese automakers continue to set up assembly lines in different African countries across various transport modes, from two-wheelers to heavy moving machinery. Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana, and South Africa remain the main hubs for these activities.

Still, exploration of more vehicle assembly and battery projects continues across the continent, with companies like BYD and Chery seeking to increase their vehicle-building capacity outside China.

Overseas, at the just-concluded 23rd China-ASEAN Expo (CAEXPO) in Nanning City, Guangxi, Chinese companies have been signing agreements with vehicle and component manufacturing stakeholders not only from Africa but also from Malaysia to Vietnam and Laos as they seek to grow their footprint beyond China, which has hit vehicle saturation amid declining car sales at home.

In South America, more Chinese vehicle investment is heading to Brazil as Chinese EVs increasingly gain ground in the region’s ride-hailing market.

Still, after-sales services and manufacturing development are likely to play key roles in the competitiveness of Chinese firms in the Global South during a key period when they face steep competition with one another.

This week in the Chinese EV scene:

Rwanda Edges Closer to Establishing a Chery EV Assembly Plant

The Rwanda Cabinet approved a strategic investment agreement under which Chinese automaker Chery will establish a local EV assembly plant. The approval on Friday, September 18, 2026, marks a formal step toward implementing the project.

Why This Matters: As a landlocked country, Rwanda’s move could become a template for how African countries without ocean access (key to easy imports) build sustainable EV businesses. Additionally, it could lead countries in the region to finally coalesce around a sustainable EV ecosystem, where interdependence creates more value.

BYD Mulling EV Assembly, Battery Projects in DR Congo

Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD could build a vehicle assembly and battery projects in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) if the exploratory stages proof the investment feasible. The company is looking at opportunities in the country’s growing electric mobility and energy sectors with discussions between BYD and the National Investment Promotion Agency (ANAPI) examining possible projects covering electric buses, local EV assembly, battery manufacturing and energy storage.

Why This Matters: If this goes through, BYD’s move could become one of the most strategic moves since the DRC supplies 70% of the world’s cobalt, a critical mineral for battery manufacturing. It could also become a catalyst for the DRC to refine its resources.

Ghana Inaugurates Phase Three of Chinese Vehicle Assembly Plant

Ghana’s Chinese-owned Zonda Tec has expanded its vehicle assembly capabilities by commissioning its third assembly plant. The new facility will support the local assembly of vehicles from Chinese automotive brands, including Great Wall Motor (GWM) and Chery.

Why This Matters: With the Chinese vehicle market reaching saturation, markets outside China are becoming more attractive as companies look for new ways to expand. In addition to bringing more Chinese vehicles into the African market, investments like Zonda’s will catalyze growth across Ghana and its intermediary markets.

Chinese Expo Showcases Electric Tuktuks Targeting African Markets

Chinese manufacturers showcased electric three-wheeler tuktuks aimed at international markets, especially in Africa and Southeast Asia, during the 23rd CAEXPO, and among the exhibitors was Guangxi Yuchai Special Purpose Vehicle Co., which displayed an electric three-wheeler with a 260 km range on a full charge. Other companies like Henan Fengshou New Energy Vehicle Group had four electric three-wheeler models on display.

Why This Matters: Two- and three-wheelers are the fastest-electrifying segment in East Africa and in Southeast Asia. Range has been the main challenge, but longer-range vehicles could accelerate the transition as more drivers feel less anxious about how far their batteries can go.

SAIC-GM-Wuling partners with Tan Chong to Manufacture EV Batteries in Malaysia

Malaysia’s Tan Chong Motor has signed an agreement with Chinese EV maker SAIC-GM-Wuling to explore the feasibility of EV battery packs and components manufacturing in Malaysia. The scope also includes recycling, reuse, and disposal of dead EV batteries.

Why This Matters: Chinese EV battery tech is increasingly expanding beyond the country, closely following vehicle trends and shifting potential markets. This expansion opens the door for other countries to benefit from skills and technology transfer, which could help build local ecosystems.

Dongfeng Signs Agreement with Vietnamese Partner

Chinese vehicle manufacturer Dongfeng Motor Group’s subsidiary Dongfeng Liuzhou Motor showcased its new EV and hybrid lineup and signed a cooperation agreement with a Vietnamese partner to jointly build a commercial vehicle knock-down kit factory.

The vehicles on display during the just-concluded 23rd China-ASEAN Expo included the Forthing Star Sea V9 hybrid camper, the Star Sea V6, the Chenglong H7 hydrogen fuel tractor, the Chenglong Yiwei 5 pure electric tractor, and the Chenglong Yiwei 2 intelligent pure electric light truck.

Why This Matters: Growing investment in manufacturing by Chinese automakers’ subsidiaries highlights the multi-pronged approaches they are taking- including selling fully built units of both electric and combustion engine vehicles as well as local assembly at different KD levels- to enter new markets and segments, expanding their reach and offerings.

SHACMAN X5000e Electric Heavy Truck Debuts in Laos

China’s heavy-duty truck manufacturer SHACMAN has introduced its X5000e in Laos. The X5000e supports dual-gun fast charging and battery-swapping capabilities and can handle complex road conditions. To simplify ownership, the company has also integrated a “purchase + finance + insurance + maintenance” solution that enables low down payment installments, battery risk assessment, an extended warranty, and rapid replacement in case of accidents.

Why This Matters: SHACMAN also plans to work with local partners to build a dedicated parts-center warehouse, train service engineers, provide 24-hour rescue, and coordinate charging piles. This approach offers assurance for buyers, which could help accelerate adoption in Laos’ logistics sector.

Chinese EVs Gain Ground in South America’s Ride-Hailing Market

Brazil’s Chinese-owned mobility platform 99, which offers ride-hailing vehicles and is operated by Chinese DiDi Chuxing, has partnered with car rental company Movida to give drivers access to lower-cost rental electric vehicles. The deal expands DiDi’s role in Brazil’s shift toward electric mobility, where 99 has more than 60 million active users and over 1 million drivers. While DiDi operates mixed fleets, it has been promoting the deployment of China-made EVs in Brazil.

Why This Matters: When Chinese businesses do business with one another in other countries, it can accelerate EV adoption, but it could also cause disquiet if localization isn’t supported. Also, if the operations become monopolistic, they may lead to fierce competition and even end up in court, as is currently happening with DiDi and Brazil’s dominant food-delivery platform, iFood, which is owned by a Dutch investment group.

In Context:

As the spread of Chinese EV technology across the Global South accelerates, the recalls by BYD and Nio show that market expansion also requires the infrastructure and expertise to keep those vehicles running throughout their life cycle. This is particularly important in African markets where second-hand vehicles are common, because without localized parts, diagnostics, trained technicians, and reliable after-sales support, technological expansion could leave buyers with vehicles that are difficult or costly to maintain once warranties expire. SHACMAN’s approach in Laos could help stakeholders elsewhere to offer comprehensive packages that “incentivize” adoption.

The Takeaway:

The emerging assembly and service projects matter not only for expanding Chinese EV access, but for determining whether Chinese technology becomes a foundation for durable local automotive ecosystems or simply another stream of vehicles flowing into markets without enough capacity to support them.

title: White House diesel tensions spill over at Climate Week - POLITICO
description:
The U.K.'s climate minister says nice things about data centers.
Asked by Surge if other White House advisers shared his view, he added that Trump “wants to see reduced pressure on diesel prices.
We’re open to any idea that’ll lower diesel prices.’” Wright’s comments show what a big difference a year makes.
High diesel prices touch a nerve politically because they push up transportation and food costs.
Trump, for example, has been hearing pleas from farm state senators to keep U.S. diesel at home.
text:
With help from Sara Schonhardt and Zack Colman in the U.S., Johanna Sahlberg in Germany, Zia Weise in Belgium, Nicolas Camut in France, Charlie Cooper in the United Kingdom, Mike Blanchfield in Canada, and Brian Dabbs in Singapore.

Surge Preview

Energy Secretary Chris Wright campaigns against his boss’s potential diesel export ban at Climate Week.

The U.K.'s climate minister says nice things about data centers.

See the sentence that PM Mark Carney removed from his speech at Climate Week.

WHO’S WRIGHT ON DIESEL?: A crack in the White House’s energy policies revealed itself at Climate Week.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright used a series of appearances at the New York event Wednesday to forcefully argue against a ban on diesel exports — a position that’s potentially at odds with his boss.

Wright’s comments came as diesel prices have soared to around $6.50 a gallon, leading to a real time debate within the White House about how to confront voter angst over spiraling cost of living expenses. President Donald Trump pledged Tuesday to make a decision “fast, one way or the other” over curtailing diesel exports to other countries.

The White House is preparing a plan to halt diesel shipments abroad for 90 days, POLITICO reported moments ago.

“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” Wright said in an event hosted by the Economist.

The public display of tension showed the mounting political pressure within the administration to alleviate high energy prices ahead of midterm elections that could remove Republicans from power in Congress.

Asked by Surge if other White House advisers shared his view, he added that Trump “wants to see reduced pressure on diesel prices. So we’re constantly talking about ways to do it. Politicians, senators, House members are constantly calling for a diesel export ban as they have for a long time. The president’s saying, ‘I hear you. We’re open to any idea that’ll lower diesel prices.’”

Wright’s comments show what a big difference a year makes. When the Energy secretary appeared at Climate Week last year, he used the occasion to question climate science and criticize countries for greening their economies.

This year, those culture war comments were drowned out by questions on energy prices.

The moderators of panels hosted by the Economist and the Wall Street Journal pressed Wright for information on the export ban, oil shipments flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and crude inventories in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Wright blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and California refinery closures for making the fuel more expensive. He said environmental regulations had made it impossible for the U.S. to build more refineries, but expressed hope a new one could be built in Texas.

Wright made the case for Washington working with oil companies and refineries to rebuild American diesel inventories, but stressed the effort should be voluntary.

“You’ll hear more from us in the coming days on this,” he added.

High diesel prices touch a nerve politically because they push up transportation and food costs. Trump, for example, has been hearing pleas from farm state senators to keep U.S. diesel at home.

But analysts say the higher costs owe to market factors and military conflicts.

“The diesel shortage has many fathers,” Kevin Book, the managing director of ClearView Energy Partners, told Surge. “Stocks were tightening on Ukrainian strikes before the Middle East disruption, and even if the California closings most directly affected the Golden State, lost capacity is lost capacity. But it is also a matter of throughput: Hormuz impairments and damage from Iranian reprisals which shuttered previously operable facilities tightened supply balances.”

Wright acknowledged that high prices are a hard problem to solve. When the Wall Street Journal asked him how long Americans would give the administration to fix the price crunch, Wright conceded, “I don’t know. That’s up to Americans.”

He argued the nuclear threats posed by Iran are “existential” and justify the temporary spike in prices.

“We’re making a trade-off that politically again is not a winner. I think it’s the right thing to do for America and Americans in the long run,” Wright told the Journal. “This conflict will pass, and you will see energy prices go down.”

WELCOME TO SURGE: I’m Ben Storrow, your lead author. Reach out with tips and ideas at bstorrow@politico.com.

Power Players

TALKING SHOP: Surge spoke to Katie White, the U.K.’s climate minister, about the COP31 goal of electrifying 35% of global energy consumption by 2035.

Is that an achievable goal?

In the U.K., we’ve very much been driven by our national interest in terms of electrification. We’ve got quite a long way to go in terms of meeting that 35 by 35 target, so it will be an ambitious target, but I think the focus on moving towards a more practical area and also threading together energy and climate is really helpful right now.

Electricity demand is surging. How will you address that?

We built quite a lot of kit in the U.K., so what we want to do is use it, and we want to use it really effectively. Now, first of all, we need to get it docked into the grid. We’re also investing in a grid upgrade, and we’re then looking at how to use the grid most effectively.

But actually, electric vehicles — the vehicle-to-grid shift, so that we can use the electric batteries to help the grid — are going to be helpful. Data centers could play a helpful role. I mean, if we get them connected to the grid and we use those data centers and that AI to manage the grid most effectively, that can be helpful.

Are you thinking about requiring data centers to use renewable energy?

My job is to support the transition towards a clean energy system. We can do that with data centers in the best way. They could be an asset. It could also be adding to our needs in a way that might not be effective. There is a lot of discussion going on in the U.K. at the moment, both within government and outside government. We are listening and we’re trying to figure out what’s the best way to do that to meet the AI growth opportunity within our carbon budgets, as well as say there’s this whole electrification opportunity which could do both.

How do you explain the benefits of electrification to consumers?

So when our new prime minister came in, one of the first things he did was take VAT off electricity. That is to meet people where they’re at now to try and give them some breathing space and reduce the pressure of the bills, but also to look at that longer-term trend that we know electrification is going to be good for communities. It’s also going to be good for businesses. So we are looking at how we do that.

But I think people know. I don’t think they need me to tell them that anybody there in the U.K. who has an EV, has had a lot cheaper driving experience than those who have had petrol and diesel cars over the summer. They’ve seen prices go through the roof. So, I think actually, quite often that talks. —Sara Schonhardt

QUOTABLE: Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, was asked at Climate Week how Congress should regulate data centers. Here’s what he said:

“I think it’s important that we do upgrade our grid. But I think those hyperscalers and the companies that are involved in getting the net benefit right now of AI are going to have to pay a big portion in terms of paying for that, because the general public right now does not see a benefit to AI, yet. And if we tell them that we’re going to go and tax them more to actually upgrade our grid in order for us to actually make sure we have a strong AI economy, we’re going to get pushback.” — Sara Schonhardt

REDACTED: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney — the former United Nations special envoy on climate action and finance — wasn’t in the mood Wednesday to dwell on the threat of climate change during an appearance at the U.N.

Check against delivery: In the prepared text of a speech Carney gave at an event on improving the monitoring of the world’s oceans, Carney skipped over this line and left it on the cutting room floor: “We are living through the consequences of a world that, collectively, hasn’t taken climate change seriously enough.”

Context: Since becoming PM a year and a half ago, Carney has faced criticism for rolling back climate change policies of his predecessor, former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. So much so that Trudeau’s former environment minister, Steven Guilbeault, quit Carney’s Cabinet earlier this year. He also skipped last year’s U.N. COP climate conference in Brazil after attending in previous years before becoming prime minister.

Today: Carney pledged a five-year CA$82 million Canadian commitment to the European Union’s OceanEye observation program.

“The ocean is warming. The Arctic Ocean is warming at four times the global average. We know the ice there is thinning. We can see the water’s opening, but we recognize our picture is incomplete,” Carney said as he announced the new funding. “We can’t protect what we can’t see. We can’t manage what we don’t understand.” — Mike Blanchfield

Driving the (global!) day

BUZZ THRILL: Electricity could meet 33% of global energy consumption by 2035, falling just shy of a 35% goal proposed by the hosts of this year’s U.N. climate talks, according to the International Energy Agency.

That’s based on current technologies and if energy prices return to where they were before the Iran war. Electricity currently accounts for 23% of total energy consumption, the IEA said.

Climate context: Faster electrification could cut climate-warming pollution 40% by 2035, in line with international climate targets, the report says. It could also slash costs of fossil fuel imports by $400 billion, removing 18 million barrels of oil per day from global markets.

But really?: Getting there won’t be easy. It would require greater investments in grids and clean energy generation, and more diversified supply chains, the IEA said. — Sara Schonhardt

TSCHÜSS TO FOSSIL FUELS: German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider presented a national road map for phasing out fossil fuels by 2045 on Wednesday at the U.N. General Assembly.. The 22-page plan was obtained by POLITICO ahead of its official release.

“Overall, the federal government will work to decarbonize the country’s power plant fleet in line with its climate targets by 2045 at the latest,” the document says. The phase-out includes all energy, not just electricity generation.

A big but: The road map does not contain new policy measures. However, it bundles the government’s existing efforts in the first comprehensive German document to lay out the country’s path away from fossil fuels.

The road map reaffirms Germany’s commitment to domestic and international climate targets. The EU’s 2050 net-zero target in particular came under scrutiny after Schneider questioned it at CERAWeek in Houston in March.

More context: Germany is the third country to present a road map for phasing out fossil fuels, following France and the Netherlands. Berlin hopes to inspire other countries in the process.

“Our roadmap is meant to send an international signal. I am sure that many more countries will follow,” Schneider said in a press release. — Johanna Sahlberg

FREEDOM GAS? A push by U.S. energy companies to deepen their influence in the Western Balkans is fueling EU concerns that the region could end up hooked on American fossil fuels — just as it attempts to reach clean energy targets.

The stakes: Albania, Kosovo, and Bosnia and Herzegovina have all signaled interest in buying up large volumes of liquefied natural gas from the U.S. or building infrastructure to support inflows. The countries say gas is needed as a transitional fuel as they reduce both Russian imports and coal consumption and switch to renewables. Both are key prongs of their EU membership bids.

Road bloc: EU officials say the plan could complicate the Balkan nations’ push to join the bloc. They question whether the projects being touted are feasible given that these countries currently have little to no domestic gas demand — meaning that flooding these markets with the fuel risks locking them into long-term gas addictions rather than helping them diversify.

“The countries ... in their wider aspiration to join the EU, have taken commitments to decarbonize, to set out the path and keep to this, to phase out basically fossil fuels,” András Hujber, who fronts the EU executive’s energy diplomacy in the Western Balkans, told a forum in Vienna in response to question from POLITICO. — Ben Munster

Our open tabs

PULLED PERK: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Wednesday called for repealing his state’s data center tax incentives, joining a wave of state officials moving to crack down on the industry ahead of the November midterm elections, reports Adam Aton.

CHINA’S ENERGY LEVERAGE: The Iran war has strengthened China’s leverage in global energy markets, giving the country little incentive to yield to Trump’s demands during Chinese President Xi Jinping‘s visit this week, write Scott Waldman and Ben Lefebvre. While the war has spiked global prices for energy and created a political albatross around the neck of the U.S. Republican Party, it has enabled China to export its clean energy technologies and present itself as a more stable geopolitical partner.

That’s all for today. Thanks for reading!
